rows.note: **Phase 6.** Beyond the photographs in row 24, there are four things no record will settle: whether the Brisbane **Donato of Pinnaroo** carrying the name Candeloro are kin; whether **Mario and Maria Mazza** of Mount Gravatt are; what the family calls the **Buenos Aires Prostamo**; and which of the **58 shared names** are one person. A short list of specific questions, with the evidence beside each, is worth more than another month of registers. **A fifth question now:** who was **Venero Crupi**, born 1935 and buried at Nudgee in December 2023 — the only Crupi in either Brisbane register, and Angela Crupi had three brothers here nobody in this archive knew about until today.

rows.what: Francesco Cichello and Vittoria Mollo — who were they?
rows.note: **Blocked behind the gap, and now demonstrably so.** Both were dead before March 1824 and neither appears in the death Tavole of 1822, 1823 or 1824 — so they died in the nine years the register does not hold. **They come back into reach only through row 59.** Note also that neither surname is rare at Zambrone: a Maria Mollo died in 1822, a Marianna Mollo and an Anna Cichello in 1823. No join on one of these names alone.

rows.what: The second copy of Zambrone's 1813–1821 deaths — and it is probably at the comune, not on film
rows.note: **Reframed, and the reframing changes who can do it.** Under the Napoleonic and Bourbon codes every act was written **twice**: one register kept by the **comune**, one sent to the **tribunale**, and the tribunale's copies are what ended up in the Archivio di Stato. **Antenati digitises the Archivio di Stato.** This volume's own manifest says so — «Archivio di Stato di Catanzaro › Stato civile napoleonico › Zambrone › 1811-1839». So the nine missing years are missing **from the court's copy**, and the copy that may still survive is **the Comune di Zambrone's own**, in its Ufficio di Stato Civile. **That is corroborated by the fact that the act existed in 1849**, when the chancery certified a copy of Domenico Ventrice's death for a marriage at Briatico. Something was still being copied from, thirty-four years after he died. **So this is a letter, not a search** — an enquiry to the Comune di Zambrone, and it is the only route to four people: Domenico Ventrice, Anna Maropoli, Francesco Cichello and Vittoria Mollo. *Noted while checking: FamilySearch's catalogue was erroring out («Something Went Wrong») on 15 September, so the film holdings for Zambrone have NOT been ruled out and should be re-checked when it is back.*

rows.what: Sweep the Zambrone death Tavole for the family surnames — 1822–24 done, and negative
rows.note: **Done for the years that matter, and negative.** The Tavole of 1822 (image 51), 1823 (65) and 1824 (78) name everyone who died at Zambrone in those years **with their parents**, and **neither Francesco Cichello nor Vittoria Mollo is among them** — nor Anna Maropoli. All three were already dead by March 1824, so **all three almost certainly died inside the missing 1813–1821**, behind the same gap as Domenico Ventrice. Four wanted people, one gap. **What it did settle:** Maropoli appears twice more in these three years, including an infant Giuseppe Maropoli dead 23 March 1824. The surname is unmistakably local. 1825–1839 remain unread but no longer urgent.

rows.what: Re-check FamilySearch's catalogue for Zambrone when it is working
rows.note: Small and specific. The catalogue UI returned «Something Went Wrong» for every query on 15 September, and its JSON endpoint accepts `q.place` but ignores it, returning two million hits. So **the film holdings for Zambrone have not actually been ruled out** — only failed to be checked. Retry, and look specifically for a Zambrone or Monteleone *stato civile* film covering 1813–1821, before concluding that row 59's letter is the only route.

rows.what: Electoral rolls are now the right instrument, not BDM
rows.note: **Promoted out of row 49 because today's sweep proved the case.** Queensland BDM cannot see this family: they arrived in 1949, married after the marriage index closes in 1951, and mostly died after the death index closes in 1996. Polistena returns **zero**; Prostamo returns **one**. **Electoral rolls have none of those limits.** They are near-annual, they run through the whole post-war period, they give **address and occupation**, and they capture people who neither died nor married inside an index window — which is precisely this family's problem. For a migration that lands in 1949, the rolls are the primary source and the registrar's index is the secondary one. Start with Brisbane 1949–1980 for Prostamo, Polistena, Mazza and Arena. **TRIED AND BLOCKED ON A SOURCE.** FamilySearch has no Australian electoral rolls for these surnames — its Australian holdings here are Victorian Petty Sessions and Find a Grave. The rolls are on **Ancestry**, which is paid, and at the **National Library of Australia**. So this needs either a subscription decision from David or an NLA route, and it is blocked until one of those exists rather than being quietly open. **UNBLOCKED 16 SEPTEMBER: David has taken a full month's Findmypast subscription, and Findmypast carries Australian electoral rolls.** See row 99. **CLOSED 16 SEPTEMBER, and the conclusion needs qualifying.** The rolls were the right instrument and they did deliver — Sebastiano Mazza at Wacol, Rosario Mazza at Leichhardt Street, both with trades. **What was wrong was the assumption that Findmypast holds them near-annually.** For Queensland it holds 1903, 1906, 1913, 1922, 1934, 1941, 1949 and 1959 and nothing after. The near-annual run is real but it is at the **NLA and on Ancestry**. See row 104.

rows.what: Ask the estate whether the kit's chart can take a second source
rows.note: **Raised by row 51, and it is not a Mazza-only problem.** `Bloodline.astro` and `lib/bloodline.js` draw one array of people — the archive's export. Any archive that also keeps **documented people the export lacks** can therefore prove an ancestor and not draw them. Here that is **fifty-four people and thirteen direct ancestors**, including three generations above Giovanni Arena. **The ask is small and probably general:** let `graph()` accept a second, clearly-styled set of nodes — drawn differently, the way a `tree` edge is already drawn dashed — so an archive can show the difference between what the family remembers and what the records prove. Worth asking before anyone builds a private fork of the chart, which is exactly how this estate got two Pedigrees 7.6KB apart. **WITHDRAWN, 20 SEPTEMBER. The ask was already answered before it was written.** `lineage()` has always taken `parentsOf()` from the caller and its own comment invites exactly this. The Mazza archive now draws its documented ancestors on `/tree/` without a line of kit change ([row 51](/worklist/)). **What may still be worth raising is narrower:** `Bloodline.astro` and `lib/bloodline.js` take one array and have no such hook, so `/bloodline/` still cannot show them. That is a real question for the estate; *«can the chart take a second source»* was not, and this row asked the wrong one.

rows.what: The processetti: the 1885/1888 bundles do not exist, and the 1851 one does
rows.note: **Phase 7. The method that has produced this archive's two biggest finds, pointed at a generation it has never touched.** Processetti carry the **birth acts of both spouses** and the **death acts of any dead parent**. Briatico 1849 broke the Calabrian line open; Scilla 1844 fascicolo 20 gave Domenico Donato's birth and Caterina Cichello's parents. **Four family marriages sit in one narrow window and none of their bundles has been opened:** Giuseppe Arena × Maria Martello (Matrimoni 1885 atto 73), Giovanni Arena × Concetta Russo (1885 atto 86), Rocco Arena × Generosa Costa (1888 atto 63), and Michele Donato × Maria Sofi. Their papers would give birth extracts for **eight people** and death acts for whichever parents had already died — including, possibly, **Filippo Arena and Domenica Costa**, whose marriage the registers cannot reach but whose deaths they can. **CHECKED 20 SEPTEMBER, AND THE ROW IS HALF WRONG AND HALF BETTER.** Listing Scilla's whole holding — **466 registers** — shows **twenty-two volumes of marriage processetti running 1810 to 1865 and then stopping**. The Italian-era fondo, all 267 registers of it, **holds no processetti at all**. So the bundles behind Giuseppe Arena × Maria Martello (1885), Giovanni Arena × Concetta Russo (1885) and Rocco Arena × Generosa Costa (1888) **are not on Antenati** and this half of the row is closed, not pending. **But the marriage that matters most is inside the window.** **Francesco Antonio Arena × Serafina Arlotta, 7 February 1851, atto 13** — the bundle is the volume **1849–1852, `an_ua2002487`**, now in `scilla-arks.tsv`. That fascicolo should carry **both spouses' birth extracts** and **the death acts of whichever of their four parents had died by February 1851** — Filippo Arena, Domenica Costa, Giovanni Arlotta, Maria Costa — and the Scilla bundle of 1842–1845 carried a dead **grandparent** as well. **One volume, three rows:** [68](/worklist/) Filippo Arena and Domenica Costa's deaths, [39](/worklist/) Giovanni Arlotta × Maria Costa's marriage, [85](/worklist/) Domenico Arlotta. **This is now the cheapest unopened thing in the archive** and it is [row 147](/worklist/).

rows.what: SAN COSTANTINO CALABRO — mapped, and it may walk round the Zambrone gap
rows.note: **Mapped for the first time, and it is bigger than expected: 205 volumes, 1810 to 1912**, including Nati 1812–24, **Morti 1813–27**, Matrimoni 1813–32 and **forty-eight processetti volumes**. **The strategic point:** Zambrone's deaths are missing **1813–1821**, and four wanted people died inside that gap. **San Costantino's Morti 1813–27 covers exactly those years.** If **Anna Maropoli** — Giuseppe Ventrice's mother, already «la fu» in March 1824 — died in her husband's own town rather than at Zambrone, **her act survives**. The gap may be walkable *round* rather than through. **Not yet swept:** the 1813–27 death volume is 325 images and **is not one comune** — image 12 is San Costantino, images 24 and 40 are **Francica**. The comune line must be read on every act. Giuseppe's own birth, about 1790, stays out of reach.

rows.what: PIZZO 1823–1860 — Maria Fragalà's death, and the Prostamo who stayed
rows.note: **Phase 7, and it is reachable where the rest of the Prostamo line is not.** Pizzo's registers begin in **1823**, and **Maria Fragalà was alive at Pizzo in June 1849** when her son married at Briatico. Her death is therefore *inside* the surviving run — one of the few Prostamo events on this line that is. The same volumes would hold any other Prostamo who did not move to Briatico. The 1837 cholera register is not digitised, but 1823–1836 and 1838–1860 are a different question and have never been opened. **Series listed: 751 volumes, earliest 1823** — the wall confirmed from the series itself. Reachable: Nati and Morti from 1823, Matrimoni 1823–29, and **thirty-four processetti volumes**. **Maria Fragalà's death is the target** and it falls inside the surviving run. Antonino Prostamo's marriage of about 1810–13 does not. **THE NAME INDEX DOES NOT REACH THEM, 21 SEPTEMBER, AND THAT IS ITSELF ODD.** Pizzo is one of only three comuni this family touches that Antenati has indexed **by name** — **births, 1868–1903**. *Prostamo* at Pizzo returns **nothing at all**, control-tested against *Arena at Scilla* (69) in the same breath, so it is a real nil and not the limiter. **Either the Prostamo had left Pizzo by 1868, or the indexing does not reach them** — and the first is checkable against what this archive already holds, since Antonino Prostamo's line is at Briatico by the 1849 marriage bundle. **Recorded so the index is not tried again for this surname.**

rows.what: THE HAMLETS — Potenzoni, Sciconi, Conidoni and Daffinà as series in their own right
rows.note: **Phase 7, and it follows from a trap already recorded.** Briatico and Zambrone searches keep returning arks that turn out to be **Daffinà, Sciconi or Conidoni** — separate comuni in the same circondario with their own registers. That has been a nuisance three times. **It is also an opportunity:** the generation-eight Briatico cluster — Fortunato Anile × Antonia Grasso, Giuseppe Barbuto × Saveria Lesto — is recorded at **Potenzoni and Mandaradoni**, not Briatico proper. Map these four series properly and the densest untouched part of the spine becomes searchable.

rows.what: Filippo Arena and Domenica Costa — alive in February 1851, and the window is 1851–1888
rows.note: **Phase 7, and the consolation prize for row 38.** Their *marriage* is pre-civil and gone. **Their deaths are not.** Both were born in the 1790s, both were alive when their son married in 1851, and Scilla's death registers run from 1816 — so they died inside a surviving run, most likely in the 1850s–1870s. A death act gives an age, a trade, an address and often the parents. **It is the only remaining route to a generation above Filippo.** **UNBLOCKED 16 SEPTEMBER.** The pre-1866 Scilla death series is now listed — **51 volumes, 1817–1865** — in `scilla-arks.tsv` ([row 130](/worklist/)). This row can start. **A CHEAPER ROUTE APPEARED, 20 SEPTEMBER.** Sweeping the annual death indexes for them means 1862–1888 — twenty-seven years, and **no container is saved for any of them**, so twenty-seven rate-limited page loads before a single image. Instead: **their son's marriage processetti**, Scilla 1849–1852, `an_ua2002487`. If either was dead by 7 February 1851 the bundle holds the death act itself. If both were alive it says so, and the sweep starts in 1851 instead of 1862. Either way one volume replaces twenty-seven. [Row 147](/worklist/). **NARROWED FROM BOTH ENDS, 20 SEPTEMBER.** The 1851 processetti give them **ages**: Filippo Arena **twenty-five** in November 1819 (b. c. 1794) and Domenica Costa **twenty-seven** (b. c. 1792). The same bundle contains **no death act for either**, where a neighbouring fascicolo binds them in when a parent is dead — so both were very likely **alive on 7 February 1851**. Filippo is called *«di Filippo»*, not *«fu»*, in act 228 of December 1861, so he was alive then too; both are *«fu»* in Francesco Antonio's death act of 1901. **The window is 1862–1888**, since the A blocks of 1889–1908 hold neither. Twenty-seven years, no containers saved. **A cheaper attack first:** their sons' and daughters' marriage processetti stop in 1865, so a family marriage in 1862–65 would carry their death acts if they had died — and the volume **1862–1865, `an_ua2002507`** is already in `scilla-arks.tsv`. **CONFIRMED ALIVE, 20 SEPTEMBER, AND NOT BY AN ABSENCE.** The **1851 annual marriage Tavola** names both spouses' parents **and marks the dead with «fu»** — the 1828 Tavola writes Giovanni Arlotta's father as *«fu Dom.co»* beside his living mother, and *«fu»* appears on the same 1851 page in other entries. **Entry 1 is «Arena Francesco e Arlotta Serafina», and its parents are «Filippo, e Costa Domenica» and «Giovanni e Costa Maria» — neither with «fu».** **So the window closes from the left.** Both were alive in **February 1851**; Filippo is still *«di Filippo»*, not *«fu»*, in act 228 of December 1861; both are *«fu»* in Francesco Antonio's death act of 1901; and the A blocks of 1889–1908 hold neither. **They died between December 1861 and 1888** — twenty-seven years, unindexed. **A cheaper instrument exists, but it does NOT reach them the way I first wrote.** Every annual **marriage** Tavola in this series dates the life status of four parents in one opening — but a marriage act names the **spouses' own parents**, not their grandparents. The Arena weddings of **1885** and **1888** are Francesco Antonio's *sons*, so those Tavole date **Francesco Antonio and Serafina Arlotta** — already known alive in 1888 — and say nothing whatever about Filippo and Domenica. *Corrected the same day it was written.* **What would actually work:** find a SIBLING of Francesco Antonio — another child of Filippo Arena and Domenica Costa, born at Scilla in the 1810s–1830s — and read the Tavola of the year that sibling married. This archive has never looked for one. Domenica Costa was twenty-seven when Francesco was born in 1819, so there are very likely elder children, and the annual birth Tavole for 1813–1818 are now reachable: **Scilla's registers begin in 1809**, not 1816 ([row 17](/worklist/)). **Otherwise it is the death indexes, 1862–1888** — twenty-seven years, an A block apiece, and no containers saved for any of them. **THE PREMISE OF THIS ROW IS HALF GONE, 20 SEPTEMBER.** It was written as the *only* route to a generation above Filippo. It is no longer: **their marriage act was found** — Scilla, Matrimoni 1815 atto 29 — and it names all four of their parents ([row 151](/worklist/)). **The row still stands, for what it was always also for:** a death act gives an age, an address and a trade, and it would settle the **five-year disagreement about Domenica Costa's birth** — twenty-eight at her wedding in 1815 (b. c. 1787), twenty-seven at her son's birth in 1819 (b. c. 1792). It is no longer urgent, and it drops behind the cheaper work the 1815 act opened up.

rows.what: SCILLA DEATHS — the Arena/Arlotta search past 1896: answered
rows.note: **Phase 7, and it is finished.** The A block of Scilla's annual death index was read for **1889–1896** without them, then the Antenati name index showed neither of them as the deceased between 1910 and 1943, which narrowed forty-seven unread years to thirteen. The twelve readable years of that window have now been swept — [row 128](/worklist/) — and **both deaths are found**: **Francesco Antonio Arena, 29 August 1901** (*Morti 1901, atto 96*) and **Serafina Arlotta, 24 April 1908** (*Morti 1908, atto 55*), **both at Via Grotte number two**. **A negative had to be narrowed on the way.** A searched row claimed 1889–1902 clear of both; he died in 1901, inside that span. The row now claims 1889–1896, which is what it can stand behind. **A negative is only worth the pages actually turned.**

rows.what: SCILLA — when and where did Michele Donato die?
rows.note: **Phase 7.** He is alive and fifty-two on the New Orleans manifest of March 1908, sailing for Quincy, Florida, and the 1910 US census shows he did not stay — his wife and household remained at Via Grotte throughout. **So he came back, and he has a death somewhere.** Scilla's death registers, or a second crossing. He is the last man on the Donato line whose end is unknown. **CLOSED 16 SEPTEMBER.** **Michele Donato died at Scilla on 10 May 1936** — «Padre Domenico, Madre Nunziata Sofi, Coniuge Maria Sofi», all three matching this archive exactly. He was fifty-two on the New Orleans manifest of March 1908 and lived another twenty-eight years after coming home. **The Donato line now has no man whose end is unknown.**

rows.what: SCILLA — Nunziata Donato × Giovanni Polistena's marriage, about 1916
rows.note: **Phase 7, and it is the act that joins two quarters.** They sailed on the same ship in February 1908 — his line immediately after her father's on the Liguria manifest — and married about eight years later. **That act would name four parents and tie the Donato quarter to the Polistena quarter with a document instead of an inference.** It would also, if his mother is named, settle whether she was a **Romano** or a **Pontillo** — which is row 41 and three ancestors. **AND HE MAY HAVE FOLLOWED THE FAMILY TO QUEENSLAND.** **NAA: BP9/3, ITALIAN POLISTENA G** — *«Polistena, **Giovanni born 1883** — arrived in **Brisbane** on the **ORMONDE**, 21 February 1928»*. This archive's Giovanni Polistena was born at Scilla in 1883, act 206; the year matches exactly and Brisbane is the right port. Graded **candidate**, because the entry carries no parents and **Polistena is a comune as well as a surname**. If it is him, he crossed to New Orleans in 1908 and to Brisbane in 1928 — and the marriage this row wants sits between them.

rows.what: SCILLA — Maria Sofi's parents, and the second Sofi marriage
rows.note: **Phase 7.** Michele Donato married a **Sofi**, as his father had. Maria Sofi sits on the spine at generation five with **no parents at all**. Given that Nunziata Sofi's parents were found in the 1844 processetti, hers should be findable the same way — their marriage act, or its bundle. **Two Donato men marrying two Sofi women in successive generations is either a close family tie or a small town, and the acts would say which.** **TRIED AND FAILED BY INDEX, 16 September.** The Scilla name index holds **four women called Maria Sofi** and not one is named as the wife of a Michele Donato; the one who died on 3 August 1913 carries no relations at all. **Her parents are not reachable this way** and the row stays a volume read — which [row 121](/worklist/) predicted, since the index is deaths only and her parents would be named in a *marriage* act.

rows.what: STRUCTURE — extend the documented line DOWNWARD as well as up
rows.note: **Phase 8.** `build_documented_line.py` walks *up* from every addition anchored to the export, and found thirteen ancestors no chart can draw. **It does not yet walk down.** Maria Donato, Fortunato Arena, Francesco Giovanni Rocco Arena and Candeloro Donato (b. 1847) are documented **children** of export people, and they are just as invisible. Same tool, opposite direction, and it would show the households whole rather than only the lines. **Done.** The tool walks both ways now: **15 documented ancestors** above export people and **4 documented children** below them, all published on /lines.

rows.what: STRUCTURE — a page for the four walls, now that all four are established
rows.note: **Done.** `data/walls.tsv` and a section on /lines: four quarters, four walls, four different causes, each with the evidence that established it and the route that remains. **Filippo Arena** — four complete years of Scilla marriages read, eighty acts, to prove an absence. **Candeloro Donato** — a province probed year by year to find registration starting in 1820. **Pasquale Prostamo** — Pizzo begins 1823. **Domenico Ventrice** — a volume opened to find nine years physically missing between two images. The page says the thing that matters: **a wall established by reading is a finding; a wall assumed from silence is a shrug**, and the difference is most of what this archive is for.

rows.what: STRUCTURE — check_links for the graves and the ships
rows.note: **Phase 8.** `check_additions` and `check_corrections` each caught real published errors the hour they existed. `data/australia-graves.tsv` and `data/naa-ships.tsv` are **still unvalidated** — no slug check, no date sanity, nothing to notice a burial dated before a birth or a grave hung on a person who died elsewhere. Today's Find a Grave double-index, the same woman in Victoria and Ohio, is exactly the shape a checker would catch. **Done.** `tools/check_places.py` is in the build. It refuses a burial before a birth, a crossing that lands before the traveller was born or after they died, a grave row with no ground, and **one person buried in two different cemeteries** — the exact Find a Grave failure found today. Tested by planting both faults. **And it caught me first:** reading `who` as a slug in `naa-ships.tsv` produced twelve confident false failures, because column 1 is the slug and column 2 is the display name. Fixed in the checker, not the data.

rows.what: Retire notes/QUEUE.md into the work list — done
rows.note: **Done.** QUEUE.md now opens «**This file is history, not a to-do list**» and says why: four items were picked up from it in one day and **three were already finished**. **Everything still live is migrated** — the Piedimonte Etneo threads as rows **89–96**, the rest already covered by existing rows. It is kept rather than deleted, because deleting the record of what was once believed is precisely what this archive tells other people not to do. **The difference that matters is the gate:** `check:worklist` refuses a row with no owner, and `check:covers` refuses an outstanding search with no row against it. The queue had neither and drifted in five days.

rows.what: STRUCTURE — give the Crupi somewhere to live on the site
rows.note: **Phase 8.** Angela Crupi's three brothers — Pietro, Antonino and Mario — went in as documented additions today, and with their parents that is **six Crupi**. They have no page, no section, and no place in the four-quarters story, because they arrived through a marriage rather than a descent. **A short section, probably on /brisbane/, saying who they were and how they reached the family.** **DONE, 21 SEPTEMBER.** A section on [/brisbane/](/brisbane/), which is where they actually are, built from `additions.json` so it cannot drift from the data. It carries what the family tree does not: that *«Angela Cupo»* is **Angela Crupi**, born 20 December 1900; that she had **three brothers in Queensland** and nobody knew; that **Pietro and Antonino** came into Brisbane together on the **Otranto** on 19 August 1930 as consecutive entries in the aliens register, and Angela followed on the **Viminale** in 1937 with two daughters; and that **Antonino was interned at Loveday**, a boot repairer at Ingham, born at **Piedimonte Etneo** — the Mazza's own town. **And it closes on the thing worth carrying away:** Pietro's missing aliens card looked like a gap and is not one — *«Alien Registration Certificate NOT ISSUED»*, because he was naturalised in 1932. **An explained absence and an unexplained one look identical until somebody checks.**

rows.what: Find the Crupi brothers' graves — not in either Brisbane register
rows.note: **Searched both registers, wildcards included, and they are in neither.** Brisbane City Council returns **zero** Crupi across its nine cemeteries. The Catholic Archdiocese returns **exactly one**, and it is none of the three: **Venero Crupi, born 14 October 1935, died 4 December 2023, Nudgee plot LA-3299**. So Pietro, Antonino and Mario are buried somewhere neither register covers — and their death registrations carry no country code, so they died in the Brisbane district, which makes the absence stranger rather than less. **Venero is left as a lead and nothing more.** Venero is a Catania name and Angela Crupi was born at Catania in 1900, so he fits the family's origin exactly — and fitting an origin is not a descent. He died in **December 2023**, well within living memory. **That makes him a question for Michael rather than for an index**, and it belongs with row 57.

rows.what: AUSTRALIA — Trove's naturalisation notices, blocked by the tool and not the archive
rows.note: **Phase 9.** Trove has already produced **Brisbane Prostamo naturalisations** and Maria Assunta's gazettal of 4 July 1966 at 3 Frank Street, Graceville — both found incidentally rather than by a sweep. **Naturalisation notices give a date, a street address and a former nationality**, which for a 1949 migration is close to what an electoral roll would give and is free. Sweep all ten surnames, not just the two that turned up by accident. **ATTEMPTED 20 SEPTEMBER AND IT WILL NOT RUN HERE.** Trove's search page loads, accepts the query and echoes it back — *«l-artType: newspapers / All of these words: Prostamo»* — and then **never renders a result list**. No count, no articles, no empty state. The console throws **«TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'clear')»** twice from Trove's own vendor bundle: a storage or cache API the browser pane does not provide, and the single-page app dies on it before it paints. **This is a tooling incompatibility, not a block and not an absence** — and it is written down that way because a blank Trove page is exactly the thing somebody records as *«nothing for Prostamo in Australian newspapers»*. That would be false: Trove has already given this archive Brisbane Prostamo naturalisations and Maria Assunta's gazettal of 4 July 1966 at 3 Frank Street, Graceville. **Two ways round, and the first is the real answer:** the **Trove API v3** is free and keyed, returns JSON, and needs no JavaScript at all — a key comes from the NLA in a few minutes and would make a ten-surname sweep mechanical. Otherwise, **David's own browser**, where the page works. **Blocked on a key, which is [row 153](/worklist/).**

rows.what: Angela Polistena × Rocco Arena — documented as a fact, still undated
rows.note: **Phase 9.** They are Michael's grandparents on the Arena side and **their marriage is not documented anywhere in this archive**. Queensland's marriage index closes in **1951**, so if they married before that it is reachable there and if after, it is not — which is itself worth establishing. Nudgee's register, the Catholic parish, or Michael. **20 SEPTEMBER: IT IS DOCUMENTED, JUST NOT DATED.** **NAA: J25 1971/3900**, Brisbane, 1953–1971: *«**Arena, Rocco; wife Angelina [or Angela] [nee Polistena]**»*. J25 is the Queensland immigration and naturalisation correspondence series and its titles name a couple together **with the wife's maiden name** — which is precisely what this row said was missing. **What it changes:** the marriage is no longer an undocumented family claim. **What it does not do:** give a date. The file is **«not yet examined»**, which means nobody has ever asked for it; an access examination is **free** and takes about ninety days, and it would very likely settle the date and place. **That is a request for David to lodge**, alongside the other Brisbane items. The Queensland marriage index still closes in 1951 and still has not produced them, which now reads as evidence they married **after** 1951 — or in the church only.

rows.what: ESTATE — offer check_corrections.py and the phase structure
rows.note: **Phase 10.** `check_corrections.py` reads the confidence vocabulary **out of the page itself**, so the legend and the data cannot drift apart — it found thirteen rows using labels the page never explained. Any archive with a corrections page has that exposure. **And the work list's phase numbering** turned 57 rows from a pile into a roadmap without changing the schema; worth passing on as a convention rather than a code change.

rows.what: ESTATE — warn about the stale Vite cache that fails a build twice
rows.note: **Phase 10, and small.** Two consecutive builds here died on «Cannot find module dist/pages/people.astro.mjs». I first diagnosed it as a race between concurrent builds. **It was not — it was a stale `.astro` / `node_modules/.vite` cache**, and `rm -rf dist .astro node_modules/.vite` fixed it immediately. Every archive in the estate runs the same Astro version and will meet it.

rows.what: Write down what today taught about instruments, not just about people
rows.note: **Phase 10.** Four findings today were about **how to read**, not about the family, and each one will otherwise be rediscovered: a Tavola may alphabetise by **given name** and change key between adjacent years; some Tavole leave the **year blank** and must be dated from the acts; **Queensland BDM cannot see a 1949 migration** because its windows close in 1926, 1951 and 1996; and **Find a Grave will index one person at two cemeteries** when the names resemble each other. Three are in memory; none is on the site. **/method/ is where a reader would look.** **DONE, 21 SEPTEMBER, AND LONGER THAN FOUR.** Nine instruments are on [/method/](/method/), built from `data/instruments.tsv`: the **annual Tavola**, the **act-head montage**, the **marriage processetti**, the **marginal annotation**, the **register index at s_size=500**, the **container fetch from inside the origin**, the **Riveli di anime e di terre**, the **Queensland BDM download endpoint**, and **NAA item titles**. **Every row carries a CAUTION and the builder refuses one without it.** An instrument described without the way it fails is how a method becomes a superstition — the best tool in this archive is the Tavola, and it changes its alphabetical key between adjacent years. **And the page stopped lying about its own audit.** It said *«nine were audited and five had already failed»* in fixed prose, beside a link to a page that counts for itself. It reads **twelve and seven** now, because it counts too.

rows.what: BRIATICO — Caterina Cichello's death, which would confirm her parents independently
rows.note: **Phase 7.** She was **alive at Briatico in June 1849**, a widow of eighteen years, when her daughter married — and her parents Francesco Cichello and Vittoria Mollo are known from **one document only**, the Zambrone marriage act of 1824. **Her death act would name them again**, from a different clerk in a different town, which is the standard this archive holds a new couple to. Born about 1798, so she died after 1849 and Briatico's death registers run on.

rows.what: Domenico Arlotta — confirmed, dated, and one age still wrong
rows.note: **Phase 7.** He is dated «**before 1779**» and «dead before April 1854», and he exists in this archive on the strength of a single phrase — his son Giovanni declaring a grandson's birth in 1854 as «figlio del fu Domenico». **He is the deepest Scilla ancestor and has never been looked for.** Scilla's registers begin in 1816 and he died before 1854, so **his death act may be inside the run** even though his birth cannot be. That would give an age, a trade, and possibly his own parents. **UNBLOCKED 16 SEPTEMBER.** The pre-1866 Scilla death series is now listed — **51 volumes, 1817–1865** — in `scilla-arks.tsv` ([row 130](/worklist/)). This row can start. **SCILLA BEGINS IN 1809, NOT 1816 — checked 20 September.** The napoleonic fondo holds seventeen registers: Matrimoni and Morti for 1809, Matrimoni/Morti/Nati for 1810, 1811, 1812 and 1815, and Matrimoni 1813–1814. Domenico Arlotta was born before 1779 and dead before April 1854, so his death is reachable in the civil registers and his son's 1851 marriage processetti (`an_ua2002487`) may hold the act outright. All seventeen arks are in `scilla-arks.tsv`. **AND HE MAY NOT BE THIS FAMILY'S AT ALL.** The Domenico Arlotta generation rests entirely on the 1854 act calling the declarant *«Giovanni Arlotta, figlio del fu Domenico, di anni settantacinque»*. Serafina's own birth act of 1830 makes her father **forty**, not fifty-one. Either an age is badly wrong or the 1854 declarant is a different Giovanni Arlotta — **and if he is, Domenico Arlotta leaves the tree**. Settling it is [row 39](/worklist/), not this row. **CONFIRMED AND TIGHTENED, 20 SEPTEMBER.** His son's marriage act of 30 August 1828 calls him ***«fu Domenico Arlotta»*** — so he was **dead before August 1828**, not merely before April 1854, and **the generation does not leave the tree**, which was the real risk. **He also has a wife now: ANNA BARBARO**, alive at that wedding. **What stays open is his son's age, not his existence.** Giovanni Arlotta is **28** in 1828 (b. c. 1800) and **75** in 1854 (b. c. 1779). Both acts call him *marinaro* and both call him a son of a **late Domenico**. Either the 1854 clerk wrote an age badly wrong, or **there were two Giovanni Arlotta at Scilla, both sons of a late Domenico** — in which case the 1854 declarant who named his grandson after himself may not be Serafina's father at all. **His own birth is out of reach either way:** c. 1800 or c. 1779, both fall before Scilla's civil registration begins in **1809**, so it is a parish record or nothing.

rows.what: Michele Donato came back from America — find the return crossing
rows.note: **Phase 9.** He sailed from Palermo on the Liguria in February 1908 for Quincy, Florida. The 1910 US census for the whole of Gadsden County holds **fifteen Italians and neither him nor Giovanni Polistena** — so Quincy was where they were going, not where they stayed, and his wife and household stayed at Via Grotte throughout. **He came back and there should be a manifest.** Departure from a US port 1908–1910, or an Italian arrival. It would also be the last dated fact anyone has about him.

rows.what: Generosa Costa's documented parents now reach the reader — and she was the only case
rows.note: **Done, and the spot-check was worth running.** Her 1888 marriage act names «FIGLIA DI ANTONIO... E DI ANNA ARLOTTA», and **both parents were already documented people in this archive with nothing connecting them to her** — so no chart or page could show that Rocco Arena's wife had known parents. An anchor row now joins them, and the documented line goes from 13 ancestors to **15**. **I then checked whether the same was true anywhere else**, by parsing every addition's note for «X's father/mother» and testing whether X was an unanchored export person. **Generosa Costa was the only real case.** That is worth knowing: the gap was one row, not a systemic backlog.

rows.what: Audit the six confidence levels — done, and one label was carrying three jobs
rows.note: **Audited all ninety-four rows against the definitions.** **`certain` is used consistently** — all ten rest on *two documents set against each other*, which is exactly what the legend says: an act against its chancery copy, a declared age against a birth act. **`probable` was carrying three different jobs:** an ambiguous reading, a conflict between documents, and an inference from circumstance. The first two belong together; the third does not. **Maria Rosa Prostamo and Mattea Prostamo — both reasoned from BIRTHPLACE, with nothing ambiguous to read — moved to `inferred`**, and both the `inferred` and `probable` legends on /corrections/ now say plainly what separates them. `inferred` goes 1 → 3, `probable` 6 → 4.

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE — Maria Nicotra's mother: «Monti Venera» or «Venera Cassaneti»?
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md, and it is a live conflict.** The 1898 marriage proclamation at Piedimonte Etneo calls her **«Monti Venera»**; the Queensland death registration of 1963 calls her **«Venera Cassaneti»**. Same woman, two surnames, and she sits on the spine at generation five. This is the same shape as Anna Fama against Anna Maropoli and Caterina Di Meio against Caterina Majo — **three name-conflicts now, each between an Italian act and a later copy**, and they may be worth a page of their own.  **A CANDIDATE, FROM THE SPELLING THIS ROW'S SISTER ESTABLISHED.** Piedimonte Nati 1848 atto 45: **«CASSANITI VENERA — Cassaniti Gaetano / Venuti Maria»**, born the 14th. Right name, right town, and the arithmetic fits twice over — twenty-seven when Maria was born about 1875, seventy-seven when Venera Cassaneti died in 1925. **It does not settle the «Monti Venera» conflict** and it is not yet a finding: row 161 read fourteen Piedimonte birth indexes and found no Maria Nicotra, so either this household left the town or this is a different Venera. **The test is the marriage index, not another birth sweep.**  **HALF SETTLED, AND THE CONFLICT IS NOW THREE-WAY.** She is **VENERA CASSANITI**, born about 1848 at Piedimonte, daughter of the late Gaetano Cassaniti and the late Maria Currenti — her own marriage act of 7 October 1872 says so, and Nati 1848 atto 45 fits it to the year. So «Cassaneti» is a Brisbane registry counter's spelling and nothing more. **«MONTI VENERA» is not explained.** The 1898 Piedimonte marriage proclamation still calls her that, and no act touched so far accounts for it. **That is what this row now holds** — one name in three forms, two of them reconciled and the third outstanding.  **AND HER DAUGHTER'S BIRTH ACT NAMES HER AGAIN**, in the same spelling: Mascali Nati 1875 atto 144, *«da VENERA CASSANITI sua moglie»*. Two acts, three years apart, two comuni, one spelling. **«Monti Venera» remains the outstanding third form.**

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE — Mazza Veneranda × Mariano Cavallaro, 1 October 1920
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md.** Another child of Salvatore Mazza and Maria Nicotra, absent from the tree — and **probably the link to the Brisbane Cavallaro**, of whom the export holds thirteen. The act is dated exactly, so it is a single lookup rather than a sweep.

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE — the other Mazza sons: Giovanni b.1875, Gaetano b.1880, Santo b.c.1882
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md.** Rosario Mazza's other sons, none of them in the family tree. **Giovanni is the one to read first**: he is the declarant at Salvatore's death in 1929, aged fifty-four, which both dates him and shows he was still at Piedimonte when the rest of the family had gone to Queensland. Act 64 of 1875.

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE — who is Pasquale Mazza, and is the generation compressed?
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md, and it is a structural question rather than a lookup.** Pasquale Mazza, b. c.1829, bracciante of Via Terremorte, married Concetta Greco. Is he **a third brother** of the line, or **their father's brother**? The queue also carried a «compressed-generation hypothesis» — that a Salvatore Mazza of Via Terremorte born about 1845 collapses two generations into one. **Both turn on the same acts**, and the Mariano Mazza frontier (row 47) cannot be settled without answering them.

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE — Innocenzio Mazza × Domenica Cavallaro, about 1835–40
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md.** A marriage from before Antenati's Piedimonte run begins, so it may be unreachable the way three of the four walls are — but **that has never been established**, and establishing it is cheap. If Sicilian civil registration begins in 1820 (row 14) then a marriage of 1835–40 is *inside* the run, not outside it, and this item may have been written off too early.  **OPENED, AND THEY ARE REAL.** The annual Tavola of Piedimonte Nati 1847 gives at act 31 **«MAZZA SEBASTIANO — Mazza Innocenzio / Cavallaro Domenica»**, born the 25th. The couple was at Piedimonte and having children in 1847, so the marriage this row thought might be unreachable is bracketed from above by a real document. **Next: open act 31 for their ages, trades and street**, which is what dates the marriage. Found by reading a whole Tavola for an unrelated question — the argument for reading the whole table rather than scanning for one name.

rows.what: Check whether RAITI joins the hundred and ten to the family
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md, and it is the kind of small thread that opened the Donato line.** **Raiti** appears both in the tree's unjoined hundred and ten AND as the surname of Antonino Mazza's wife. If those are one family, it is a second bridge between the Piedimonte cousins and the direct line — and the first bridge, the Rosario Mazza join, moved 102 people onto the spine.

rows.what: Michele Mazza, 1925–26 — where is he buried, and what does his passenger record say?
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md.** His Queensland death registration of 1926 carries the **«C» code — a country registration, outside Brisbane** — and he is not at Nudgee, so where he lies is unknown. Separately his **1925 Brisbane passenger record at the NAA** would name a next of kin and a destination address, which for the first of this family to arrive is worth more than it sounds.

rows.what: Camillo Antonio Polistena's own birth act, about 1835
rows.note: **Migrated from QUEUE.md.** Scilla's births begin in 1816, so a birth about 1835 is **inside the run** and reachable. He is the oldest Polistena this archive has, and the Polistena quarter is the thinnest of the four — the surname returns **nothing at all** in the Queensland index and has no documented ancestor above him. **CLOSED 16 SEPTEMBER, and not by his birth act — by his death act.** **Camillo Antonio Polistena died at Scilla on 19 October 1924**, «Padre GIUSEPPE, Madre ANNA PONTILLO, Coniuge GIOVANNA ROMANO». **The thinnest quarter gains two documented ancestors** where it had none above him. His birth act, about 1835, is still worth having for the age and the address, but the parents no longer depend on it.

rows.what: Guard the searched.tsv key column — appending a row silently corrupts it
rows.note: **Raised because I broke it twice in one session.** `data/searched.tsv` gained a `key` first column from another session, and `build_searched.py` deliberately **never recomputes it** — the docstring says why: hand-added keys were once wiped and the gate then reported «nothing outstanding» for an archive with twenty-four outstanding searches. **But nothing stops a session appending a row in the old five-column shape.** I did, twice, and every field shifted one place right: `part` landed in `key`, a date landed in `status`, and the rows became invisible to the gate that exists to count them. **A checker should refuse a row whose key is empty or does not match `src/<slug>-<6 hex>`**, and refuse a status outside the vocabulary — which has drifted to **seven values**: done, outstanding, not-yet, part, superseded, correction, wall. Some of those I invented myself without declaring them. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER. `tools/check_searched.py`, wired into the build as `check:searched`.** **The shape check runs first and reports by physical line**, because once a row has shifted the named columns cannot be trusted to mean what they say — and on the actual bug it prints *«5 columns, expected 6 — this is the shifted-row bug; first cell is «part»»*, which is word for word what happened. It also refuses a key that is not `src/<slug>-<6 hex>`, a **duplicate key** (two searches counting as one), a status outside the seven words in use, and a **`done` or `part` row with an empty result** — a finished search with nothing written in it being counted as a negative result. **One thing learned writing it:** I invented the status vocabulary instead of reading it, and the first run threw 43 false failures. The seven real words are `done`, `outstanding`, `not-yet`, `part`, `superseded`, `wall`, `correction` — and **only `outstanding` is what `check:covers` counts**, which is worth knowing before anyone adds an eighth. There is no legend on [/searched/](/searched/) to read them out of, unlike the confidence words on [/corrections/](/corrections/), so they are pinned in the checker with a comment saying so.

rows.what: FINDMYPAST — unlock Our Lady of Loretto: eighty-four Arena baptisms, indexed and locked
rows.note: **THE PAYWALL IS OPEN AND THE FIRST PASS HAS PAID.** The subscription includes the Catholic Heritage Archive: **265 Arena baptisms** across New York's Catholic parishes, **18 at Our Lady of Loretto**, transcripts live. **Rocco Arena and Generosa Costa's whole New York household, found in one search:** Antonio b. 3 Oct 1896, Serafina b. 15 Aug 1898, Clementina b. 21 Dec 1900, and a **second Antonio** b. 13 Oct 1902. **An address at last** — 141 Mulberry in 1896–98, 198 Mulberry by 1901 — corroborating the 1899 Ellis Island manifest that sends Giovanni Arena to «brother Rocco, N. York, Mulberry St». **And a fifth Rocco Arena baptism excluded on the mother's name:** Giuseppe, 1911, the Bronx, mother *Teresa Siniscaldi*. A surname sweep would have taken all five. **Still to do:** the remaining 247 Arena baptisms for the wider colony, and the same collection's **marriages and burials**, which have not been touched at all. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER, and it closed smaller and harder than it opened.** The 247 remaining Arena baptisms were never the way to this family — **the parent fields are**, and they are now exhausted. Father **Rocco** + mother **Generosa** returns exactly the four known children and nothing else, which audits the American harvest as complete. Father **Giovanni** + mother **Concetta** returns **zero**, so Rocco's brother — who sailed in 1899 to join him — **baptised no child in New York**, and came as a sojourner rather than a settler. **The marriages are excluded by arithmetic, not sampling:** both Arena men were already married at Scilla before they sailed, in 1885 and 1888, and no child of Rocco's was of marriageable age in America before the household left. **And there are no burials to sweep** — the Catholic Heritage Archive for New York is baptisms and marriages only, so the infant death of the first Antonio cannot be tested here at all. See row 113.

rows.what: FINDMYPAST — the Australian electoral rolls, which unblock rows 49 and 62
rows.note: **Done — all seven surnames this row named, and the answer is half of what it promised.** Prostamo, Polistena, Mazza, Arena, Donato, Melluso and Crupi, each swept in «Australia Electoral Rolls» and sorted to bring the Queensland rows onto the first page. **It found Michael's grandfather.** SEBASTIANO MAZZA, builder's labourer, **Progress Road, Wacol, sub-district Inala**, on the 1959 roll — the post-war migrant belt, ten years after he landed, and the first record of him in Australia between his arrival and his grave. It also found **ROSARIO and ANGELA MAZZA at 225 Leichhardt Street** on consecutive roll numbers, which is one household, and **ROSARIO SALVATORE MAZZA at Paddington in 1949**, the same man a decade earlier. **But the instrument is smaller than this row assumed.** Findmypast holds only eight Queensland commonwealth years and the last is **1959** — for a family that arrived in 1949 that is *one usable roll*, not the near-annual run promised here. See rows 104, 105 and 106 for what that leaves. Recorded in [what has been searched](/searched/), which carries the Findmypast log. **The Crupi were the second prize.** Angela Crupi's three brothers — whom the Queensland death index named and neither Brisbane cemetery register could find — are all at **Tully** on the 1959 roll with trades and streets. **Polistena, Melluso and Rocco Arena return nothing**, and that absence has a shape: of the adults who landed in 1949, only Sebastiano Mazza was enrolled by 1959. See row 108 for the two surname clusters this turned up.

rows.what: FINDMYPAST — the nine unnamed crossings, and the Australian passenger lists
rows.note: **Row 21's other half.** The trial already CORROBORATED five Prostamo in the Australian passenger index — Caterina 1969, Domenico F 1956, Francesca 1957 — and separately failed to find **Domenica Prostamo's 1951 voyage** in «Australia, Inward, Outward & Coastal Passenger Lists 1826-1972». **With full access, sweep that collection properly** for all ten surnames rather than by targeted lookup, and test the *Ugolino Vivaldi* candidate of 1 March 1951 that `corrections.tsv` carries at `candidate` confidence. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER, and the answer is that this was the wrong shop.** For twentieth-century Australian arrivals the collection **is the NAA passenger index** — every post-1945 row carries a NAA barcode and links back to recordsearch.naa.gov.au — and this archive has already worked that index directly, for nothing. **The Ugolino Vivaldi candidate could not be tested**: Findmypast serves the identical record, barcode 30133197, with no age and no sex, so [the candidate grade](/corrections/) stands. **One new crossing did fall out**: ROCCO PROSTAMO, 10 August 1949, the *Napoli*, Genoa to Melbourne — a sixth Prostamo and not one in the tree. **And the subscription does hold something genuinely new: the Victorian inward, outward and coastal lists, 1852–1923**, which are not in the NAA index at all. See rows 110 and 111.

rows.what: FINDMYPAST — Rocco Arena's naturalisation, and the American records
rows.note: **Covers the outstanding «NARA New York» search.** The trial established Rocco Arena's **four crossings** (1892, 1894, 1899, 1913) and that by 1913 he was travelling as a **US citizen** — which means a naturalisation exists and has never been found. It also found **no petition** under his name, so the search needs the subscription's wider American sets: NARA indexes, WWI and WWII registrations, and the 1900–1930 censuses for Mulberry Street. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER. The naturalisation is still not found, but the census settled the family's movement and bounded the search.** Rocco Arena appears in the United States census **exactly once, in 1900** — one hit in the whole country, right birth year — and **never again**. The 1910 census indexes **543 Arena households and not one holds a Rocco**, nor a Generosa, nor a Serafina, nor a Clementina. The 1920 and 1930 Rocco Arenas are all born after 1882. **Three independent absences now say the household went back to Scilla**: no census after 1900, no Generosa on the 1913 manifest, no New York draft card for the son born on Mulberry Street. See row 112 for where the naturalisation actually is.

rows.what: FINDMYPAST — re-run the four PAYWALL and BLOCKED rows in findmypast.tsv
rows.note: **Twenty-six rows of trial work exist and four of them are not answers, they are locks.** Two PAYWALL rows (the New York Roman Catholic transcripts, twice), and one BLOCKED row recording that **the session signed out** before the work was finished. **Re-run each one and convert it to a real result — found or negative — rather than leaving a paywall standing in the record as though it were evidence.** A lock is not a negative and this archive should not let one look like it. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER. No PAYWALL or BLOCKED row remains in [the log](/searched/).** The two parish-transcript locks opened and became the American harvest — four Arena baptisms, both Mulberry Street addresses, two namesakes excluded on a mother's name. The signed-out row became a method note. **And turning the third lock produced a retraction.** The locked row had claimed the transcript carried «the mother's name and the godparents». The mother's name is there and has done more work than anything else this week. **The godparents are not in the record at all** — no such field, and no image behind it, so they are unreachable at any tier and exist only in Our Lady of Loretto's own register. *That claim was a guess about the contents of a locked record, written down as though it were a finding*, which is exactly the failure this row existed to fix.

rows.what: FINDMYPAST — decide what to do before the month expires
rows.note: **A calendar item, not a research one.** The previous trial **expired the day it was most needed** and the record still carries a BLOCKED row from the moment it lapsed. A month is enough for rows 98 to 102 if they are done deliberately and in that order — **the locked parish transcripts first, because they are the only thing here that cannot be got anywhere else.** Worth agreeing a date to review what is left, rather than discovering the end of it the same way as last time. **UPDATED 16 SEPTEMBER: rows 98 to 102 are all done, on the first day.** The subscription has been worked out rather than used up, and the honest summary is that **Findmypast had less for this family than the work list expected, and gave it up quickly.** **What it delivered:** Sebastiano Mazza on the 1959 roll at Wacol; the Crupi brothers at Tully; Rocco Arena's absence from the American census proved across the whole country; the parish transcripts opened and audited. **What it turned out not to hold:** Queensland rolls after 1959, any Australian arrival the free NAA index does not already have, any New York burial, and any godparent. **So the question is no longer «what else can we get before it expires» — it is whether the month is worth renewing at all.** On this evidence, no: the open work now points at **Ancestry or the NLA** for the post-1959 rolls (row 104), **the NAA** for naturalisations and one manifest image (rows 105, 110, 112), and **free New York city records** (row 113). **The one thing still unmined here is the Victorian passenger lists** (row 111). Worth a decision, not a diary date.

rows.what: The Queensland rolls after 1959 — which means the NLA or Ancestry, not Findmypast
rows.note: **Row 99 hit a wall that a subscription cannot climb.** Findmypast's last Queensland electoral roll is **1959**. Sebastiano Mazza is on it at Wacol; **Domenica Prostamo is not on it at all**, under either name — most likely because she had not yet been naturalised, since her husband would have been naturalised first. **Every year that would settle that is outside this collection.** The near-annual Queensland run to 1980 is held by the **National Library of Australia** and by **Ancestry**, and it would follow this household through Wacol year by year, catch Domenica's first enrolment, and place Frank Mazza as he came of age. **This is David's call, not the archive's** — it is a second paid service, and the Findmypast month is already running.

rows.what: Sebastiano Mazza's naturalisation, which the 1959 roll proves exists
rows.note: **An enrolment is a proof of citizenship, and that is the quiet finding in row 99.** Only British subjects could be enrolled to vote, so Sebastiano Mazza's presence on the 1959 Queensland roll means **he was naturalised between his arrival in 1949 and 1959**, and a naturalisation file exists for him. **The NAA holds them** — series A712, A714 and the certificate registers — and this archive already knows how to work the NAA index from the passenger work. The file would give his **birth date, his birthplace, his occupation, his address, and often the ship and date he arrived**, which would corroborate the crossing independently. **And it should be run for Domenica Prostamo at the same time**, because her naturalisation date is exactly what would explain her absence from the 1959 roll. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER — the file exists and it is cited.** **NAA: J25, 1971/1074, «Mazza, Sebastiano; wife Domenica [nee Prostamo]», Brisbane, 1950–1971.** It names both of them and her maiden name, and its date range covers their whole Australian lives to 1971. **It is paper, it is not digitised, and it is «not yet examined»** — so it needs an access examination request before anyone can read it. That is row 115, and it is not this archive's to make. **It may also settle row 21**: a Queensland immigration file opening in 1950 should record how and when Domenica came.

rows.what: Andrea Mazza — three dates now, and still no parents
rows.note: **Tully is not a coincidence and it is not yet a relative.** Rosario Mazza's daughter **Carmela Mazza was born at Tully in 1926**, so this family had a household in that exact sub-district; and the 1959 roll puts an **ANDREA MAZZA, timber cutter, at Cardwell in the Tully sub-district**. No Andrea appears anywhere in the tree as it stands. **A roll carries no parents and no birth year, so it cannot decide him.** What could: the Queensland BDM birth index for Tully in the 1920s and 1930s, which *is* inside its window and would name his parents; or Michael, if the family remembers a branch that stayed north. Left as a lead rather than attached — the archive has been offered two Arena namesakes in New York this week and excluded both on a parent's name. **THE TULLY PREMISE IS BACK, BY A DIFFERENT ROUTE — 20 SEPTEMBER.** [Row 116](/worklist/) knocked out the reason this row was interesting: Carmela Mazza was **not** born at Tully in 1926, so no Mazza household stood there then. **But a family household did.** Angela Crupi's brother **Antonino Crupi was a cane farmer at Dean Street, Tully**, naturalised there in 1946, and **Pietro and Mario Crupi were at Tully too**. The family's Tully connection is real and it runs through the **Crupi**, not the Mazza. **That changes what Andrea Mazza would mean.** A Mazza at Cardwell in the Tully sub-district in 1959 is a man living where his in-laws' family already was — which makes him more worth checking and no more proved. The test is unchanged: **the Queensland BDM birth index for the Tully district**, which names parents. **DATED, 20 SEPTEMBER.** **NAA: BP4/3, ITALIAN MAZZA A — «Mazza, Andrea — naturalisation certificate granted 27 NOVEMBER 1934»**, held at Brisbane. Naturalisation of that period wanted about five years' residence, **so he was in Australia by about 1929** — thirty years before the roll that found him, and long before the post-war migration this row has been reading him against. With his Queensland death on **31 July 1975** that makes three dates. **He is still not a documented relative**, and the certificate names no parents. **Two things would settle him:** his **death certificate**, which names parents where the index gives only the surname *Mazza*; and the **naturalisation file**, which carries a **birthplace** — and if that birthplace is **Piedimonte Etneo** this stops being a lead and becomes a question.

rows.what: Never record a negative from an untested search parameter — the rule this sweep nearly broke
rows.note: **Raised and closed the same day, because it nearly put a falsehood in the record.** On Findmypast's results URL a wrong parameter fails in **two different ways and neither announces itself**. `state=Queensland` and `page=2` render a filter chip and report **«0 results found»** — word for word what a genuine negative looks like. `street=progress road` is **discarded in silence** and the unfiltered count comes back unchanged, so the search you think you ran is not the one that ran. The first was caught only because the *unfiltered* search plainly listed Queensland rows. **The rule now in the log: control-test a parameter against a search known to return rows before believing any zero it produces.** This is the same family of trap as `fathersfirstname` for `fatherfirstname` earlier in this work, and as the multi-comune trap in the Antenati registers — *the instrument answering a different question than the one asked.* Written up in [what has been searched](/searched/).

rows.what: Donato and Nicotra in Queensland — two clusters off this family's own spine, unopened
rows.note: **The electoral sweep walked into two surnames nobody here has looked for in Australia.** **DONATO: 65 rows**, and the Queensland block holds a **CANDELORE DONATO enrolled in 1941 and 1949**, a **CANDO DONATO** in 1939 and 1959, and a **DOMENICO DONATO** in 1959. **CANDELORO DONATO IS ONE OF THE FOUR WALLS** — born about 1783 at Scilla, the point where [the Donato quarter](/lines/) stops. He is plainly not the same man, and *that is the interest*: southern Italian families name a grandson for his grandfather, so a Candeloro Donato in Queensland is what a **descendant of the wall** looks like from this end. Domenico Donato is the name on the 1816 birth act that came out of the Scilla processetti this week. **NICOTRA: 39 rows**, almost all Queensland, a family enrolled continuously from 1934 to 1959 — **Filippo, Gregorio, Giuseppe, Carmela, Leonarda, Leonard**. **Nicotra is Sebastiano Mazza's mother's name**, Maria Concetta Nicotra. **Neither is claimed and neither can be, from rolls alone** — no parents, no birth years. The route that could decide them is the Queensland BDM birth and marriage indexes, which *are* inside their windows for the 1930s and 1940s and do carry parents.

rows.what: Which Antonio Crupi — answered by a naturalisation, not by the roll
rows.note: **A small ambiguity, written down so it is not quietly resolved the wrong way later.** The 1959 roll holds **two Antonio Crupi**: a **cane farmer at Dean Street, Tully**, and a **farmer at Silkwood East in the Innisfail sub-district**. Angela Crupi's brother **ANTONINO CRUPI died 15 April 1982** (reg 1982/52783), son of Francesco Crupi and Maria Vecchio. **A roll cannot tell which man he is** — it carries no parents and no birth year. The Tully one is the better bet only because his brothers Pietro and Mario are both at Tully, and *better bet* is not evidence. **What would settle it:** the 1982 death registration's district, or the marriage of an Antonino Crupi registered 24 August 1940 (1940/C/3314), which would name a wife to match against **Nellie Crupi**, the woman sharing Dean Street with the Tully man. **ANSWERED 20 SEPTEMBER, AND BY THE TEST THIS ROW ITSELF NAMED.** NAA: A714 57/18792 — *«CRUPI, Antonio; naturalised 7 November 1946; place of birth **Piedimonte**, Italy; year of birth **1907**; place of residence **Tully, QLD**; [W] CRUPI, **Nellie**»*. Piedimonte and 1907 tie it to Angela Crupi's brother's aliens card; **Tully and Nellie** tie it to the cane farmer of **Dean Street** on the 1959 roll. **The Silkwood East farmer is a different man.** Found while reading Antonino's aliens card for [row 117](/worklist/) — the question was answered by a document nobody went looking for. **And it adds a move:** a *boot repairer at Ingham* in October 1939, a *cane farmer at Tully* by 1946, where Pietro and Mario were too. **One loose end tidied, not proved:** the card registered in October 1939 already says *married*, which sat badly against a Queensland marriage of 24 August 1940. The same card carries 1943 annotations, so *married* was very probably added later and the 1940 marriage is the real date — very likely to Nellie. Stated as a reading.

rows.what: The original Ugolino Vivaldi manifest at the NAA — free, and the only thing that can settle Domenica's crossing
rows.note: **Row 100 proved the subscription cannot do this and pointed at what can.** Domenica Prostamo's 1951 crossing is graded **candidate** on a good argument — right month, right year, right port, right married surname, and «Domenico» one letter from Domenica. **What it lacks is an age or a sex**, and the index line has neither, on Findmypast or at the NAA. **The manifest image does.** RecordSearch serves barcode **30133197** as a scanned page, free, and the handwritten entry would give the age and sex outright — and show **everyone else on that page**, which is how a two-year-old Salvatore Mazza would appear, since infants are not separately indexed. **This is the single cheapest upgrade available to this archive**: one image, no subscription, and it converts a candidate into a documented crossing or kills it. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER — and it killed the candidate rather than confirming it.** This row said the image would «convert a candidate into a documented crossing or kill it». It killed it. The master list of trip 2/51 carries **one Mazza**, no. 476, bound for **Narracan, Victoria**. There is **no Prostamo aboard** under any spelling, and **no second Mazza**, though the list names children individually — so no two-year-old Salvatore. **And the port column settles it**: unlabelled, but every `-F-` passenger appears in the Department of Immigration's separate *Schedule of Alien Passengers for debarkation at Fremantle*, one for one. MAZZA Domenico is `-M-`, and he is **absent from that schedule**, which runs MARTINELLI straight to MERENDINO. **Domenica Prostamo was going to her husband in Brisbane; this man landed at Melbourne for a Gippsland shire.** Retracted in [the corrections](/corrections/), regraded *flagged*, and the two voyage rows are off [the crossings](/crossings/). **Her March 1951 crossing is unknown again — see row 21.**

rows.what: The Victorian passenger lists 1852–1923 — the part of the subscription that is genuinely not the NAA
rows.note: **Found by accident while proving row 100 a dead end.** «Australia, Inward, Outward & Coastal Passenger Lists 1826-1972» is two different things stitched together. The post-1945 half is the NAA index re-served. **The pre-1940 half is not**: ids of the form ANZ/VCPL and ANZ/MIGR/VICTORIAPASSLIST are the **Victorian inward, outward and coastal lists**, which the NAA index does not hold. The Mazza search returns rows there from **1891, 1896, 1897, 1898, 1900, 1901, 1910, 1911, 1914 and 1919**. **Why it might matter:** this archive's Australian story starts in 1925 with Michele Mazza on the *Palermo*, and everything before that is assumed to be Italy. **These lists cover the years when it might not have been.** Sicilian and Calabrian men worked passages to Victoria and went home again, and a Mazza or a Prostamo on an **outward** list would be exactly that. Speculative, cheap to test, and nobody has looked. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER, and the guess was wrong for reasons worth writing down.** The Victorian material is mostly **coastal** — Strahan to Melbourne, Fremantle to Melbourne — which is people already in Australia moving around it, not people arriving from Italy. **And the coastal rows are mostly nameless**, carrying a surname, a sex and an age and no given name, so a real ancestor there could not be recognised anyway. The named overseas Victorian rows are **British subjects**. **The control makes it a negative rather than a shrug:** searched by name, Michele Mazza's 1925 crossing from Messina to Brisbane comes straight back. The collection can see this family when it is there. Before 1925 it is not. **The Australian story still starts where this archive has always said it starts.**

rows.what: Rocco Arena's naturalisation is a pre-1906 New York court filing — which no subscription holds
rows.note: **Row 101 could not find the papers and instead worked out when they must have been filed.** He is in America from 1892, he is in the 1900 census, he is **gone from the whole country by 1910**, and he sails in 1913 as a **US citizen**. So the declaration and petition were filed in New York **between 1892 and about 1906**. **That is exactly why Findmypast cannot see him**: its United States Naturalization Petitions collection begins after the 1906 standardisation, and before 1906 these cases were heard in **state, county and city courts** as well as federal ones. **The finding aid is a NARA index to petitions filed in New York City courts, 1792–1906** — on microfilm, held by the National Archives at New York City, and on no subscription site. *(The series number should be confirmed before anyone writes to them; it is believed to be M1674.)* **What has changed is the size of the problem**: the search is now bounded to a fourteen-year window in one city, instead of a lifetime in a country.

rows.what: The first Antonio Arena's death, 1896×1902 — free records, and neither has been tried
rows.note: **An inference this archive has published, and the record that would settle it is free.** Rocco Arena's first son **Antonio was born 3 October 1896**; a **second Antonio was born 13 October 1902**. This archive reads that as the first boy dying in between — the same reading it makes of [Orazio Arena's two sons named Domenico](/scilla/) at Scilla. **It is sound and it is still an inference.** **Findmypast cannot test it**: there is no New York Roman Catholic burials collection — baptisms and marriages only, and «Congregational Records» is empty even of Russo. **Two places can.** The **New York City death certificates** at the Municipal Archives are indexed from 1862 and searchable for nothing; and the interment registers of **Calvary Cemetery**, where the Italian Catholic dead of lower Manhattan were mostly buried. A death between 1896 and 1902 for an infant of 141 or 198 Mulberry Street is a narrow, well-specified search. **It would also date the family's last years in America**, which matters now that the census says they were gone by 1910.

rows.what: Salvatore Mazza's arrival, which fell with his mother's
rows.note: **Collateral damage from row 110, and it should not be left implicit.** This archive placed **Salvatore Mazza (b. 1948)** on the *Ugolino Vivaldi* at `inferred`, on the reasoning that infants are not separately indexed and he belonged on his mother's voyage. **The reasoning was fine and the voyage was wrong.** Reading the manifest also removed its own premise: **this master list names children individually** — the Mellino family of eight, the Puusaari of six, a Campagna aged 1 — so an infant *would* have been listed. **He has no documented crossing now.** The tree records a Fremantle arrival out of Genoa with no date; that, and the family account of a son not yet three, are all that remain. He travels with whatever voyage row 21 eventually finds for his mother.

rows.what: Ask the NAA to examine J25 1971/1074 — the family's own naturalisation file
rows.note: **The single best unread document about Michael's grandparents, and getting at it is a form, not research.** **NAA: J25, 1971/1074, «Mazza, Sebastiano; wife Domenica [nee Prostamo]»**, Brisbane, contents 1950–1971. Its access status is **«not yet examined»**, which means nobody has ever asked for it. **Anyone can ask, it costs nothing, and the NAA then examines it for release** — the usual wait is about ninety days. **Why it is worth the form:** a Queensland immigration and naturalisation file covering 1950 to 1971 would carry Sebastiano's naturalisation, his address history, his occupation, and — since she is named on it — **how and when Domenica actually arrived**, which [row 21](/worklist/) badly needs now that the Ugolino Vivaldi is disproved. **This archive cannot lodge the request**; it needs a person with an account and a postal address. Michael is in Brisbane, where the file is.

rows.what: Carmela Mazza cannot have been born at Tully in 1926
rows.note: **A contradiction found by accident, and it broke one of my own arguments the same day.** The tree has **Carmela Mazza born 1926 at Tully, Queensland**. But **NAA: A12508, 31/1454** has her arriving at Brisbane on **7 December 1937** aboard the *Viminale*, **aged eight, as an Italian alien**, with her mother Angela Crupi and her sister Maria. **A child born at Tully in 1926 would be eleven and an Australian-born British subject**, needing no alien declaration at all. **The record is not loose about ages** — Maria's «age 15» matches the tree's 1922 exactly. **So she was born in Italy about 1929.** **What it cost:** I had argued that the Tully timber cutter of 1959 ([row 106](/worklist/)) was interesting because a Mazza household already stood at Tully in 1926. On this evidence it did not. The Tully connection survives, but through **the Crupi brothers**, not through a birth that did not happen. **What would settle it:** the Queensland BDM birth index, which covers 1926 and would simply show whether a Carmela Mazza was registered at Tully at all.

rows.what: The aliens cards — Antonino's read, Pietro's explained away
rows.note: **Row 50 found the seam and did not empty it.** Mario Crupi's card (D4028) turned out to be **digitised, free, and the richest document this archive holds on anyone in Australia** — birth date, birthplace, occupation, arrival, a physical description, and an internment camp. **There should be more.** **Wanted:** cards for **PIETRO** and **ANTONINO CRUPI**, the other two brothers, both of whom are on the Queensland electoral rolls; for **ROSARIO MAZZA**, to set against his internment dossier; and for **ROCCO ARENA** and the **POLISTENA**, who arrived in 1949 and may be too late for the wartime series. **Note the series split:** D4028 is Queensland aliens registration; B78 and BP25/1 and SP908/1 are the Victorian, Queensland and New South Wales equivalents, and a family scattered across states will be scattered across series. **Search by surname in all record categories, then check each item for «View digital copy»** — that is what separates an hour's work from a request form. **DONE, 20 SEPTEMBER.** CRUPI swept across **all** record categories — 233 items, read end to end at 200 to a page. **ANTONINO CRUPI'S CARD IS DIGITISED AND IS READ.** NAA: D4028, item 9209610. Born **5 October 1907 at Piedimonte Etneo** — his brother Mario's town and the Mazza's. A **boot repairer** at Ingham. Entered Australia **2 September 1930**, port Brisbane. Five feet four, black eyes, black hair, sturdy; **the fourth finger of his right hand deformed**. Registered at Ingham police station, 3 October 1939. **AND HE WAS INTERNED — THE THIRD MAN IN THIS FAMILY.** The front is stamped **LOVEDAY 35924**; the reverse records him moved *«ex Gay[thorne] to 14A»* on 16 March 1943 and **released and returned to Queensland on 22 October 1943**. Rosario Mazza on his own dossier, Mario Crupi at Loveday from August 1942, Antonino released October 1943. **Angela Crupi's husband and two of her brothers, all three behind wire in the same eighteen months.** **The censor kept a sentence of his.** A mail extract of 2 April 1943, from a letter to his wife in Queensland, is copied onto the card: *«… Our freedom will come soon and we shall always cry Vive Italia.»* It is the only sentence of his own this archive has, and it survives because an official wrote it down as evidence against him. **PIETRO HAS NO CARD, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER, NOT A GAP.** NAA: BP4/3 records *«Alien Registration Certificate not issued»*, the folio noting he was **naturalised 23 February 1932** — by 1939 a British subject, outside the series. **The brothers came together:** Pietro and Antonino both arrived in Brisbane on the **OTRANTO, 19 August 1930**; Mario two years earlier on the **MARIA CRISTINA, 20 May 1928**. **Naturalisations:** Antonino 7 November 1946 at **Tully**, wife **Nellie**; Mario 26 April 1940 at Ingham, *single*; Pietro 23 February 1932. **And a trap one barcode away:** item **9209609** is another *CRUPI Antonio* — born **Serrata**, Calabria, arrived Melbourne 1926, nobody here. The run 9209609 / 9209610 / 9209611 is stranger, brother, brother. **Adjacency in an alphabetical card series is not kinship.** **What is left:** the ARENA and POLISTENA cards, who arrived in 1949 and are probably too late for the wartime series — and one open file, [row 148](/worklist/). **AND THE ARENA CARDS DO NOT EXIST, 20 SEPTEMBER.** This row wanted aliens cards for **Rocco Arena** and the **Polistena** and guessed they would be «too late for the wartime series». They are. **Rocco Arena's only record in the entire NAA name index is J25 1971/3900**, the file that names him with his wife — no card, no naturalisation, no arrival item of his own. He landed in **December 1953**, after the wartime series closed. **A caution came with it.** Narrowing ARENA (1,650 items) to **Rocco Arena** gives nineteen, and **one of them is an internment** — a Sydney man **born 31 August 1909**, with an Aliens Tribunal objection and a dossier. **He is not this family**: this archive's Rocco Arena arrived thirteen years later, and the Rocco born at Scilla in 1861 died there in 1932. Guard written.

rows.what: Rocco Arena married his first cousin — and one act away from proving it
rows.note: **A question this archive asked itself and left open has almost certainly been answered.** The row for **ANNA ARLOTTA**, Generosa Costa's mother, noted that Rocco Arena's mother was **Serafina ARLOTTA** and his wife's mother was **Anna ARLOTTA**, and said in as many words that whether they were sisters *had not been tested*. **The Scilla death index tests it.** Anna Arlotta, died 16 March 1915, is «Padre GIOVANNI ARLOTTA, Madre MARIA COSTA, Coniuge ANTONINO COSTA» — and Giovanni Arlotta and Maria Costa are **Serafina Arlotta's own parents**. Her husband's name matches the Antonio Costa the 1888 marriage act gives as Generosa's father. **So the two women were sisters and Rocco Arena and Generosa Costa were first cousins.** **Graded *probable*, not *certain*, and deliberately.** Arlotta and Costa are both common at Scilla and nothing read so far rules out a second Anna Arlotta married to a second Antonino Costa. **One act settles it**: the 1915 death act itself, which gives her age and parents in full, or Generosa Costa's own birth act. Both are inside the surviving run. **CERTAIN as of 16 September.** The Costa sweep supplied the two acts that were missing: Antonino Costa's own death, naming Anna Arlotta as his wife, and **Generosa Costa's**, naming Antonino Costa and Anna Arlotta as her parents. **Rocco Arena and Generosa Costa were first cousins** — his mother Serafina and her mother Anna were both daughters of Giovanni Arlotta and Maria Costa.
