**202 lines of prose.** Shape: the question, what is known, what has been tried, and the record that would answer it. `kit/components/Questions.astro`.

**Raised by the UI alignment pass, 2026-09-16.** It is recorded here because it is research this archive owns, not something to guess at from outside. **[State corrected from «open» to «next» on 16 September — «open» is not in the estate vocabulary and the build gate refuses it. Twenty-five sources: **six read in the original**, fifteen index-only, two walls. **And extracting it exposed a page that had been underselling this archive by a year's work.** It opened *«almost every source below is an INDEX cited by the family tree, not a document this archive has seen»* and listed **no Italian civil register at all**; it closed under the heading *«What is not here yet»* with *«No Italian civil register has been read for this family. That is the largest single gap.»* Both were true on the day the archive was built. **The old headline is kept on the page, struck** — an archive that quietly deletes its own wrong headline is harder to trust than one that shows the correction.

rows.what: Does Antenati's name index cover BIRTHS and MARRIAGES too, or only deaths?
rows.note: **The single highest-value question in the work list, because the answer re-prices a dozen rows.** Today's sweep queried `/search-nominative/?cognome=X&localita=Scilla` and every result came back an **atto di morte**, 1910–1943. **That may be all Scilla has indexed, or it may be all that these four surnames happened to return.** Not the same thing, and the difference is enormous: if **marriages** are indexed, [row 71](/worklist/) — Nunziata Donato × Giovanni Polistena, about 1916 — is answered by a query. If **births** are, so is Camillo Antonio Polistena's birth act and half of [row 4](/worklist/). **Test it properly:** query a surname with no locality and read the *tipologia* facet, which will say what act types exist and how many of each. **ANSWERED 16 SEPTEMBER, and the answer is no.** Every act in Scilla's name index, across every year from 1880 to 1943, is an **atto di morte**. There are **no births and no marriages in it at all**. **Coverage is 1911–1943 solidly** — between 279 and 704 indexed persons a year — with only a scatter before that: four in 1880, one in 1885, a handful each in 1902, 1905, 1906, 1908, 1909, 1910. **What it costs:** [row 71](/worklist/), [row 137](/worklist/) and half of [row 4](/worklist/) stay volume reads. The hope that one query would answer them is gone. **What it gains:** the window it does cover is exactly when this family's Italian relatives were dying, which is why it gave up four deaths in an afternoon. **And `anno=` is the year parameter**, control-tested — `anno=1880` returns 4, matching the facet, while `estremoRemoto=` is silently ignored and returns all 13,777.

rows.what: The Scilla surnames are all swept — and the summaries cost a second sweep
rows.note: **DONE, AND IT WAS ALREADY DONE.** This row was written when four surnames had been swept and listed eight more as wanted: Costa, Sofi, Zirilli, Martello, Russo, Paladino, Romano, Pontillo. **Every one of them was run by [rows 128, 130, 131 and 132](/searched/) within the following two days**, and this row was never closed. It has now been checked by re-running seven of them. **What the re-run bought, and what it cost.** It bought a NEGATIVE that answers [row 131](/worklist/) — **Mariantonia Musolino is not in the index at all**, Scilla having only seven Musolino records — and four households written out into `corrections.tsv`: Giovanna Romano's three sisters, the four children of Lorenzo Costa and Generosa Polistena (including **Generosa Costa's own father Antonio, d. 1 June 1915**), Domenico Arlotta's wife **Maria Pontillo**, and the guard now standing on the two Generosa Costas ([row 139](/worklist/)). **It cost seven rate-limited queries that had already been paid for once**, because the first pass wrote «69 indexed persons, 26 of them the deceased» and then named eight. **The rule, and it is the second time today it has been bought: when a query returns a BOUNDED set, write the set down.** A paragraph is cheaper than a second search, and the second search is rate-limited.

rows.what: Generosa Costa's death — absent from the Arena index, so look under Costa
rows.note: **Her husband's death act of 1932 names her as his wife, so she was alive or recently dead in February 1932.** She does not appear as *the deceased* anywhere in the Arena results, which is expected — she would be indexed under **COSTA**. Worth doing on its own because she is the last of the New York household whose end is unknown: Rocco died in 1932, their daughter Serafina in 1912, and the two Antonios and Clementina have no recorded end at all. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER. Generosa Costa died at Scilla on 6 June 1916** — «Padre ANTONINO COSTA, Madre ANNA ARLOTTA, Coniuge ROCCO ARENA». **She died sixteen years before her husband**, who followed on 8 February 1932. Her parents are exactly those the 1888 marriage act gave, now from a second and independent document. **And her father's own act came with it:** Antonio Costa, died 1 June 1915, «Padre LORENZO COSTA, Madre GENEROSA POLISTENA» — **two new ancestors** on a line that stopped dead at him, and the reason for his daughter's name.

rows.what: Read the four acts the index only summarises
rows.note: **An index line is not an act — this archive says so about NAA item titles and the same rule applies here.** Four acts are now identified and none has been opened: **Rocco Arena, 8 February 1932**; **Giovanni Arena, 31 March 1936**; **Michele Donato, 10 May 1936**; **Camillo Antonio Polistena, 19 October 1924**. Each would give an **age** — which dates a birth — plus an address, a trade, and the two declarants. **Camillo Antonio's is the most valuable**: his age would date the birth this archive has only as «about 1835». **ONE OF THE FOUR READ, 16 September — Camillo Antonio Polistena, and it was worth it.** His age is **eighty**, so he was **born about 1844, not 1835**: the archive's figure was inferred from his son's birth and is nine years out. He was a **pescatore**, he died at **fifty minutes past midnight at Rione Monacina**, and the act calls his parents *«dal fu Giuseppe»* and *«dalla fu Pontillo Anna»* — both already dead — and him *«marito di Romano Giovanna»*. **A witness is «ARENA ROCCO FU FILIPPO, di anni trentasei»** — not this family's Rocco Arena, who was sixty-three in 1924, but the one who died in 1938. Exactly the namesake [row 132](/worklist/) warns about. **The method is now cheap:** the volume's own *indice annuale* is the last image, it gives the act number, and the acts run **two per image** — three downloads instead of seventy-five. **Still to read:** Rocco Arena 1932 (`an_ud16599915`), Giovanni Arena 1936 (`an_ud16600296`), Michele Donato 1936 (`an_ud16600302`). **TWO OF FOUR READ. Rocco Arena, Scilla Morti 1932 parte I atto 9:** he died at **Via Prof. Zagari** at **18:15 on 8 February 1932**, a **pescatore**, **«vedovo di Costa Generosa»** — a widower of fifteen years and eight months. Both parents and the wife match the archive exactly. **One tension recorded rather than smoothed:** the act says *settantuno*, seventy-one, which would put his birth before February 1861 — but his birth act is Nati 1861 **atto 228**, late in the year, and the 1900 US census says September 1861, making him seventy. **The birth act wins**; a death-act age is what two elderly neighbours told the registrar. **Still to read:** Giovanni Arena 1936 (`an_ud16600296`), Michele Donato 1936 (`an_ud16600302`). **ALL FOUR READ, 16 September.** Giovanni Arena died at **Via Grotte 72** on 31 March 1936, a **marinaio**, aged eighty-one — exact against his birth of 30 April 1854 — **«marito di Russo Concetta»**, so his wife outlived him. Michele Donato died at **Via Grotte 66** on 10 May 1936, also a **marinaio**, aged **eighty**. **That is a correction:** the tree has Michele born in 1851, which would make him eighty-five here and fifty-seven on the 1908 New Orleans manifest that calls him fifty-two. **Both records point at 1855–56 and the tree is five years out.** **And the four acts together produced something none of them says alone:** Giovanni Arena at Via Grotte 72, Michele Donato at Via Grotte 66, Fortunato Arena born at 70, Giuseppe Arena at 75, Maria Donato at 21, Giovanni Polistena at 47. **Three of the four Scilla quarters lived on one street** — which is how they kept marrying each other, and it was sitting in the archive unnoticed.

rows.what: Serafina Arena's death act, 1912 — does it record that she was born in America?
rows.note: **A small question with a large answer if it goes the right way.** She was baptised at Our Lady of Loretto, Manhattan, on 15 August 1898 and died at Scilla on 15 August 1912. **If the Scilla act names her birthplace as New York, that is the return migration written down in an Italian register** — the only document here that would state it outright rather than by inference from three absences. If it simply says Scilla, that is worth knowing too, because the index's «Nascita: Scilla» field may be a default rather than a claim. **ANSWERED 17 SEPTEMBER, and the answer is that it is a different child.** The act says «di **mesi tre**, residente in Scilla, **nata in questo Comune**» — **three months old and born at Scilla**. **So this archive's row about her was wrong and is retracted.** The Serafina baptised at Our Lady of Loretto on 15 August 1898 did not die on her fourteenth birthday; the matching dates were a coincidence and I built on it. **What the act found instead is a child nobody here knew of:** Rocco Arena and Generosa Costa had a **second Serafina**, born at Scilla about May 1912 in the **Quartiere Chianalea**, dead at three months — the name given again fourteen years after the first, exactly as they did with their two sons named Antonio. **And it answers the row's real question better than a birthplace line would have:** the household was at Scilla and *still having children* in 1912. That is the return from America seen from the inside. **The New York Serafina has no known fate again.**

rows.what: Domenico and Anna Arlotta died two days apart — read both acts
rows.note: **14 and 16 March 1915, brother and sister, both children of Giovanni Arlotta and Maria Costa.** Two deaths in one family in one week is not ordinary and the acts will say why: an epidemic, a fire, or a boat. **Scilla is a fishing town** and the sea takes siblings together. Whatever the cause, both acts carry ages, which would date Serafina Arlotta's siblings and bracket the marriage [row 39](/worklist/) wants. **DONE 17 SEPTEMBER, and the row's premise was wrong.** Both acts are read. **Neither gives a cause** — Italian civil death acts do not record one. **And the arithmetic removes the mystery:** Scilla registered about **125 deaths in 1915**, one every three days, so *two deaths in a week is the ordinary rate*. A third, **Arena Filippo on 17 March**, makes three in four days and means nothing either. I called it «not ordinary» and it was. **What the acts do give is better than a cause.** Both name **«da fu Giovanni e da fu Costa Maria»**, so the sibling link — and the whole cousin chain resting on it — now stands on the **acts** rather than an index line. Their ages date them: **Anna about 1835, Domenico about 1842**, against Serafina's documented 13 June 1830. Domenico was a **marinaro**, husband of Maria Pontillo; Anna a **casalinga**, wife of Antonino Costa. **And the address is the real find:** both died in **CHIANALEA**, the fishing quarter — where Rocco Arena and Generosa Costa's infant daughter had died three years before. An eighty-year-old and her brother of seventy-three, same quarter, two days apart, is most simply one household and one illness. **The register will not say so and neither will this archive.**

rows.what: Settle whether Rocco Arena married his first cousin — one act
rows.note: **[Row 118](/worklist/) grades it *probable*; this is the act that would make it *certain*.** Either **Anna Arlotta's death act of 16 March 1915**, which gives her age and parents in full, or **Generosa Costa's own birth act**, which would name her mother with a patronymic. **Both are inside the surviving run.** What is being ruled out is a second Anna Arlotta married to a second Antonino Costa — unlikely, and *unlikely* is not *ruled out*. **SETTLED 16 SEPTEMBER, and not by reading an act — by the Costa side of the index falling into place.** **Four acts now agree and none contradicts.** Anna Arlotta's death of 16 March 1915 names her parents as **Giovanni Arlotta and Maria Costa**, who are Serafina Arlotta's parents, and her husband as **Antonino Costa**. His own death of 1 June 1915 names her back. **Generosa Costa's death of 6 June 1916 names that same couple as her parents.** And the 1888 marriage act gave them in the first place. **[Row 118](/worklist/) is upgraded from *probable* to *certain*.** What would still break it — two different couples named Giovanni Arlotta and Maria Costa at Scilla in the same decades — would have to be pointing four mutually consistent acts at the wrong pair.

rows.what: Francesco Antonio Arena and Serafina Arlotta — both found, in the same house
rows.note: **DONE, 20 SEPTEMBER 2026, AND THEY DIED AT THE SAME ADDRESS.** **FRANCESCO ANTONIO ARENA died 29 August 1901** at seven ten in the morning — *Morti 1901, parte I, atto 96* — a *pescatore* of eighty-two (eighty-one and nine months in fact), son of the late Filippo and the late Domenica Costa, **husband of Serafina Arlotta**. **SERAFINA ARLOTTA died 24 April 1908** at four in the morning — *Morti 1908, parte I, atto 55* — a *filatrice* of seventy-seven (exact), daughter of the late Giovanni Arlotta, *pescatore*, and the late Maria Costa, ***tessitrice***, and **widow of Arena Antonio**. **Both at Via Grotte number two, Scilla**, six years and eight months apart. She kept the house and died in it, with Rocco in America and Giovanni home from it. **Twelve annual indexes read, 1897 to 1908.** 1909 is not on Antenati at all ([row 129](/worklist/)) and did not need to be. **THE CATCH THAT NEARLY HID HER.** The 1908 index enters her as «**Arena** Serafina, fu Giovanni» — her *husband's* surname over her *father's* forename — while the act says **Arlotta**. Eleven A blocks were swept for an Arlotta and she was found only because Arena is also an A. **When sweeping an index for a married woman, read her husband's initial too.** **Six Arena leads came out of the sweep and none is read** — [row 144](/worklist/).

rows.what: The two Scilla death volumes Antenati does not hold — 1888 and 1909 (no longer blocking)
rows.note: **Found by listing the series rather than by failing to find someone in it, which is the better way round.** The Morti run is complete from 1866 to 1943 **except for 1888 and 1909** — and 1909 sits inside the thirteen-year window where Francesco Antonio Arena and Serafina Arlotta must have died. **This is the same shape as the Zambrone gap**: a hole in the digitisation, not necessarily in the record. **The second copy is the route** — these registers were kept in duplicate, one at the comune and one at the Tribunale, and it is the Tribunale copy Antenati filmed. Belongs with [row 9](/worklist/). **AND THE INDEX IS NOT A BACK DOOR INTO THEM, checked 16 September.** The name index lists two acts under **1909**, which looked at first like content from a volume browse cannot reach. It is not: their document arks — `an_ud16595370` and `an_ud16595649` — fall **inside the ark ranges of the 1911 and 1912 volumes**. They are 1909 deaths written into later registers, which is ordinary. **The 1888 and 1909 volumes are genuinely absent** and the second copy remains the only route. **THE URGENCY IS GONE, 20 SEPTEMBER.** This row mattered because 1909 sat inside the window in which Francesco Antonio Arena and Serafina Arlotta had to have died. **They did not die in it.** He died **29 August 1901** and she **24 April 1908**, both found in volumes Antenati does hold ([row 128](/worklist/)). The two holes are still real and still worth recording as holes — 1888 is the year of Rocco Arena's own marriage, so a death in his household that autumn would be unreachable — but nothing this archive is currently looking for is behind either of them. **Downgraded from a blocker to a note about the digitisation.**

rows.what: List the Scilla death series BEFORE 1866 — rows 68 and 85 cannot start without it
rows.note: **`scilla-arks.tsv` holds 55 Nati and 54 Matrimoni volumes for 1816–1865 and NOT ONE Morti volume.** The restaurazione death series has never been listed, and two rows depend on it entirely: **[row 68](/worklist/)**, Filippo Arena and Domenica Costa, who died most likely in the 1850s–70s, and **[row 85](/worklist/)**, Domenico Arlotta, dead before April 1854. **One page load does it** — the same `s_size=100` trick that returned all 81 post-1866 volumes this afternoon. **Do it before either row is attempted**, for the reason [row 17](/worklist/) gives about mapping before sweeping. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER: 51 volumes, 1817–1865, in one page load**, now in `scilla-arks.tsv`. **The deaths begin in 1817, a year after the births** — so anyone reasoning «Scilla's civil registration begins in 1816» about a *death* is reasoning one year wrong. 1846 and 1854 are doubled. **The reusable part is the series id:** `serie=2002440` carries all three act types for the restaurazione period and is filtered by `tipologia=`, exactly as `16594786` does for the italiano period.

rows.what: Orazio Arena's second wife is not in the index — the marriage act is the only route
rows.note: **A whole second marriage, found as a by-product.** The Scilla death index gives Orazio Arena four children by **Giovanna Zirilli** — Teresa (d. 1913), Giuseppe (d. 1922), Maria Annunziata (d. 1933) and Alessandro Antonio (d. 1936) — and a fifth, **DOMENICO ARENA (d. 30 December 1923), whose mother is MARIANTONIA MUSOLINO**. **Musolino is a name this archive has never held.** Either Orazio married twice or there are two Orazio Arenas at Scilla — and this archive already knows this man had *two sons both named Domenico*, which is exactly the situation where a second wife gets overlooked. The marriage act would settle it. **CHECKED 20 SEPTEMBER, AND SHE IS NOT THERE.** The name index holds **seven Musolino records at Scilla in total**, of which two are the deceased — Domenico Musolino (d. 17 April 1911, son of Bruno Musolino and Grazia Longordo) and Francesca Musolino (d. 7 November 1928). **Neither is Mariantonia.** She exists in the index only as a name inside her son Domenico Arena's act of 1923. So she died outside 1911–1943, or away from Scilla, and **the index route is closed**. What is left is **Orazio Arena's second marriage act** — Scilla's civil marriages 1866–1913 are all on Antenati, his first wife Giovanna Zirilli bore children to 1860, and Domenico Arena (d. 1923) is the only known child of the second marriage, so the wedding sits somewhere after 1866. The annual marriage indexes are one A-block read apiece.

rows.what: The two Antonio Arenas — the guard is written
rows.note: **A collision to guard before it does damage, in the spirit of [row 97](/worklist/).** This family's **FRANCESCO ANTONIO ARENA** married **SERAFINA ARLOTTA**, and the index renders him simply «Antonio» on his sons' death acts. **But the same index holds an ANTONIO ARENA married to a SERAFINA DE LUCA** — parents of Grazia (d. 1913), Anna (d. 1917) and Annunziata (d. 1919). **Same given name, same wife's given name, same town, same decades.** Anyone sweeping «Antonio Arena + Serafina» will merge two families. **The mother's surname is the discriminator and it must be checked every time** — which is exactly how two Arena namesakes were excluded in New York this week. **WRITTEN, 20 SEPTEMBER.** `corrections.tsv` now carries the separation, graded **certain**. It names the discriminator — **Arlotta or De Luca, read every time, never inferred** — and it records that **this archive has already sprung this trap once**: the Orazio Arena who died at Scilla in August 1895 was taken for the tree's Orazio, the supposed father of Rocco. He is the son of **Antonio Arena and Serafina *De Luca***, a different household entirely. The second family is now fully drawn from the index: three more children, **Grazia** (d. 14 February 1913), **Anna** (d. 8 March 1917, wife of Rocco Paladino) and **Annunziata** (d. 12 April 1919). **And the collision is worse than the row knew**, because the whole Arena surname at Scilla resolves into **at least seven households** — see the map filed under the name index. Antonio × Serafina is one collision in a field of them. **AND NOW IT IS A DOCUMENT, NOT A GUARD.** The **1828 annual marriage Tavola** names all four parents: **«Arena Antonio e De Luca Serafina — Orazio e Morabito Letteria / Filippo e Alfonzetti Anna — 10 Ag.o 1828 — atto 26»**. So the other Antonio Arena married his Serafina in **August 1828** and was the son of **Orazio Arena and Letteria Morabito**, while this archive's Francesco Antonio married his in **February 1851** as the son of **Filippo Arena and Domenica Costa**. Different decade, different parents, different wife's family. **And it explains the name that caused the trouble:** their son Orazio, who died at Scilla in 1895 and was once taken for the tree's Orazio, is named for **his own grandfather** — the custom working exactly as predicted.

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE ETNEO — is it name-indexed? The Crupi are from there too
rows.note: **The NAA card gave Mario Crupi's birth as 28 November 1905 at Piedimonte, province of Catania — the Mazza's own town.** So the Crupi and the Mazza came from one village, and **Angela Crupi's birth of 20 December 1900** with her parents **Francesco Crupi and Maria Vecchio** should be reachable in the registers the Mazza line already uses. **First test whether Piedimonte Etneo is in the name index at all** — if it is, two birth acts and a set of parents come back for two queries. If it is not, the acts are still there to be read by volume, **with exact dates in hand**, which is the cheapest register work there is. **ANSWERED 16 SEPTEMBER: Piedimonte Etneo is NOT name-indexed.** «Nessun risultato trovato» on a locality-only query. **Angela Crupi's birth of 20 December 1900 and Mario Crupi's of 28 November 1905 are not reachable this way** — but the NAA card gave both dates to the day, so the volume read is as cheap as a register read ever gets: a known comune, a known year, a known date.

rows.what: Are Briatico, Zambrone and Pizzo name-indexed?
rows.note: **The Calabrian half of this family has been worked entirely by volume-reading, and it may not have needed to be.** Scilla turned out to be name-indexed for deaths 1910–1943; nobody has checked whether **Briatico**, **Zambrone**, **Pizzo** or **San Costantino** are. **If any is, several open rows collapse into queries** — [row 84](/worklist/) (Caterina Cichello's death), [row 44](/worklist/) (the Melluso), [row 66](/worklist/) (Maria Fragalà's death at Pizzo). **One paced fetch per comune answers it.** Do it before any further Calabrian volume sweep. **ANSWERED 16 SEPTEMBER, and mostly no.** **Briatico, Zambrone, San Costantino Calabro and Potenzoni are NOT indexed** — all four return «Nessun risultato trovato». **Pizzo IS**, but for **births**, about 5,900 of them across 1868–1903 — and it holds **no Prostamo**, which is expected since the family was at Briatico by then. **So [row 84](/worklist/), [row 44](/worklist/) and [row 66](/worklist/) all stay volume reads.** **The important by-product:** Pizzo being indexed for *births* while Scilla is indexed for *deaths* proves the act type varies by comune, so «deaths only» was never an Antenati fact.

rows.what: Build the name-index coverage map: comune × act type × years
rows.note: **The same argument as [row 17](/worklist/), one level up, and it will pay better.** Row 17 wants to know which Scilla volumes carry an annual index; **this wants to know which comuni and which years Antenati has indexed by name at all** — because where it has, the volume index does not matter. **Today's work was done blind**: the coverage was discovered by querying four surnames and noticing every hit was a death between 1910 and 1943. **One table, built once**, and every later question becomes «is it indexed» before «which volume». **FIRST PASS DONE 16 SEPTEMBER — the eight comuni this family touches.** **Indexed:** Scilla (deaths, 1911–1943), Pizzo (**births**, 1868–1903), Catania (deaths, 1911+). **Not indexed:** Piedimonte Etneo, Briatico, Zambrone, San Costantino Calabro, Potenzoni. **Two rules fall out of it.** The **act type varies by comune** — assuming Scilla's «deaths only» held everywhere would have been wrong at Pizzo. And **`localita=` does not mean «registered here»**: it matches any place attached to the person, and `localita=Catania` returns people who died at **Vicopisano in Tuscany**. It read cleanly at Scilla only because those people were born and died in one town. **Still to do:** turn this into the actual table, and extend it past this family's comuni if the estate wants it. **FOLDED INTO THE HOLDINGS TABLE, 21 SEPTEMBER.** The name-index map is published beside the volume holdings on [What Has Been Read](/searched/), because the two questions are one question asked at different heights and a reader should not have to hold both pages open. Indexed: **Scilla deaths 1911–1943, Pizzo BIRTHS 1868–1903, Catania deaths 1911 onward**. Not indexed: Piedimonte Etneo, Briatico, Zambrone, San Costantino Calabro, Potenzoni. **The act type differs between comuni and that is the trap** — assuming Scilla's «deaths only» held everywhere would have been wrong at Pizzo, where it is births.

rows.what: The Loveday records — Mario Crupi's internment, from the camp's own side
rows.note: **His aliens card says «18.8.42 LOVEDAY INTERNMENT CAMP / 30/12/43 Released and entrained for Brisbane» and that is all it says.** The NAA holds the camp's own series — nominal rolls, internee service and casualty forms, and the objection and appeal files that record **why** a man was interned. **The why is the part worth having**: north Queensland Italians were interned on the word of neighbours, and the files carry the allegation and sometimes the appeal. **Rosario Mazza's dossier (MP1103/1 Q8110) should be worked the same way**, and [row 7](/worklist/)'s Trove search now has two names and two dates to search on. **DONE 16 SEPTEMBER, and the «why» turned out to be a different question than expected.** His **service and casualty form (MP1103/1, Q30124) is digitised** and gives the whole arc on one sheet: **taken at his own address, Bemerside, Ingham, on 20 April 1942**; Gaythorne, then **Cowra on 5 May**, then **Loveday on 17 August 1942**; a **tribunal in January 1943**; **released 29 December 1943** — twenty months. **And the record that makes it bite is the other one.** NAA **A714, 9/4300**: he was **naturalised on 26 April 1940**, two months before Italy entered the war. **It did not protect him** — the casualty form still records his nationality as «Italian (Nat.)». **It also proved something this archive had refused to claim.** The 1959 roll put a Mario and a Maria Crupi at Tully with **both address columns blank**, and I declined to pair them on adjacency. The next-of-kin line pairs them properly: *«Maria CRUPI … Relationship: Wife»*. **And it dates the marriage** — he is *Single* in April 1940 and married by April 1942. **Five files remain unopened**: BP242/1 Q25743 (his Queensland investigation case file, which is where an allegation would be), A435 1946/4/2800, D1901 C594, MP1103/2 Q30124 and J25 1955/16646.

rows.what: Camillo Antonio Polistena — born 21 September 1844, found
rows.note: **[Row 96](/worklist/) closed on his death act, which gave his parents. His birth act would give the arithmetic a check and the parents a second witness.** Scilla's births begin in 1816, so a birth about 1835 is inside the run. **What makes it worth doing now rather than before:** we know the parents to look for — **Giuseppe Polistena and Anna Pontillo** — so the read is a confirmation with a known answer, which is the kind that catches a wrong identification. **His age at death in 1924 will narrow the year first**, which is [row 124](/worklist/). **THREE YEARS READ ACROSS, 20 SEPTEMBER, AND HE IS IN NONE OF THEM.** His son's 1883 birth act makes him forty-eight, so about 1835; the complete **P section** of the annual Tavola was read for **1834, 1835 and 1836** — **629 births** — and there is **no Camillo Antonio Polistena**. **The shape of the absence is the finding.** Those 629 births hold **exactly one Polistena**. The P section at Scilla in the 1830s is Paladino, Pirrotta, Patafio, Papalia, Pizzarello. **The Polistena are barely there**, which may be why this quarter stops where it does — and *Polistena* is itself a comune in the province of Reggio Calabria. **The one entry is a lead with a flaw.** Entry 191 of 1836: *«**Polistina Annunziata, di Giuseppe e Martello Anna**, 2 Dicembre»*. Right given names for his parents, **wrong surname for the mother** — the death act says **Anna Pontillo**. And four entries earlier stands *«Pontillo Giovanni, di Giuseppe e Paladino Giuseppa»*: a clerk copying that column had both surnames under his hand. **Act 191 of 1836 settles it and is three images away.** **Then widen.** A declared age is a range, and this archive has already been burned reading three points inside a window as a search of the window. **1830–1833 and 1837–1840** are next; the containers are not bought. **THE LEAD WAS OPENED THE SAME HOUR AND IT PAID.** The act is **204**, not 191: that Tavola's *«Num. d'ordine»* is an **index row** and the index **carries no act number at all** — act 191 is a Squillaci birth at Solano. The acts run in date order, so the **birth date** is the only key, and two probes found it. **Scilla, atto 204 of 1836.** On **2 December 1836** the midwife **Teresa Arena**, forty-four, declared a girl born that morning at eight, in her parents' own house, to **ANNA PONTILLO, thirty-five**, lawful wife of **GIUSEPPE POLISTINA, thirty-eight, *marinaro*** — and named **Annunziata Polistina**. **So the index was the liar and the death act was right.** The mother is **Pontillo**, not Martello, and **Annunziata is Camillo Antonio's sister** — the first sibling he has ever had in this archive. The guess about *why* the index erred held too: four entries earlier in the same P section stands *«Pontillo Giovanni, di Giuseppe e Paladino Giuseppa»*. **And the Polistena quarter gets its first two dates.** Giuseppe Polistena born about **1798**, a **marinaro** — a third Scilla sailing family beside the Arena and the Arlotta — and Anna Pontillo about **1801**. **Camillo Antonio's own birth is still not found.** With his parents dated, a son born about 1835 fits them exactly; the years still to read are **1830–1833 and 1837–1840**. **SIX CONSECUTIVE YEARS NOW, 1833–1838, AND HE IS IN NONE OF THEM.** The complete P section of every annual Tavola. **But his parents are in two.** **Rocco Polistina, 13 December 1833** — *«Giuseppe e Pontillo Anna»*, the index spelling her correctly this time — and **Annunziata Polistina, 2 December 1836**. **The three years between hold no Polistena birth at all**, and they are not thin years: 201, 206 and 222 births. **A child born to this couple about 1835 is simply not there.** **So «forty-eight» in September 1883 is out by at least two years**, and he was born **before 1833 or after 1838**. The search moves to **1830–1832** and **1839–1840**, and it should not stop at the first year that fits. **One thing to carry:** the 1837 Tavola has *«Pirrotta Salvatore — Rocco, e **Polistina Annunziata**»* — an **adult** Annunziata Polistina bearing children two months after the infant one was born. The baby was very likely named for her, and she is a relative this archive has not identified. **1839 ADDED: SEVEN CONSECUTIVE YEARS NOW, AND A SECOND POLISTENA HOUSEHOLD.** Entry 153 of 1839 is *«**Polistina Maria — Francesco e Longardo Giuseppa** — 30 Maggio»* — **not** Giuseppe and Anna Pontillo, so not a sibling. **Seven years, about 1,450 births, four Polistena in total:** Rocco (1833) and Annunziata (1836) to this archive's couple, Maria (1839) to the other, and nothing else. **With a surname that scarce the temptation to join any two bearers is strong and must be resisted — the discriminator is the mother.** Guard written. **What is left:** **1830, 1831, 1832** and **1840 onward**. Containers bought for 1832, 1840 and 1839; 1830 and 1831 are not. **The naming custom argues he is older, not younger:** Rocco is the eldest son found and under Calabrian custom the first son takes the father's father's name, which would make **Rocco Polistena** the grandfather — leaving *Camillo Antonio* as a second son named for the **mother's** father, i.e. a **Camillo Pontillo**. That reading puts him after December 1833, which the register denies. **So either the custom is not being followed here, or he is the elder and 1830–1832 is where he is.** **1832 ADDED: EIGHT CONSECUTIVE YEARS, 1832–1839.** Entry 152 of 1832 is *«Polistina Domenica — **Francesco e Longordo Giuseppa** — 17 Dicembre»* — the other household again. **Eight years, about 1,630 births, five Polistena in total:** Domenica (1832) and Maria (1839) to Francesco and Giuseppa Longordo; **Rocco (1833)** and **Annunziata (1836)** to Giuseppe and Anna Pontillo. **Two households running in parallel, and between them they account for every Polistena birth in eight years.** Camillo Antonio is not one of them. **So he was born in 1830 or 1831, or in 1840 or later**, and «forty-eight» in September 1883 is out by at least three years. **Containers bought:** 1832, 1839, 1840. **Not bought:** 1830, 1831. **Take 1840 first** — it is in hand and costs nothing but images. **FINISHED THE WINDOW: ELEVEN CONSECUTIVE YEARS, 1830–1840, AND HE IS IN NONE OF THEM.** **1840 gives a third sibling** — *«Polistina **Fortunata**, di Giuseppe e **Pontillo** Anna, 28 Gennaro»*. So this archive's couple have **Rocco (Dec 1833), Annunziata (Dec 1836) and Fortunata (Jan 1840)** — **three years apart, twice** — with **1830, 1831, 1832, 1834, 1835, 1837, 1838 and 1839 all read and empty of them**. **So Rocco is the eldest and Camillo Antonio cannot be earlier. He must be 1841 or later**, and «forty-eight» in September 1883 is wrong by **at least six years**. **The naming custom agrees:** a first son takes the father's father's name — making Giuseppe's father a **Rocco Polistena** — and a later son the mother's father's, which would make **Camillo Antonio** the namesake of a **Camillo Pontillo**. Both point forward. **The eleven years also map the surname.** Eight Polistena births in about 2,100 children, across **three households**: Giuseppe × Anna Pontillo, Francesco × Giuseppa Longardo, and **Luigi × Marianna Baviera — whose son born 21 June 1831 is called *Francesco Antonio Polistina***, one word from our man, right town, right decade, different parents. Guard written. **Next: 1841–1848.** Anna Pontillo was about thirty-five in 1836 and could bear to about 1846. **No container for any of those years is bought.** **THE NEW WINDOW IS STARTED: 1841 AND 1842 ARE CLEAR.** 1841 holds **no Polistena at all**; 1842 holds one, *«Polistina Salvadore, di Domenico e Costa Caterina»* — **a fourth household**. **1843 is a doubled year and the index is in the other ark.** `an_ua2002874` holds the acts and closes at act 200 with no Tavola; `an_ua2002877` is where the *indice* will be — the same split this archive met in 1852 and 1875. Its container lookup returned **403**, caught by the control test and recorded as a block. **AND THE METHOD ITSELF HAS A HOLE IN IT.** Entry 160 of 1841 reads *«**Palmisano** Gio. Battista — **Giuseppe e Anna Pontillo** — 26 Agosto»*. A Giuseppe married to an Anna Pontillo, right town, right decade, **wrong surname**. The way these Tavole are being read is by scanning the *parents* column for «Giuseppe e Pontillo Anna» — which walks straight into this entry, because what separates them is the **child's surname**, the column a parent-scan skips. Guard written. **Still to read:** 1843 (needs the second ark), 1844–1848. **AND ROCCO POLISTINA'S ACT IS READ — atto 174 of 1833.** It confirms the parents from a second independent document (**Giuseppe thirty-four, *marinaro*; Anna thirty-three**, against thirty-eight and thirty-five in 1836 — both landing on Giuseppe b. 1798–99 and Anna b. 1800–01), and it shows **the same midwife, Teresa Arena**, delivered both children. **Its margin carries a marriage added thirty-six years later:** *«L'anno 1869, il giorno 12 Luglio … ha contratto matrimonio in questo Comune con **Colorina Bri[…]**»*. **Rocco lived to thirty-five and married at Scilla on 12 July 1869.** **That opens [row 154](/worklist/)** — these acts annotate themselves, and nobody here has been reading the margins. **1843, 1844 AND 1845 ADDED — SIXTEEN CONSECUTIVE YEARS NOW, 1830 TO 1845.** 1843: no Polistina child (one as a *mother*, the third sighting of the adult Annunziata). 1844: two Polistina, both from the **other** households — Domenico × Costa Carolina, Francesco × Longordo Giuseppa. 1845: **partial** — seven of eighteen lines in the P block are too faint to read, and that is recorded as partial rather than as a negative. **The family's shape is now fixed.** Giuseppe Polistena and Anna Pontillo have children in **December 1833, December 1836 and January 1840** — and in the twelve other years read, nothing. Anna was about thirty-five in 1836, so her childbearing plausibly ends around 1840–42, which is exactly what the register shows. **Which leaves a contradiction worth stating rather than smoothing.** His 1924 death act names these two as his parents; his son's 1883 act makes him forty-eight. **There is no year in their childbearing window where he fits, and the window has been read across.** Four readings, none preferred: he was born elsewhere and the family came in; the death act's parents are wrong; the Tavola omitted him (these indexes *do* drop entries); or he is a child already found under a name nobody has connected. **The test that separates them is [row 155](/worklist/).** **THE SEARCH WAS AIMED AT THE WRONG DECADE, AND HIS MARRIAGE ACT SAYS SO** ([row 155](/worklist/)). He was **thirty-six on 23 January 1881**, so **born about 1844** — not 1835. Eleven years of Tavole were read around a figure that was nine years out. **He was born at Scilla**, on his own sworn word, so the act exists. **And 1844 and 1845 are both already in hand and both incompletely read:** 1844's P block was covered for entries 127–138 without establishing where it ends, and **1845 is recorded as partial** with seven of eighteen lines too faint. **Go back to those two years first.** **FOUND. 1844 TAVOLA, ENTRY 142: «Polistina Camillo — Giuseppe e Pontillo Anna — 21 Settembre».** **Born at Scilla on 21 September 1844.** **The arithmetic is exact, which is what makes it safe.** Thirty-six years and four months at his marriage on 23 January 1881 — the act says *trentasei*. Thirty-eight years and eleven months at his son's birth on 16 September 1883 — that act says **forty-eight**, ten years wrong, and it is the figure this row searched around. **And the reason it took sixteen years of sweeping is mine.** The 1844 P block was read **earlier the same day**; the crop covered entries 127–138 and stopped, and this row was written saying the end of the block had not been established. **He is four entries past where I stopped.** Instead of one more crop on the year already open, I swept 1845, 1830–1832 and five marriage years. **The rule it buys:** *a partial reading recorded as a negative is the same error as a 403 recorded as a nil.* Where a section is read, **find its end** — the next section letter — before writing «not there». **1845 is still marked partial** and should be finished on the same principle. **A fifth Polistena household came with it:** entry 143 is *«Polistina Tommaso — **D.** Antonio e Paladino Annunziata»*, the *D.* being **Don**. **Next, and cheap:** the act itself — [row 156](/worklist/).

rows.what: Donato–Polistena — four ties, and the first one now has a date
rows.note: **The index turned up a second one and the archive only knew the first.** [Row 71](/worklist/) is about **Nunziata Donato × Giovanni Polistena**, about 1916. But the Scilla deaths also give **MARIA DONATO (d. 3 April 1911), «Padre Candeloro Donato, Madre Domenica Romano, Coniuge GIUSEPPE POLISTINA»** — a Donato woman married to a Polistena man a generation earlier. **Her father is a Candeloro Donato**, which is the name of both this archive's wall and Domenico Donato's son of 1847. **Two families that intermarried twice are usually close to begin with**, and the earlier act would say how. **MORE THAN TWO, CHECKED 20 SEPTEMBER.** Writing the Polistena and Donato index sets out in full turns two ties into **four**: **(1)** Maria Donato, d. 3 April 1911, «Padre Candeloro Donato, Madre Domenica Romano, Coniuge **Giuseppe Polistina**» — the one this row was written for. **(2)** **Raffaele Polistena × Teresa Donato**, whose three children all die at Scilla — Santa (12 July 1926, wife of Rocco Catalano), Maria (19 July 1927, wife of Camillo Matia) and Luigi (8 December 1933, husband of Annunziata Matrà). **(3)** **Giovanni Polistena × Annunziata Donato**, whose daughter Teresa dies 5 January 1933. **(4)** Nunziata Donato × Giovanni Polistena, about 1916 — [row 71](/worklist/). **And a fifth pattern worth naming:** Rocco Polistena, d. 7 August 1923, is the husband of a **Nunziata Polistena** — a Polistena married to a Polistena, the same surname endogamy this archive has already met among the Bueti and the Vizzari. **Two families that intermarry four times in two generations are one neighbourhood**, and the Romano are in it too: Maria Donato's mother is a **Domenica Romano**, and Giovanna Romano's sister Concetta married a **Rocco Donato**. **SIX, NOT FOUR — 20 SEPTEMBER.** The National Archives adds two more, in **Queensland**: **NAA J25 1967/9873**, *«Polistena, Giuseppe; wife **Maria Maddalena [nee Donato]**»*, and **NAA J25 1970/3023**, *«**Donato, Concetta [nee Polistena]**»*. **Two families that intermarry six times over two generations and two hemispheres are not two families who happened to meet.** They were one neighbourhood at Scilla — **Via Grotte** — and they were still one neighbourhood in Brisbane. **ONE OF THEM IS DATED, 20 SEPTEMBER.** **Scilla, Matrimoni 1882, atto 48: LUIGI CARMELO POLISTINA × ANNUNZIATA MATRÀ, 23 November 1882** — and he is *«figlio di **Raffaele** e di **Teresa Donato**»*, matching the name index's *«Luigi Polistena, d. 8 December 1933 — Padre Raffaele, Madre Teresa Donato, Coniuge Annunziata Matrà»* across fifty-one years. **Note which generation it dates.** Teresa Donato is the **mother** here, so the Donato–Polistena join in this line happened a generation **earlier** than this row had it — **Raffaele Polistena × Teresa Donato, before about 1852**, is now a named target. And both of them were **alive in November 1882**, which is the first date either has ever had.

rows.what: The two Generosa Costas — the guard is written
rows.note: **Rocco Arena's wife was Generosa Costa. So was Pasquale Donato's.** The death index gives **PASQUALE DONATO (d. 20 April 1937), «Padre Domenico, Madre Annunziata Sofi, Coniuge GENEROSA COSTA»** — and Pasquale is Michele Donato's brother, so this is inside the family, not a stranger who happens to share a name. **That is exactly the circumstance in which two women become one in a tree.** They are almost certainly different: Rocco's Generosa was born about 1868 and married in 1888. **Write the distinction down now**, while it is obvious, rather than discovering the merge later. **WRITTEN, 20 SEPTEMBER.** `corrections.tsv` now carries the separation explicitly, against `generosa-costa`, and it is graded **certain** rather than inferred, because the two women are separated by evidence and not by assumption: **Rocco's Generosa was already dead on 6 June 1916**, twenty-one years before the other's husband died in 1937, and their parents differ — Antonino Costa and Anna Arlotta for the first, unknown for the second. **A third Generosa sits a generation above them**: GENEROSA POLISTENA, Antonino Costa's mother, for whom Rocco's wife was almost certainly named. Three women of one name in three generations of one town, and the guard names all three.

rows.what: Tell the estate that Antenati has a name index
rows.note: **This is not a Mazza finding, it is an estate finding, and the other archives are working Italian registers too.** `/search-nominative/?cognome=X&localita=Y&s_size=100` returns acts with **father, mother and spouse** already extracted, and for Scilla it covers deaths 1910–1943. **Falco and Defranceschi have been reading volumes the same way this archive has.** Worth a note carrying the query form, the `localita=` caution — `fq=` and `facets=` are **silently ignored** and return the unfiltered count — and the parsing rule that **only rows with a `p.morte` value are the deceased**; the rest are relatives seen from inside someone else's act, and reading them as deaths invents people. **SENT, 21 SEPTEMBER**, to the landing site for circulation, with the query form and all three cautions — and with the one this row did not have: **the act type differs by comune.** Scilla is indexed for **deaths** 1911–1943 and **Pizzo for BIRTHS 1868–1903**, so an archive carrying «deaths only» across from one to the other would produce a confident negative on a series that is indexed the other way round. Five of the eight comuni this family touches are not indexed at all, so the annual Tavola remains the instrument for those — and that is written up on [/method/](/method/) beside it. **AND THE FORM WAS TESTED BEFORE IT WAS ALLOWED TO STAND.** The Booyzen session's rule, arriving the same hour: *«a method note is code, and an untested method note is untested code»* — they had recorded archive.org identifiers with a suffix that does not exist and every id in their own note returned nothing. This archive had just sent a query string to three other archives. **It was re-run: it works**, and the `p.morte` caution is now confirmed **by example** rather than asserted — the index returns *«Rocco Arena — Figlio Serafina Arena — Atto di morte 15 Agosto 1912»* beside *«Serafina Arena — Morte: Scilla 15/08/1912 — Padre Rocco Arena»*. The dead child is Serafina. Reading the first row as a death would have killed Rocco Arena twenty years early, with a plausible date.

rows.what: The two Queensland investigation case files — why these men were interned
rows.note: **The casualty form says what happened to Mario Crupi. These files would say why.** **NAA: BP242/1, Q25743** — «Crupi, Mario — Queensland investigation case file», 1942–1948, **Brisbane, Box 152**. And **NAA: BP242/1, Q21227** — the same series for **Rosario Mazza**, 1940–1948. **Both are Access status OPEN**, so neither needs an access examination — unlike [row 115](/worklist/). They are simply **paper, in Brisbane, undigitised**, and someone has to ask for them. **Why they matter more than the camp records.** North Queensland Italians were interned largely on the word of neighbours and informants, and it is the investigation file that carries **the allegation, the evidence offered for it, and sometimes the appeal**. Mario Crupi had been **naturalised since April 1940** and was taken anyway; this is the file that would say on what grounds. **Michael is in Brisbane, where both files are.** A reading-room visit would open both in an afternoon, or the NAA will quote for copies.

rows.what: The spine still calls Antonino Prostamo untested, and additions.json says he is proved
rows.note:
Two files in this repo disagree about the same man. **`spine.json` gen 6, `antonino-prostamo-1785`, is drawn on /direct-line/ as a joint that will not bear weight** — one of the four above 1785 said to rest on the family tree alone. **`additions.json` says the opposite**: «The fourth generation, carried as UNTESTED until 14 September 2026 and now documented four times over. A MARINARO like his father and his son.» It gives a source (Briatico, Matrimoni 1849, atto 1 — Antenati an_ua87663), a trade, and a death: 31 December 1837 at Pizzo, in the cholera, at two in the morning on the last night of the year. It also carries `inTree: antonino-prostamo-1785`, so the two files certainly mean one man. 

**Which is right is this archive's to say, not mine.** Raised because it travels: Our-Family reads this spine to decide what a child is told, and it currently tells them that generation is only what the family says. If the spine is the stale one, the children's page is repeating a caution the archive has already retired — and the 1697 line is one generation shorter in doubt than it looks.

**ANSWERED 17 SEPTEMBER, and the spine was not the stale one — the person page was.** **`spine.json` is right to show what it shows.** It is built from Michael's export, and this archive's standing rule is that [the charts draw the export as given](/corrections/) because the corrections are proposals, not edits. So the two files are *meant* to differ. **What was wrong is that the difference never reached the man.** `build_person_extras.py` gathered a person's records from four places — Nudgee, the NAA index, the tree's own citations and `read-people.tsv` — and from nowhere else. **It never read `documented-additions.tsv` or `corrections.tsv`**, which is where most of this archive's evidence lives. So Antonino Prostamo's page carried the sentence *«No record has been read for this person. What is known of them is what the tree asserts, and it is unverified»* — about a man documented four times over. **Twelve people were in that position**, including Giovanna Pontillo, whose surname six records settled yesterday, and Salvatore Mazza, Sebastiano's own father. **Fixed:** both files are now read, keyed the way each keys a person — additions by `inTree`, corrections by `slug`. Citations go to `records`, prose to `corrections`, under the heading the page already had for it: *«What a register says about this person, which the tree does not»*, followed by its own statement that the chart above still draws the tree. **Nothing is applied. The archive just stops being silent about it.** **Guarded:** `check_links.py` now refuses the build if a person named in either file has a page carrying neither a record nor a correction. Verified against a reintroduced bug — it exits 1 and names them. **And the caller was right about the reach:** Our-Family reads this spine, so the children's page was repeating a caution this archive had already retired. Raised by the estate, not by us, which is the argument for the landing page existing.

rows.what: The merchant seamen series at Kew — the one thing the UK archives might hold
rows.note: **Raised by David, and the only part of his suggestion that survives testing.** A sweep of The National Archives' Discovery API found **nothing at all** for this family — Prostamo, Polistena, Cichello, Zirilli, Fragalà, Briatico and Piedimonte Etneo all return **zero**, and the handful of Crupi, Arlotta and Melluso hits are provably other people. **That is structural:** this family went Italy→Australia and Italy→New York and never through Britain, and Kew's passenger series (BT 26, BT 27) cover **UK ports only**. **But the seamen series are a different matter.** **BT 372** registry cards and **BT 99** crew agreements record an Italian **place of birth** — the sweep turned up entries reading «place of birth, Napoli» and an Arlotta born at Udine. **And this family is full of mariners:** Giovanni Arena and Michele Donato are both **«marinaio»** on their 1936 acts, Domenico Arlotta on his of 1915, Antonino Prostamo **«marinaro»**, Rocco Arena **«pescatore»**. **If any of them ever signed on a British-registered ship, they are in these series.** **Two cautions before anyone spends a day on it.** Most nineteenth-century crew agreements are **not at Kew at all** — the bulk went to the Maritime History Archive in Newfoundland, and Kew keeps a sample. And a Scilla fisherman working the Strait is a far likelier thing than one signing British articles. **Long shot, cheap to test, and the API makes it a query rather than a trip.**

rows.what: Three Arena leads read and closed; three left
rows.note: **Fallout from [row 128](/worklist/).** Sweeping twelve annual death indexes for two people turned up **six other Arena acts**, each with a patronymic. **Three are read, 20 September, and all three close.** **~~ARENA GIOVANNA, *di Rocco*, 1908 parte II atto 2~~ — NOT ROCCO'S DAUGHTER.** Nine, born at Scilla, dead **at Marseille** 1 February 1905; mother **Francesca Martello**. What it opened instead is [row 145](/worklist/). **~~ARENA NICOLINA, *di Giuseppe*, 1906 atto 41~~ — NOT GIUSEPPE'S DAUGHTER.** She was **forty**, born about 1866, when Rocco's brother Giuseppe was six. Via Grotte 17; mother the late **Marianna Romano**; husband Giuseppe Cesoriero. **~~ARENA COSMO, *di Filippo*, 1904 atto 122~~ — NOT ROCCO'S NEPHEW.** Three months old, Vico San Michele 13, son of Filippo and **Clementina Furfari**. The act gave the father no age, so the plan was to sweep ten years of marriage indexes — **seven of them with no container saved, a rate-limited page load each.** Instead the **Antenati name index**, which carries the spouse, answered in one GET: **Filippo Arena died at Scilla 17 March 1915, «Padre Giovanni Arena, Madre Natalina Longordo, Coniuge Clementina Furfari»**. A different Filippo. **The order of operations is the lesson:** when the question is *whose son was this man*, ask the name index before planning a volume sweep. **The three unread:** Arena Raffaele *fu Giuseppe* (1901, atto 63); Arena Rocco *di Alessandro* (1906, atto 141); Arena Santo *fu Rocco* (1908, atto 108). All three now look like other households — see the seven-household map filed under the name index — so they are **low priority**, kept because a named act should not be silently dropped. **What the three closures cost and bought:** they cost nine image fetches and they bought the question on [row 146](/worklist/).

rows.what: PARTE II — the deaths abroad, in eighty-one volumes nobody here has opened
rows.note: **Found by accident chasing a lead from [row 144](/worklist/), and it is the biggest thing the Scilla death series has left to give.** Every Scilla death volume has a **parte II** at the back, just before the annual index, and **parte II is where deaths abroad are transcribed** — on the order of the *Procuratore del Re* at Reggio Calabria, from certificates issued by foreign authorities, at a family's request. **The 1908 parte II runs to five acts and three of them are foreign:** GULLI ROCCO, 27, a *bracciante*, husband of Lofaro Maria, dead in **NEW YORK** on 17 August 1907 **of a fractured skull** — transcribed from an English-language certificate *with a translation*, at his widow's own request; **ARENA GIOVANNA**, nine, dead at **MARSEILLE**; and CACCIOLA CARMELA, seven, dead at **TUNIS** at ten at night. Three continents in four acts, in a town of a few thousand. **Why it matters here.** Rocco Arena crossed to New York four times between 1892 and 1913 and Giovanni Arena followed him in 1899. This archive has always treated the American end as the American record's problem. **If any Arena, Arlotta, Donato or Polistena died outside Italy and the family asked for it, the act is in a parte II — and it names the foreign city, the date, often the cause, and the parents.** A New York death certificate, in other words, sitting in a Calabrian register. **The sweep is affordable.** Parte II is a few acts per volume, at a fixed position — the last images before the *indice annuale*, which `tools/antenati_index.py sheet` already finds. The annual index lists parte II entries in its own column (*Parte* = 2ª), so the index alone says whether a year has any worth opening. **Eighty-one volumes, 1866–1943, and none read.** **AND [ROW 146](/worklist/) GIVES IT A TARGET.** Three of Rocco Arena's four brothers vanish from Scilla's registers after 1898. Parte II is the first place to look for them.

rows.what: Two of Rocco Arena's brothers vanish after 1898 — the third was a sister
rows.note: **A silence, not a gap — and it took two complete searches to see it.** Francesco Antonio Arena and Serafina Arlotta had five known sons: **Filippo** (b. 14 Feb 1852), **Domenico** (b. 24 Mar 1853), **Giovanni** (b. 30 Apr 1854), **Giuseppe** (b. 5 Mar 1860) and **Rocco** (b. 20 Dec 1861). **Only Rocco and Giovanni die at Scilla.** Rocco on 8 February 1932, Giovanni on 31 March 1936 — both in the Antenati name index with their parents named. **Filippo, Domenico and Giuseppe are in none of it.** Not among the twenty-six indexed Arena deaths of 1910–1943. Not in the A block of any annual index from 1897 to 1908 ([row 128](/worklist/)). Not in 1889–1896 either. **And Giuseppe was certainly still there in June 1898**, burying his own ten-month-old son Francesco Giovanni Rocco at Via Acquagrande 30. Then nothing. **The reading that fits is that they left.** Their brothers Rocco and Giovanni both crossed to New York — Rocco four times from 1892, Giovanni in 1899 to join him — and Giovanni's bride's father, Paolo Martello, was already in America in 1885. Scilla was going before this family went. **Where to look, cheapest first.** **1.** [Row 145](/worklist/) — **parte II** of Scilla's own death volumes, where deaths abroad are transcribed at a family's request. If one of them died in New York and the family asked, the act is there and it names the parents. **2.** The Ellis Island and NARA manifests for a **Filippo, Domenico or Giuseppe Arena of Scilla**, 1892–1914 — the same route that documented Rocco's four crossings and Giovanni's one. **3.** Their **marriages at Scilla**: Giuseppe married Maria Martello in 1885 (atto 73) and Giovanni married Concetta Russo the same autumn (atto 86). **Filippo and Domenico have no marriage in this archive at all**, and a marriage act would give a wife whose own death may be indexed. **The negative that would be worth as much as a finding:** if none of the three is in parte II and none is on a manifest, then they died somewhere that never told Scilla, and the archive should say so plainly rather than leave three men trailing off. **ONE MORE STRAW, 20 SEPTEMBER.** **Filippo Arena's birth act, Nati 1852 atto 48, has a blank margin.** Scilla's birth acts carry marriage annotations for marriages celebrated **in the same comune after 1866** ([row 154](/worklist/)), and any marriage of his falls in that window. **A blank margin does not prove he never married** — it is consistent with a marriage somewhere else, which is precisely what «he left Scilla» predicts. Set beside his absence from the death index 1889–1943 and from the name index of 1910–1943, it is a third silence pointing the same way. **The same test is worth running on Domenico Arena (b. 1853)**, whose act has not been opened in the register at all. **ONE OF THE THREE WAS NEVER A BROTHER, 20 SEPTEMBER.** *«Domenico Arena, b. 24 March 1853»* is **DOMENICA ARENA**, a daughter: act 53 of 1853 says *«una femina»*, *«di dare alla fanciulla il nome di Domenica»*, and the baptism column names **Domenica Arena**. **A married daughter leaves the Arena surname and stops appearing under it, which is not a disappearance at all.** So the row is **two** men, not three: **Filippo** (b. 1852) and **Giuseppe** (b. 1860). **And Filippo's silence got louder.** His birth act's margin is **blank** in a volume where other acts carry marriages written back in 1876, 1881 and 1883 — so **he did not marry at Scilla**. Third silence, same direction. **AND THE MARGIN STRAW IS WITHDRAWN, SAME DAY.** I wrote an hour ago that Filippo Arena's blank margin was evidence he did not marry at Scilla. **Giuseppe Arena's birth act is blank too, and Giuseppe married at Scilla in 1885.** The annotation was simply not always made. **Filippo's blank margin means nothing**, and this row rests where it did: on his absence from the death index 1889–1943 and from the name index of 1910–1943. **RE-TESTED AGAINST A SET NEARLY THREE TIMES LARGER, 21 SEPTEMBER, AND IT HOLDS.** The name index was re-queried in full — not to redo the search but to **test the query form this archive had just broadcast to three other archives**, on the principle that an untested method note is untested code. It works, and it returns **152 rows for Arena at Scilla, about sixty-nine people**, where the earlier sweep saw twenty-six. **Only two carry «Madre Serafina Arlotta»** — Rocco, 8 February 1932, and Giovanni, 31 March 1936. **Neither Filippo nor Giuseppe is anywhere in the sixty-nine.** A negative that survives the set trebling is worth more than the first one was, and it points the same way. **And the pull paid sideways**, which is what a full index read does: **GIUSEPPE ARENA, died 27 March 1925, «Padre Domenico, Madre Teresa Polistena»** — the first evidence that [Filippo's brother Domenico's 1838 marriage](/corrections/) produced anyone, and an independent confirmation of Teresa Polistina eighty-seven years later in a different series. His daughter **Teresa Arena** died there in 1943, named for her grandmother.

rows.what: The 1851 processetti bundle — opened, and it dated two generations
rows.note: **The cheapest unopened thing in this archive.** **Francesco Antonio Arena married Serafina Arlotta at Scilla on 7 February 1851, atto 13.** Antenati holds the *processetti* volume for that window — **1849–1852, `an_ua2002487`** — found by listing Scilla's 466 registers in one page load ([row 64](/worklist/)). **What a processetti fascicolo carries:** the **birth extracts of both spouses**, and the **death acts of any parent already dead**. The Scilla bundle of 1842–1845 carried a dead **grandparent** as well, and the Briatico bundle of 1849 broke the whole Calabrian line open — a cholera death, three generations of descent, a birth act, an *atto di notorietà* and five new names, in twenty minutes after two days of sweeping the wrong comuni. **The four parents it could name, with their death acts attached:** **Filippo Arena** and **Domenica Costa** ([row 68](/worklist/) — otherwise twenty-seven years of unindexed sweep), **Giovanni Arlotta** and **Maria Costa** ([row 39](/worklist/)). And possibly **Domenico Arlotta** ([row 85](/worklist/)), the deepest name on the Scilla side, dead before April 1854. **What it cannot do:** these bundles stop in 1865. The 1885 and 1888 Arena marriages have no processetti on Antenati at all. **Method:** the ark is in `scilla-arks.tsv`; the container costs one rate-limited page load, then manifests and images are free. Bundles are filed **in act order**, so fascicolo 13 of 1851 is found by reading the act numbers on the wrappers rather than by counting images — and the volume spans four years, so find the 1851 block first. **OPENED 20 SEPTEMBER, AND IT PAID.** Container `58rXBoX`, 1845 images; **fascicolo 13 of 1851 begins at image 1190**, wrapper reading *«Volumetto de documenti pel matrimonio di Francesco Arena e Serafina Arlotta — fogli quattro»*. **Foglio 1 is Francesco Antonio Arena's birth act itself**, act 186 of 1819 — the act, where this archive has always cited the Tavola. **Filippo Arena, twenty-five, marinaro** (b. c. 1794) and **Domenica Costa, twenty-seven** (b. c. 1792): two generation-seven people who had no dates at all. Born at twelve o'clock in the family's own house; baptised next day. **And Filippo signed it**, in a register where almost every act ends *«perché illetterati»*. **Foglio 2 is Serafina Arlotta's, and it is act 89, not act 2** — this archive has been citing a Tavola row number in three places. **Maria Costa, twenty-three** (b. c. 1807), her first date of any kind; **Giovanni Arlotta, forty** — which **conflicts by eleven years** with his own 1854 declaration of seventy-five, and is flagged rather than averaged. **And the absence is evidence:** four sheets, no death act of any parent, where fascicolo 3 of the same year binds in *«Atto di morte del padre e dell'avo paterno dello Sposo»*. The ordinary reading is that all four parents were alive on 7 February 1851 — graded *inferred*, because the bride was twenty and no consent sheet is listed either. **Navigation, which is the reusable part:** fascicolo wrappers are findable **by shape** in a montage of thumbnails at width 430, no text read. In 1851 they fall at images 1100 (n. 3), 1190 (n. 13), 1280 (n. 24), 1430 (n. 37). **Do not** navigate by the *Num. d'ordine* on the atti di notificazione bound inside — a separate series at a different rate. **What is left in this bundle:** sheets 3 and 4, the banns and the certificate of canonical celebration. Low value beside the first two, but unread. **AND THE INFERENCE IT RESTED ON IS NOW CONFIRMED.** The bundle's four-sheet index held no death act for any parent, which was an argument from absence and graded *inferred*. The **1851 marriage Tavola** settles it positively: entry 1's parents are written without *«fu»*, in a series that marks the dead with it. **All four were living in February 1851**, and the correction is now graded *documented*.

rows.what: Antonino Crupi's Queensland investigation file — open access, unread
rows.note: **NAA: BP242/1, Q16634 — «Crupi, Antonio and Maria — Queensland investigation case file», 1939–1957, held at Brisbane, access status OPEN.** Found while reading Antonino Crupi's aliens card ([row 117](/worklist/)). **Why it matters.** The card says only that he went into Loveday compound 14A in March 1943 and came out in October. **The investigation file is the document that put him there** — BP242/1 is the Queensland series of the Commonwealth Investigation Branch, and its files carry the informant's allegation, the police report, the internment recommendation and the objection hearing. Mario Crupi has one too — **BP242/1 Q25743**, also open, also unread. **«Antonio and Maria»** is the file title; Antonino's wife was **Nellie** by 1946, so the Maria may be his mother **Maria Vecchio**, an earlier wife, or a different couple entirely. **The title is a finding aid, not a record** — it has to be opened before anything is claimed from it. **Neither file appears to be digitised**, so this is a reading-room request or a digitisation order, not an afternoon's work. Worth putting on David's list beside the other Brisbane items.

rows.what: Two Prostamo in Western Australia in the First World War
rows.note: **Thirty years earlier than anything this archive holds in Australia, and in the wrong state.** NAA series **PP14/3** — applications for registration as an alien, Perth — holds two items: **`ITALIAN/PROSTAMO G`, GABRIELE PROSTAMO** (item 5137304) and **`ITALIAN/PROSTAMO F`, FRANCESCO PROSTAMO** (item 5137303), both dated **circa 1916–1920**, both **access status Open**. **Why this is worth opening.** This archive's Australian story starts in 1937 with Angela Crupi and runs through the post-war assisted passages. **Prostamo is a Briatico and Pizzo surname** and it is not common. Two men of it registering as enemy aliens in Perth during the First World War means an Italian migration this family knows nothing about, a generation before the one it has documented — and the registration form of that period carries **birthplace, date of birth, arrival, occupation and address**. **What it is not, yet.** A surname and a state. Neither man is in the tree, and Western Australia is not where this family settled. **The test is the birthplace on the form:** if either says **Briatico**, **Potenzoni** or **Pizzo**, it is the same stock; if it says somewhere else, Prostamo is a wider surname than this archive assumed, which is worth knowing too. **Check the item detail for «View digital copy» first** — PP14/3 may not be scanned, in which case this is a Perth reading-room request rather than an afternoon.

rows.what: Four Brisbane files that name this family and nobody has ever asked for
rows.note: **These are requests, not searches.** Four National Archives files name people on this archive's spine, are held at **Brisbane**, and carry the access status **«not yet examined»** — which means **nobody has ever asked to see them**. An access examination is **free** and takes roughly ninety days, and anyone can lodge one. **1. NAA: J25 1971/3900** — *«Arena, Rocco; wife Angelina [or Angela] [nee Polistena]»*, 1953–1971. **Michael's grandparents on the Arena side**, whose marriage is documented nowhere else ([row 80](/worklist/)). **2. NAA: BP242/1 Q16634** — *«Crupi, Antonio and Maria — Queensland investigation case file»*, 1939–1957, **access Open**. The file behind **Antonino Crupi's internment** ([row 148](/worklist/)); his brother Mario's is **BP242/1 Q25743**, also open. **3. NAA: J25 1962/5930** — *«Prostamo, Domenico Francesco; wife Assunte Maria [nee Melluso]»*, 1952–1966. The marriage of **Maria Assunta Melluso**, buried at Mount Gravatt in 1991 under a surname nobody could attach to a man. **4. NAA: J25 1972/23086** — *«Melluso, Gregorio; wife Carmela; and children Giuseppe, Maria [surname Prostamo]»*, 1959–1974. **Gregorio Melluso's household**, which Queensland's own index cannot show — it holds exactly one Melluso registration in its entire run. **Why they are worth the wait.** J25 is Queensland immigration and naturalisation correspondence: the files carry arrival details, addresses, sponsors, and the family relationships spelled out. BP242/1 is the Investigation Branch: informant, police report, internment recommendation, objection hearing. **Every one of these would answer a question this archive currently records as open.** **Owned by David** because lodging the examination request is his to do, and the ninety days start the day it is lodged.

rows.what: Filippo Arena × Domenica Costa's marriage — the only route to generation nine
rows.note: **This archive reaches generation eight on the Scilla side and stops.** Filippo Arena was **twenty-five** and Domenica Costa **twenty-seven** when their son Francesco was born on 25 November 1819 — ages read today off the act itself, in the 1851 processetti. **Their own parents are unknown**, and there are only two documents that would name them: **their marriage act**, or **Filippo's death act** ([row 68](/worklist/), a twenty-seven-year unindexed sweep). The marriage is the cheaper of the two. **The window is about 1812–1819**, and four years are now read: **1819 — no Arena.** Tavola alphabetised by **surname**; its A section holds one entry, Abbate Grazia. **1818 — no Filippo Arena.** Tavola alphabetised by the **groom's given name**, so Filippo sits under **F**, and the F section is Migliarino, Polimeni, **Pizzarello**, La Valle. *Searching the A section here would have produced a confident, complete and entirely false negative* — the caution this archive already wrote, paying for itself. **1817 and 1816 have no Tavola at all.** 1817 runs to act 41 then blank forms; 1816 to act 42, and the archivist's card reads **VOLUME TARLATO** — worm-eaten. Each costs a full read of about forty openings, one act to an opening. **What is left, cheapest first.** **(1)** The **napoleonic** marriage volumes — 1809, 1810, 1811, 1812, 1813–1814, 1815 — whose arks are in `scilla-arks.tsv` and whose containers have not been bought. Scilla's registration begins in **1809**, so those years exist and nobody here has opened one. **(2)** The unindexed 1816 and 1817, act by act. **(3)** The **processetti** for the same window — `1810–1814` and `1815–1816` are held, and a bundle carries the death acts of dead parents, which would reach generation nine even if the Tavola does not. **Containers in hand:** 1816 `wQYJYDb`, 1817 `5K9P9J9`, 1818 `LPaGar8`, 1819 `0AJEJ8b`. **THREE MORE YEARS FALL, 20 SEPTEMBER.** **1812** (Tavola, seventeen marriages, all read), **1811** (Tavola; F section is di Franco, Arbitrio, Bova) and **1810** (indice; F section is Filippo **Laganà**, Vita, Martello, Zirilli, Fava) hold **no Filippo Arena**. **1809 has no Tavola.** All three napoleonic indexes use the **groom's given name** as well. **So the marriage is not in 1810, 1811, 1812, 1818 or 1819.** What is left is **1809, 1813–1814, 1815, 1816 and 1817 — every one of them without an index.** **All nine containers are now saved.** **The cheapest remaining route is therefore the processetti**, not the acts: bundles are found by their **wrappers**, which name the couple in three words, and Scilla holds `1810–1814` (`an_ua2093352`), `1815–1816` (`an_ua2093354`) and `1817–1819` (`an_ua2002455`) — **the whole remaining window, in three volumes**. A bundle also carries the death acts of dead parents, so it reaches **generation nine** even where a Tavola would only name them. **And the sweep paid for itself sideways:** the 1811 Tavola gave **Candida Costa**, daughter of Rocco Costa and Pasqualina Idone — **Maria Costa's sister**, found in an index opened for somebody else. A Tavola that names four parents will keep doing that, which is an argument for reading the whole section rather than scanning for one surname. **THE PROCESSETTI ARE BOUGHT AND SIZED, 20 SEPTEMBER, AND THE ROUTE IS CONFIRMED BUT NOT CHEAP.** Containers: **1810–1814 `LaNPkQJ` (947 images)**, **1815–1816 `LqA4a7D` (364)**, **1817–1819 `02Ro183` (880)** — **2,191 images for the five unindexed years**. **Wrappers exist and are the finding aid.** Image 22 of the 1815–1816 volume reads *«Anno 1815, N.o 4 — Documenti pel Matrimonio di …»* over a mostly blank left page — the same form as the 1849–1852 bundles. **But a twenty-point sample at nine-image spacing surfaced only one clearly legible wrapper**, so they are neither evenly spaced nor reliably distinguishable at thumbnail size in this volume, which is catalogued *VOLUME TARLATO* and heavily stained. **So this is a deliberate pass, not an afternoon:** roughly 250 thumbnails at nine-image spacing across the three volumes, read in montages of twenty, with each candidate wrapper cropped to confirm the names. **Start with 1815–1816** — it is the smallest and covers two of the five years. **Everything needed is now in hand and nothing here needs buying again.** **CLOSED, 20 SEPTEMBER, AND NOT BY THE PLANNED ROUTE.** The processetti were never opened. **Filippo Arena married Domenica Costa at Scilla on 12 NOVEMBER 1815 — Matrimoni 1815, atto 29**, in the napoleonic volume `57O1erJ`, one of the five unindexed years. What cracked it was not a new source but a **new way of reading an unindexed volume**: in these registers an opening puts the *end* of one act on the left page and the *head* of the next on the right, and that head carries the act number, the date, the groom's name, his age, his trade and his father. Cropping that band and tiling it ten to a sheet reads a whole volume in four montages. **Three volumes — 1815, 1816, 1817, one hundred and eleven acts — fell in an afternoon**, where this row had budgeted 2,191 processetti thumbnails. **All three were read to the closing statement**, so each volume's end was found before anything was written about it; 1816 and 1817 are **complete negatives**. **The act names four people this archive had never seen:** **ORAZIO ARENA**, marinaro, and **SETTERIA MORABITO** — Filippo's parents, both alive, both standing beside him and consenting, because at twenty-two he was still a minor under the code; and **GIOVANNI COSTA**, dead at Scilla on **29 March 1790**, and **MARTA ALFONZETTI**, Domenica's parents. **Filippo signed the act**, in the same hand that signs his son's birth in 1819. **Two things this row got wrong, recorded rather than quietly fixed.** Its header promised **generation nine**; Filippo is generation seven here, so his parents are **generation eight** — the same depth already reached on the Arlotta–Costa side. And the wall it was built to climb was **this archive's own mistake**: the marriage was called pre-civil and lost only because the search had started in 1816. Scilla begins in 1809. **The sea trade now runs four generations — Orazio, Filippo, Francesco Antonio, Rocco — and above Orazio there is no civil register at all.** What is left is parish, and that is [row 158](/worklist/).

rows.what: The Civil Aliens Corps — Rosario Mazza is in it and the Crupi are not
rows.note: **Internment was not the end of it, and this archive stops at the camp gate.** **NAA: J1737, MAZZA R — «Mazza Rosario, CAS 15000 — Civil Aliens Corps (CAC)», Brisbane, 1944, access OPEN.** The CAC was the labour corps that interned Italians were released *into* rather than freed from — road, timber and farm work under military administration — and **CAS 15000 is Rosario Mazza's service number in it**. **The three men line up.** Mario Crupi was at Loveday from 18 August 1942 and released 30 December 1943. Antonino Crupi was moved to compound 14A in March 1943 and released 22 October 1943. Rosario Mazza's Corps file is **1944**. They were moving through the same machinery within months of each other — Angela Crupi's husband and two of her brothers. **TESTED THE SAME DAY AND THE GUESS WAS WRONG.** I wrote here that the Crupi brothers would have J1737 files too. **They do not.** The complete CRUPI name index — 233 items — holds **no J1737, no Civil Aliens Corps and no CAS number** for any Crupi. Rosario Mazza has one; neither of his wife's brothers does. Why is unresolved: the Corps was not universal, and men released in October and December 1943 may simply have gone back to the cane. **What the test found instead** is that both Crupi internment dossiers exist and are open — **MP1103/1 Q7838** for Antonino and **MP1103/2 Q30124** for Mario — and that **those serials are the ones written on their aliens cards**, which ties card to camp for both men. **What to look for now:** **NAA: BP628/5**, the *«Name Index and registration cards for internees dossiers Queensland — MACAUDO to MYSLIM»* (1939–1962, Brisbane, **open**), which is the finding aid to the Queensland dossiers and whose range covers **Mazza**. **This is the part of the story the family is least likely to have been told**, and it is on open access.

rows.what: A Trove API key — five minutes of David's time, and it unblocks a whole source
rows.note: **Trove will not run in this session's browser** ([row 79](/worklist/)): its single-page app throws inside its own vendor bundle on a storage API the pane does not provide, and never paints a result list. **The fix is not another attempt at the page.** **The Trove API v3 is free**, returns JSON, and needs no JavaScript. A key is requested from the National Library of Australia at **trove.nla.gov.au** under *For developers*; it takes a few minutes and asks only for a name and what the key is for. **What it would unblock.** Trove holds Australian newspapers and the **Commonwealth of Australia Gazette**, where **naturalisation notices give a date, a street address and a former nationality** — for a family that arrived in 1937 and 1949, that is close to what an electoral roll gives, and free. This archive has already had two finds out of Trove *by accident*: the Brisbane Prostamo naturalisations, and Maria Assunta Melluso's gazettal of **4 July 1966 at 3 Frank Street, Graceville**.
