Neither came from a sweep. **Ten surnames are waiting:** Mazza, Crupi, Arena, Polistena, Donato, Prostamo, Melluso, Cavallaro, Bova, Armanno. **Once the key exists**, put it somewhere this project can read and the sweep is mechanical — one GET per surname, no browser involved.

rows.what: The margins — worth reading when full, worth nothing when empty
rows.note: **This archive has read a dozen Scilla birth acts and never once looked at the left margin.** Atto 174 of 1833 has written down its edge, in a different hand: *«L'anno 1869, il giorno 12 Luglio … **ha contratto matrimonio in questo Comune con Colorina Bri[…]**»*, signed by the Uffiziale and dated from Reggio on 26 August 1869 — **thirty-six years after the birth**. **The printed form asks for it.** The left column is headed *«MARGINE per scriversi alcune notizie riguardanti gli atti di nascita»*; the right is the baptism, which this archive does read. One column is the sacrament; the other is everything that happened to the person afterwards. **What a margin can hand over free:** a marriage date and a spouse, with no marriage register opened at all — and for years where the marriage Tavola is missing or the volume is unindexed, that is the whole answer. **The acts to go back to, all already fetched and all free to re-crop:** **Francesco Antonio Arena**, Nati 1819 atto 186 (read in the 1851 processetti — *and the processetti copy may not reproduce the margin, so the register itself must be opened*); **Serafina Arlotta**, Nati 1830 atto 89; **Rocco Arena**, Nati 1861 atto 228; **Giovanni Arena**, Nati 1854 atto 76; and the Arena births of 1852, 1853 and 1860. **Cheap, mechanical, and it uses containers already bought.** **THREE TESTED THE SAME HOUR, AND THE RULE IS NARROWER THAN IT LOOKED.** **Rocco Polistina** (1833): margin carries his 1869 marriage. **Serafina Arlotta** (1830): **blank** — she married in 1851. **Filippo Arena** (1852): **blank** — any marriage of his falls after 1866. **The reading that fits all three:** the annotation is an **Italian-era habit**, absent from an 1851 marriage and present on an 1869 one, **and** it is written only when the later act is registered in the **same comune** — the note says *«ha contratto matrimonio in questo Comune»* in so many words. **So a blank margin is weak evidence.** For a pre-1866 marriage it means nothing at all. For a post-1866 one it is consistent with a marriage **elsewhere** — which for Filippo Arena is the reading the rest of the evidence already supports ([row 146](/worklist/)). **Still worth doing** for **Rocco Arena** (b. 1861, m. 1888 at Scilla), **Giovanni Arena** (b. 1854, m. 1885 at Scilla) and **Giuseppe Arena** (b. 1860, m. 1885 at Scilla) — all three married **at Scilla after 1866**, which is exactly the case where the annotation appears. And for **Domenico Arena** (b. 1853), where a blank would be one more straw and an annotation would be a marriage nobody has. **THE CONTROL IS RUN AND THE GRADING GOES UP.** The 1852 volume **does** annotate margins — act 55 carries *«Scarfone Rocco contrasse matrimonio in Scilla con Vita Maria»*, 1881 — and 1853 does it twice on one opening (1876 and 1883). **So Filippo Arena's blank margin is evidence: he did not marry at Scilla.** *(And a correction of my own inside the hour: I first took writing at the edge of the 1852 act-48 opening for act 49's margin. It is act 49's **baptism** column. The control had to be run on a different opening before the blank meant anything.)* **And chasing a margin turned up something far bigger — see [row 137](/worklist/) and the retraction filed against Domenico Arena.** **AND THEN THE CONTROL FAILED, WHICH IS WHY YOU RUN CONTROLS.** **Giuseppe Arena married Maria Martello at Scilla on 12 September 1885** — act 73, read here in the original — **and his own birth act, Nati 1860 atto 45, has an empty annotation box.** A man who demonstrably married in the comune after 1866 was never annotated. **So a blank box is not evidence of anything, and the reading filed against Filippo Arena is withdrawn in full.** **What survives:** a *present* annotation is free evidence — Rocco Polistina's 1869 marriage came that way, and marriages of 1876, 1881 and 1883 sit on other acts. **A bonus when it is there, silence when it is not.** **And the box moves between volumes.** 1852–53 use a **left** column headed *«MARGINE per scriversi alcune notizie…»*; 1860 uses a **right** box headed *«MENZIONI prescritte dagli articoli 64, 65 e 106»*. Same purpose, opposite side of the page — so anyone reporting a blank must say which side they looked at.

rows.what: Camillo Antonio's marriage — FOUND, 23 January 1881, and he is nine years younger
rows.note: **Sixteen years of Scilla's birth register have been read and he is in none of them** ([row 137](/worklist/)). His parents' children come in 1833, 1836 and 1840; there is no year he fits. The birth register cannot settle it, so stop asking it. **His marriage act can.** He married **Giovanna Romano** — her death act of 15 July 1930 names him as her husband, and their son Giovanni was born at Via Grotte 47 on 16 September 1883, when Camillo Antonio was entered as forty-eight. So the wedding falls roughly **1870–1882**. **What a Scilla marriage act of that period gives:** both spouses' ages, **both birthplaces**, and all four parents. That is his age a third time, from his own mouth, and — decisively — **whether he was born at Scilla at all**. If the act says he was born somewhere else, sixteen years of negative reading stop being a puzzle and become the answer. **The ground is already bought.** Scilla's Italian-era marriages run **1866–1913** without a gap and every ark is listed in `scilla-arks-italiano.tsv`; containers are saved for 1874–1877 and 1885–1890. The annual index of each year is one A-block read, and **P for Polistena is a short section at Scilla** — eight births in eleven years, so the marriages will be sparse too. **Start at 1875 and work outward**, since a man of about forty in 1883 marrying a woman young enough to bear a son that year most likely married in the middle of the window. **STARTED 20 SEPTEMBER. 1876 IS CLEAR; 1875 HAS NO INDEX.** **1876** carries an *«Indice annuale per gli Atti di Matrimonio»* in a **good format** — every spouse alphabetical, the two halves of each couple **braced together** against one register number, so one reading gives both names and the act. Its P range is Pirrotta, Patafio, Paladino ×3 and Piemi. **No Polistena.** **1875 has no Tavola at all** — the volume ends in blank forms and a printed *Parte II* title page, and there is only **one ark per Italian-era marriage year** at Scilla, so no second volume carries the index. 1875 must be read act by act, about forty openings. **So the indexes are not uniform across this series either** — 1876 and 1877 have them, 1875 does not. **Check the tail before promising a year.** **Left:** 1870–1874, 1875 (by acts), 1877–1882. Containers saved for 1874–1877. **1874 AND 1877 ADDED, BOTH CLEAR.** 1874's P section is Parisi, Pizzarello ×2, Piria, Pirrotta, Patafio; 1877's is Patafio, Paladino, Panuccio, Pirrotta, Papalia, Parisi. **No Polistena in either.** **The index format is the same good one in all three years** — every spouse alphabetical, the two halves of each couple **braced against one register number** — so a year costs **one crop** once the container is in hand. That makes the rest of this window cheap. **Noted and not joined:** act 44 of 1877 marries an **Arlotta Maria Concetta** to Pietro Panuccio. Serafina Arlotta's known siblings are Anna, Domenico and Giuseppe Antonio; a Maria Concetta is not among them and nothing here makes her one. **Left:** 1870–1873 and 1878–1882 (containers not bought), and 1875 act by act. **1879 AND 1880 ADDED, BOTH CLEAR.** 1879's P is Procopio, Papalia ×3, Paladini, Paladino, Prigandè; 1880's is Paspiglia, Piria, Pirrotta, Paladino, Patafio, Papalia ×2. **No Polistena in either.** **Five years read and clear: 1874, 1876, 1877, 1879, 1880.** 1875 has no index; 1878's container lookup hit a 403 and was not retried. **Left: 1870–1873, 1878, 1881, 1882.** **Three things noted and not joined.** **1879 act 22 marries an Arlotta Giuseppe** — Serafina's brother Giuseppe Antonio Arlotta is recorded here as the husband of Angela Nunziata Pizzarello and the bride in this index does not obviously match, so the act is wanted before anything is claimed. **1879 act 8: Russo Giovanni × Arena Fortunata** — the Russo–Arena pairing again, six years before Giovanni Arena married Concetta Russo. **1880 act 40: Riganatì Antonio × Arena Teresa** — and the Teresa Arena this archive holds, Orazio's daughter born 1853, died in 1913 as the wife of *Pietro Bova*. A different woman or a first marriage; nothing decides it here. **1878 AND 1882 ADDED.** 1878 is clear — Paladino, Porpiglia, Palermo, Pizzarello. **1882 holds two Polistina and neither is him:** *«Polistina Giuseppe × Zagari Giovanna»* and *«Polistina Luigi Carmelo × Matrà Nunziata»*, act 48. **That is worth more than a negative.** Seven years of this index are now read and **1882 is the first to hold the surname at all** — so the Polistena were marrying at Scilla by 1882, and the earlier silence is not an artefact of the index. And **«Luigi Carmelo» fits a household already known**: the 1831 birth Tavola gives *«Polistina Francesco Antonio, di **Luigi** e Giovanna Baviera»*. **Both 1882 acts are worth opening regardless.** A Scilla marriage act of that date gives both spouses' ages, **both birthplaces** and all four parents — so either one would say whether the Polistena of Scilla were born there or came in, which is the question [row 137](/worklist/) could not answer from sixteen years of births. **Left:** 1870–1873 and 1881 (not bought), 1875 (no index, act by act). **AND A NAVIGATION NOTE, BOUGHT WITH FOUR WASTED PROBES.** The 1882 volume is **split into two series and both are numbered from one** — image 33's margin reads *«Numero 4 — Colosi Giuseppe Luigi Vincenzo / Zagari Giuseppa Maria Raffaela»*, which is **Parte II** act 4. Parte II begins around image 31. **The index gives a «Numero di Registro» without saying which part**, so an index number cannot be resolved to an image without checking both series; and several images in the thirties are blank versos showing only bleed-through. **The cheap way in:** every act carries a **margin label with its number and both spouses' names**, so a montage of the narrow left-margin strip across a run of images identifies every act without reading a single act body. That is the trick that worked on the 1874 volume and it should have been used here first. **AND THE TRICK WORKED.** A montage of the narrow left-margin strip across images 24–32 read the whole volume's act numbers **and both spouses' names** in one look: acts 45, 47, 49, 51 on successive images, and **Parte II beginning at image 30**. **Act 48 is the second act on image 25**, and it is read — see the 1882 row in scilla-reads. **FOUND. SCILLA, MATRIMONI 1881, ATTO 4 — 23 JANUARY 1881**, six seventeen in the evening. *«**Polistina Camillo Antonio, di anni trentasei, marinaro, nato in questo Comune**, figlio del **fu Giuseppe** e della **fu Anna Pontillo**»*; *«**Romano Giovanna, di anni ventisei, filatrice, nata in questo Comune**, figlia di **Annunziato** e di **Angela Zirilli**»*. **THE AGE IS THE FINDING. Thirty-six in January 1881 is a birth about 1844** — and his son's 1883 act makes him forty-eight, a birth about 1835. **Nine years apart**, and the 1835 figure is what [row 137](/worklist/) swept eleven years of birth Tavole around. The answer was never in them. **He was born at Scilla** — *«nato in questo Comune»* — so the birth act exists and the sweep missed it. **And 1844 is inside the swept range**: that year's P block was read for entries 127–138 **without establishing where the block ends**, and **1845 is on record as partial**, with seven of eighteen lines too faint. Those two years are the shortest road left and are already paid for. **Three more things it gives.** **Giuseppe Polistena and Anna Pontillo were both dead by January 1881** — the first bound either has had, against their last sighting alive in January 1840. The parentage is confirmed from a **second** document, forty-three years before the 1924 death act. And **Giovanna Romano is dated**: twenty-six, born at Scilla about 1854, with both her parents living — the **fourth** record to call her a Romano and the first in which she is the subject.

rows.what: Camillo Antonio's birth act — read: atto 137 of 1844
rows.note: **His birth is dated — 21 September 1844 — but only from the index** ([row 137](/worklist/)). **The act has not been opened**, and this archive's own standing rule is *read the act, not the index*: that rule has been vindicated four times here, most recently when a Tavola line read as *Domenico* turned out to be **Domenica**, a daughter. **It is cheap.** The 1844 Tavola carries **no act number**, but the register runs in **date order**, so a birth of 21 September sits two or three probes into container **`LNolOVK`**, which is already bought. **What the act would add.** **Both parents' ages** — dating **Giuseppe Polistena** and **Anna Pontillo** a third time, against *thirty-four and thirty-three* in 1833 and *thirty-eight and thirty-five* in 1836. The **house**, the **hour**, the **declarant** (a midwife delivered both his siblings), and the **witnesses**. And its **margin**, which on a man who married at Scilla in 1881 may carry that marriage — though [row 154](/worklist/) records that a blank there proves nothing. **It would also confirm the given name.** The index says **Camillo**; every later record says **Camillo Antonio**. The act will say which he was christened. **HUNTED THE SAME HOUR AND NOT FOUND — five acts eliminated.** The 1844 volume maps cleanly: **image N carries folio N−2**, with the **even** act on the left page and the **odd** act on the right. Image 73 = acts 140/141, image 74 = acts 142/143. **Checked and excluded, all in the September run:** **138** (declarant Domenico Spoletti), **139** (child Giuseppe), **140** (declarant Cosmo Bellantoni, child *Marianna Violante*), **141** (declarant Domenico Calarco, baptised at the parish **of Solano**), **142** (declarant Giovanni Macrì, child *Rosantonio*, born the 28th). **None is Polistina.** **So either the act sits outside 138–142** — the September run plausibly spans acts 135 to 145 — **or the Tavola's «21 Settembre» is the birth date against a later declaration**, or that faint line reads a different day. **The finding does not depend on it:** the Tavola gives the parents and the date, and the marriage act's *trentasei* is exact for September 1844. But **the act has not been read**, and this archive's own rule is that the index is not the source. **Next pass, and do it this way:** montage the act-number-and-date band — region `pct:50,10,48,20` at width 900 — across **images 68–76**, which covers acts 132 to 149 **in one look**, instead of opening them one at a time as I did. **FOUND — ATTO 137, not 142.** Two montages did what five one-at-a-time probes could not: the **even** acts across images 68–77 mapped September to acts **129–143**, and the **odd** acts across 68–73 put a **Polistina at act 137**. *«È comparso **Giuseppe Polistina, di anni cinquanta, marinaro** … quale ci à presentato un **maschio** … nato da **Anna Pontillo, filatrice**, sua moglie legittima … **nel giorno ventuno corrente mese** … di dare al fanciullo **il nome di Camillo Antonio**.»* The baptism column names **Camillo Antonio Polistina**. **So the Tavola was right about the date and the parents and wrong about the number** — 142 was its row, 137 is the act. **Third time today.** And the act gives the **full given name**, where the index gives only *Camillo*. **And the margin carries his marriage**, annotated *«Scilla 25 Gennaio 1881»* — two days after the wedding of 23 January 1881. **The birth act and the marriage act point at each other across thirty-seven years**, and the identification is closed from both ends. **One figure recorded and not averaged:** Giuseppe Polistina is **fifty** here, against thirty-eight in 1836 and thirty-four in 1833 — births of 1794, 1798 and 1799. The two earlier agree; this one does not.

rows.what: Orazio Arena's other children — the Scilla birth registers, 1809 onward
rows.note: **A new surname to sweep, and the cheapest lead the 1815 act opened.** Orazio Arena and Setteria Morabito were both alive and living at Scilla in November 1815, and their son Filippo was their **minor** child — the word the act uses is *«figlio minore»*, meaning under twenty-five, not youngest. **Scilla's birth registers run from 1809** and its marriage registers from the same year, so any child of theirs born or married from 1809 on is in a volume this archive can already reach, and most of those volumes have an **annual Tavola**. A sibling of Filippo is worth more than a name: **the Tavola of the year a sibling married dates the life status of Orazio and Setteria**, which is the instrument [row 68](/worklist/) wanted and could not use on Filippo's own children. **Start with the marriage Tavole 1816–1840 under A**, which are one page each, before touching the birth registers; the marriage index is alphabetised by the groom's given name in some years and by surname in others, so **read the whole section, not the letter you expect**. Containers for 1816–1819 are already in `scilla-arks.tsv`. **THE VOLUMES ARE OPEN, 20 SEPTEMBER.** Twenty-one marriage containers, **1820 through 1843**, were fetched in one sitting from inside the antenati origin -- six at a time, five seconds apart -- with **no 403**, and their image counts came free off the IIIF manifests. `scilla-arks.tsv` now holds every Scilla marriage volume from 1809 to 1845 with a container against it. **Nothing in this row needs buying again; what is left is reading.** **AND THE NAPOLEONIC SWEEP FOUND AN ARENA HOUSEHOLD NOBODY HAD MET.** Scilla **Matrimoni 1813, atto 21**: *«DIEGO ARENA, di anni trentasette, di professione SARTORE … figlio maggiore di **DOMENICO ARENA, di anni SETTANTA, di professione BARBIERE**, domiciliante in questo Comune, e di **ANNA MELIDONI**, di anni cinquantaquattro»*, both present and consenting; the bride **Maria Giuseppa Pontillo**, sixteen, daughter of Giovanni Pontillo, commerciante, and Diana Idone. Banns at **Campo** as well as Scilla. **Domenico Arena was born about 1743** — earlier than any Arena in this archive, Orazio included — and he is a **barber**, where the spine is four generations of sailors. **He is NOT claimed as Orazio's father, and the temptation to claim him is the point.** Scilla has more than one Arena family; a shared surname in a small town is how this archive nearly hung a birth act on the wrong Mariano Mazza. **What would settle it is Orazio Arena's own marriage, which is pre-1809 and parish** — [row 158](/worklist/). In the meantime the household is recorded as three documented people with no edge to the spine. **Also banked from the same two volumes:** the first year of the register marries a **Fortunata Donato** (1809 act 2) and a **Giacoma Arena** (1809 act 10) — both brides, both surnames present in the town from the beginning. **AND THE SAME THREE INDEXES GIVE THE SHAPE OF THE SURNAME.** Read whole, the napoleonic years hold **six Arena** and not one of them is Filippo's household: **Diego Arena** the tailor as a groom (1813), with his father **Domenico Arena the barber, seventy, born about 1743**; **Giacoma Arena** (1809) and **Giovanna Arena** (1812, daughter of **Carlo Arena** and Eugenia Ateja) as brides; **Natalina Arena** as a mother (1811); and **Antonia Arena**, *«fu»* and so dead before February 1811, wife of Domenico Falcomatà, whose two daughters marry in 1811 and 1812 — the same parents in both entries, so two sisters and one household. **That is THREE Arena fathers at Scilla in one decade** — Domenico the barber, Carlo, and Orazio who is Filippo's — **with nothing between them.** The finding is not a line; it is the shape of a surname in a town, and a standing warning against the join this archive would most like to make. **DONE, AND ON THIS ROW'S OWN STATED METHOD.** The row said: *find a sibling of Filippo, and the Tavola of the year that sibling married will date Orazio and Litteria.* **It did exactly that, in the second year opened.** **Scilla, Matrimoni 1821, atto 29 — GIUSEPPE ARENA, twenty-seven, MARINARO**, *«nato in questo Comune … figlio di **ORAZIO ARENA**, di professione **marinaro**, domiciliato ivi, e di **LITTERIA MORABITO**, domiciliata ivi»*, married **Maria Teresa Polistina** on 13 November 1821; the promessa was taken six days earlier before **Tommaso Cutelli** — *the same sindaco who married Filippo in 1815*. **Three things at once.** A **brother** for Filippo, the first sibling this archive has ever found for him. **Orazio and Litteria alive on 7 November 1821** — named with no *«fu»* on either, six years past the only other date for them. And **LITTERIA confirmed a third time**, after the 1815 act and the baptism extract, which retires the last doubt about this morning's correction. **And the Tavola was enough on its own** — 1821 alphabetises by **surname**, so Arena sits at the top of the book and the whole test was one crop. The A section also holds **ARENA ROCCO × COSTA DOMENICA** (act 20) with different parents: a **fourth** Arena family at Scilla, and a second Domenica Costa. **What is left is not this row:** Orazio's own marriage is pre-1809 and parish ([row 158](/worklist/)), and the remaining Tavole 1822–1843 would find more siblings but cannot go higher.

rows.what: Above Orazio Arena there is no civil register — the parish records of Scilla
rows.note: **The Arena spine now ends at a man born in the 1760s or early 1770s, and the state was not yet writing.** Civil registration in the Kingdom of Naples begins in 1809; everything above Orazio Arena and Setteria Morabito, and everything about **Giovanni Costa**, who died at Scilla on **29 March 1790**, is **parish**. **There is one concrete handle.** The 1815 marriage act does not merely say Giovanni Costa was dead — it cites his death record and says it *«si conserva»*, is preserved. So a Scilla parish death register covering March 1790 existed in 1815. Scilla's parishes fall under the **Archdiocese of Reggio Calabria–Bova**; its historical archive is not on Antenati and not on FamilySearch's Italian civil collections. **Blocked, and honestly so:** this archive has no access, no catalogue and no evidence of digitisation, and the 1908 Messina earthquake, which levelled much of the strait, is a real risk to the holdings themselves. **The next step is not a search, it is a question:** write to the Archivio Storico Diocesano at Reggio and ask what survives for Scilla before 1809. That is [row 150](/worklist/)'s kind of task — a human one — and it is offered to **David**, not claimed here. **AND IT IS NO LONGER A BLIND QUESTION, 20 SEPTEMBER.** The 1815 marriage bundle ([row 159](/worklist/)) quotes the Scilla parish books **by name** and names the men who held them: the *«liber Baptizatorum»* and the *«liber Defunctorum»* of the **Chiesa Matrice**, kept by the archpriest **D. Giuseppe Ingigneri** and searched for these extracts by the economo curato **Leonardo Cantore Bandiera**, who signed all three in May and October 1815. The baptism book was open at **1787** and **1793**, the death book at **1790**. **So the letter to Reggio can name books, custodians and years instead of asking a general question** -- which is the difference between an enquiry that gets answered and one that does not.

rows.what: The 1815 marriage file — three leaves that reach 1787, 1790 and 1793
rows.note: **Opened the same day the marriage act was found, and worth more than the act.** [Row 151](/worklist/) had budgeted a blind sweep of 2,191 processetti thumbnails across three volumes to *find* the marriage. Once the act was found in the register instead, the bundle stopped being a search and became an **address**: year 1815, number 29. **The wrappers are the index** — each carries the year, the folio range, the bundle number and the couple in three words — so a scan at five-image spacing, then two passes at step two, landed on it in about forty thumbnails. **Image 149 of `LqA4a7D`:** *«1815 | 114 a 116 | N.o 29 | Scilla | Documenti per il Matrimonio di FILIPPO ARENA E DOMENICA COSTA | fogli tre».* **Three Latin extracts, and every one of them paid.** **Folio 114** — Filippo's baptism: *«Die vigesima quinta mensis Martii ... millesimo septingentesimo nonagesimo tertio, Scyllae ... infantem HODIE NATUM ex Horatio Arena et LITTERIA MORABITO coniugibus, cui nomen imposuit PHILIPPUS NUNTIATUS».* **Born and baptised 25 March 1793**, godmother Rosaria Bombarda — and his mother's name is **Litteria**, not the «Setteria» this archive read off the civil act six hours earlier. **Folio 115** — Domenica's baptism, **16 June 1787**, by the archpriest Giuseppe Ingigneri himself, *«cui imposui nomen DOMINICA JOSEPHA»*, godmother Giuseppa Cotronei. **That settles the five-year dispute**: twenty-eight at her wedding was right, and the twenty-seven her husband gave at their son's birth in 1819 was five years wrong. **Folio 116** — her father's death, **29 March 1790**, aged about forty: *«Joannes de Costa ... FILIUS QUONDAM JOSEPHI ET JACOBAE TURCO, legitimus vir Marthae Alfonzetti»*, ill in bed, confessed to Rev. D. Paolo Turco, given the Viaticum, anointed, and buried in the church of S. Maria di Porto Salvo. **One word does the work.** *Quondam* — the late — makes **GIUSEPPE COSTA and GIACOMA TURCO generation nine**, the first time the Scilla side has reached that far, and dates them both dead before March 1790. **And the lesson is the reverse of the one row 151 taught.** There the register beat the bundle. Here the bundle beat the register: it corrected a given name, corrected two birth years, and reached two generations the civil registers cannot touch, because it copies **parish** books that begin nineteen years before the state did. **Where a marriage bundle survives, read it even when the act is already in hand.**

rows.what: Piedimonte Etneo relisted — the archive held 103 of 457 registers
rows.note: **Asked why the Sicilian generations were still stuck, the first honest answer was: nobody had finished looking at what exists.** `pe-arks.tsv` held **103** Piedimonte Etneo registers. The comune has **457**. One page load of the register index at `s_size=500`, parsed in page context and **reconciled group by group against the live listing** — every fondo, type, ark range, count and year list — before a row was written. **What had never been listed at all:** every *stato civile italiano* year after 1863; all the **allegati** and **pubblicazioni**; the *Diversi* and *Cittadinanze*; and **twenty volumes of `Matrimoni, processetti` 1841–1860** — the exact instrument that broke the Scilla wall this afternoon ([row 159](/worklist/)), sitting unopened for the other half of the family. **And nine volumes nobody knew were there:** *«Riveli di anime e di terre»* of the **Deputazione del Regno**, **1714** and **1747–1752** — Sicilian household tax returns that list a head of household with his wife, his children and their ages. [Row 162](/worklist/). **One hard limit, recorded so it is not rediscovered:** the holding **stops at 1893**. Venera Cassaneti's death in 1925 and Salvatore Mazza's marriage to Maria Nicotra about 1900 are **not on Antenati and never were** — those are the comune at Piedimonte, or the Tribunale copy at Catania.

rows.what: John Nicotra and Venera Cassaneti — the side nobody has ever searched
rows.note: **Two of the three cards in generation three are blank, and it is not because the records are gone.** Searching this archive for *Cassaneti* returns **nothing at all** — not a read, not a negative, not a work-list row. Maria Nicotra (1875–1963) married Salvatore Mazza and is buried at Nudgee; her parents come to us only through a **Queensland death registration**, which is also where the «Maria Concetta» comes from, and where *Nicotra* is garbled to *Lecota* on her son Michele's. **Nobody has opened a Sicilian act for any of them.** **1875 is read and eliminated, 20 September.** The annual index holds exactly one *Nicotra Maria*, act 34, born 6 March 1875 to **Alfio Nicotra**, sixty-eight, and **Angela Previtera** — and her margin reads *«unita in matrimonio con Nicito Giuseppe fu Vincenzo, atto del 29.7.91»*. She married at Piedimonte in 1891 and stayed. **The method is now fixed and it is cheap.** Piedimonte's Italian-era birth volumes each carry an **Indice Annuale** alphabetical by surname in the last three images. For each year: read the index for *Nicotra Maria*, then crop that act's **margin**, which names the husband. Ours married a **MAZZA**; every other Maria Nicotra at Piedimonte will name somebody else. **One index page and one margin crop per year.** **The window is 1870–1885** — the tree's years are wrong often enough in this family that a single year is not a search ([the range rule](/searched/)). Containers for 1866–1893 are one batched fetch away; only 1875 is bought. **And if she is in none of them she was not born at Piedimonte**, which would itself be the finding, because it would mean the Nicotra came in from another comune. **1879 GOES TOO, AND IT COST ONE INDEX READ.** The N section of the 1879 Indice Annuale holds Neri, Nicodemo and Nucifora and **no Nicotra whatever**. The same page also closed a second question for free: its M section has **no Salvatore Mazza**, which excludes the tree's «Salvatore Mazza 1879» at this comune and leaves [Nati 1873 atto 3](/corrections/) standing with a negative behind it. **Fourteen containers are now banked** — 1870–1874, 1876–1883 — so the remaining years are reading, not fetching. **One route tested and closed:** Salvatore's own birth act carries a **marginal annotation column**, and in this series those name the spouse and the comune of the marriage. **His is empty.** The act four lines below it carries a full one, so the practice existed and was simply not applied to him — and [a blank box proves nothing](/searched/). **His birth act will not tell us where he married.** **And the post-1893 half needs a different archive entirely.** Antenati's Piedimonte holding stops at 1893, so the Mazza–Nicotra marriage of about 1900 and Venera Cassaneti's death in 1925 are not there. The route is the **Tribunale copy** — «Italy, Catania, Catania, Civil Registration (Tribunale), 1866–1929», already cited elsewhere in this archive — which runs thirty-six years further than the Archivio di Stato's filming. **SEVEN YEARS CLOSED, 20 SEPTEMBER: 1870, 1871, 1873, 1874, 1875, 1876, 1879.** Every N section read in the original and quoted whole on [what has been read](/searched/). The Nicotra ARE at Piedimonte — a Filippa in 1870, a Salvatore and a Giovanni in 1871, an Ignazio in 1873 — **and in seven years they produce no Maria** except the 1875 one whose margin marries her to a Nicito. **That is now worth saying out loud as a hypothesis, not a conclusion:** her birthplace in the family tree may be her *husband's* town copied across. Salvatore Mazza was born at Piedimonte; their son Rocco was born at **CATANIA** in 1899. If the household had already moved down to the city, Maria may be a Catania girl and no amount of Piedimonte sweeping will find her. **Do not act on that yet** — seven years is seven years, not the whole window, and 1872, 1877, 1878 and 1880–1884 are still unread with containers in hand. **But read them to close the hypothesis, not in hope.** **A cheaper instrument for the rest:** the 1870 and 1872 indexes are written *«Surname Given DI FATHER»*, so where a year does that, a *«Nicotra Maria di Giovanni»* would identify itself in the index without opening an act. **1872 MAKES EIGHT, AND ITS M SECTION PAID BETTER THAN ITS N.** No Maria among *Nicotra Angelo 147, Nicotra Giovanna 158, Nucifora Francesca 162* — but the same index gave **«Mazza Mariano — 32»**, and act 32 read in the original is **Salvatore Mazza's elder brother**, born 12 February 1872 to *«Rosario Mazza DI MARIANO, d'anni ventisette»* and *«Leonarda Bonanno di Gaetano»* ([row 163](/worklist/)). **And the Catania hypothesis just got weaker, not stronger.** That Mazza birth is in **CONTRADA SAN BASILIO**; the 1875 Maria Nicotra who is *not* ours was born in **VIA SAN BASILE** to Alfio Nicotra, bracciante. **The Mazza and the Nicotra were neighbours in the same lane.** That is not evidence of anything on its own — half the town were braccianti and lanes are long — but it is a reason to finish reading Piedimonte before reaching for a city of a hundred thousand people. **1877, 1878 and 1880–1884 remain, containers in hand.** **THE WHOLE DECADE IS NOW READ, AND IT IS EMPTY.** 1877 holds a single N entry, *Nicodemo Maria 85*, and **no Nicotra at all**; 1878 holds *Nicotra Alfio* twice and *Nicodemo Giuseppe*. With the eight already done that is **1870 through 1879 complete** — ten consecutive annual indexes, every N section read in the original and every entry named on [what has been read](/searched/). **The Nicotra are there the whole time and never produce her.** A decade is not a sample, and the year the tree gives her is the year she is most clearly absent from. **Still to read before anything is concluded: 1866–1869 and 1880–1884.** **And 1877 cost nothing and paid twice**, because its M section gave a **second Rosario Mazza** whose wife is also a Leonarda — Leonarda **Monacorso**, in via Grotta Nicodemo — which is exactly the act that would have been hung on the tree's Orazio Mazza. [Recorded as a correction](/corrections/). **TWELVE CONSECUTIVE YEARS, 1870–1881.** 1880's N section is one line, *Nucifora Francesco 92*; 1881's runs *Nicotra Antonina 24* across a page break into *Nucifora Concetta, Nucifora Agata, Nicotra Mariano, Neri Concetta*. **Both halves of that split section were read** — a section that ends at the foot of a page is exactly where a partial reading becomes a false negative, which this archive has paid for once already. **A lead left standing:** the 1880 M section carries **«Mazza Gaetano — 66»**, and *Gaetano* is what the custom gives a **second son**, after the mother's father — and Leonarda Bonanno's father is **Gaetano Bonanno**. It may be another child of Rosario and Leonarda or another of the town's Mazza households. **Not opened, nothing claimed.** — **OPENED, AND IT IS THEIRS.** *«Mazza Rosario, di anni trentadue, bracciante … da BONANNO LEONARDA, industriosa, sua moglie … via S. Basilio … il nome di GAETANO»*, born **5 May 1880**. The street and the mother's surname are what settle it against the other Rosario-and-Leonarda in the town. [Row 165](/worklist/). **AND THE OTHER SIDE OF THE QUESTION ANSWERED BETTER THAN THE FIRST.** Twelve years of Italian indexes have not produced her; **her own Australian file names her in one line.** **NAA: BP25/1, ITALIAN MAZZA M**, Brisbane, Item ID 5041955, access **Open**: *«Mazza [nee Nicotra], Maria — Nationality: Italian — arrived Sydney **20 April 1962** on PHDCG».* **Three things at once.** It confirms **Nicotra** as her maiden name from an Australian government record rather than from the family tree. It gives an **arrival this archive did not have** — widowed in 1929, she came out at about eighty-seven to her sons and died at Brisbane the next year. And an alien registration file of this kind routinely carries a **date and place of birth**, which is the one fact the whole Piedimonte sweep is trying to reach. **It is not digitised**, so it is a copy request at Brisbane and not a search — [row 164](/worklist/), offered to David alongside the four files already waiting in [row 150](/worklist/). **FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE YEARS, 1870–1883.** 1882 gives *Nicotra Nunzia 65, Nucifora Rosaria 103, Nicodemo Francesco 114*; 1883 gives *Nicotra Rosa 27* and four Nucifora. **The Piedimonte hypothesis has now been tested across the whole plausible window** — she died in 1963 at eighty-eight, which puts her birth about 1875, and 1870–1883 brackets that by five years either side. **This row now waits on [row 164](/worklist/)**, her own alien registration file at Brisbane, rather than on more Italian indexes: 1866–1869 and 1884–1893 remain, but reading them would be sweeping outside the window rather than closing it. **And the same two pages answered a question nobody had asked of them:** the 1883 M section holds *Mazza Rosaria 117* and *Mazza Venera 118* — consecutive numbers — and **no Orazio**, so the tree's «Orazio Mazza, born 1883» has no act there. [Flagged, not disproved](/corrections/). **AND THE SURNAME THIS ARCHIVE HAS BEEN SEARCHING IS PROBABLY WRONG.** The Queensland index was swept by surname: **«CASSANETI» returns nothing at all** — Maria's own 1963 death registration is the only instance of that spelling in the entire Queensland index, taken down from an informant at a Brisbane registry — while **«CASSANITI» returns five**, and Cassaniti is the ordinary Catanese form. It is also what the **Piedimonte birth index** writes: a *Cassaniti Sebastiano* and a *Cassaniti Leonardo Maria* in 1875 alone. **A Sicilian register searched for «Cassaneti» will return nothing and the negative will mean nothing.** **The same sweep also closes a question nobody had asked:** eighteen Nicotra registrations in Queensland and **not one other names John Nicotra or Venera Cassaneti as a parent**, so Maria seems to have had no sibling who died or married there. The Queensland Nicotra are Maccarone, Patanè, Scalia and Carbone households, and none of them is hers. **AND THE NAME INDEX CANNOT REACH HER EITHER, 21 SEPTEMBER.** *Nicotra* at Catania returns eight deceased and not one is hers — Concetta at Catenanuova, three Giuseppe and a Nunziata at **Vicopisano, which is in Tuscany**. That is this archive's own `localita=` caution demonstrated in its own data: the parameter matches any place attached to a person, not the place of death, so a query scoped to Catania returned people who died four hundred miles away. *Cassaniti* at Catania returns **nothing**, control-tested in the same breath against *Arena at Scilla*, which returns sixty-nine. **This row still waits on [row 164](/worklist/)**, the Brisbane file.  **AND THE MARRIAGE INDEX IS A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT FROM THE BIRTH INDEX.** Fourteen years of BIRTH indexes produced nothing. Piedimonte's annual **«Indice Annuale per gli atti DI MATRIMONIO»** names **both spouses** — groom above, bride below — on **one page-pair for the whole year**, so a year is eliminated without opening an act. **1871 is read in full: twenty-six acts, all twenty-six couples written out on [what has been read](/searched/), and NO Nicotra groom and no Cassaniti bride.** (There is a «Cassanoti Giovanni» at act 12; he marries an Amante Rosaria.) **Sweeping 1866–1885 is about twenty crops**, and only the 1871 container is bought. **AND THE BIRTH TAVOLA HAS HANDED OVER A CANDIDATE FOR HER MOTHER:** Nati 1848 atto 45, **«Cassaniti Venera — Cassaniti Gaetano / Venuti Maria»**. [Row 89](/worklist/). **This row no longer waits only on [row 164](/worklist/).**  **FOUND, AND THE FOURTEEN EMPTY YEARS HAVE AN EXPLANATION.** **Piedimonte Etneo, Matrimoni 1872 atto 20, 7 October 1872:** *«sono comparsi **GIOVANNI NICOTRA**, di anni trentuno, bracciante, **domiciliato e residente a MASCALI**, figlio di **ROSARIO** … e di **VENERA MURABITO**, contadina, domiciliati e residenti pure in Mascali. E **VENERA CASSANITI**, di anni ventiquattro, qui domiciliata, figlia del **fu GAETANO** e di **fu MARIA CURRENTI**.»* **Four new people at generation six** and the two blank cards on `/tree/` are filled. **HER FATHER WAS A MASCALI MAN.** This row read fourteen consecutive Piedimonte birth indexes and the Nicotra never produced her — because a wife went to her husband's comune, and **the children of this marriage were registered at MASCALI**, which this archive has never opened and never listed. The Catania hypothesis is retired: it was invented to explain a silence that has a simpler cause. **This row no longer waits on [row 164](/worklist/) at all.** [Row 173](/worklist/) opens Mascali.  **AND SHE IS FOUND.** **Mascali, Nati 1875, atto 144** — born **8 December 1875**, father Giovanni Nicotra, mother Venera Cassaniti. This row's fourteen consecutive Piedimonte indexes were read in the wrong town, and the 1872 marriage act said so in six words: *«domiciliato e residente a MASCALI»*. **Closed.**

rows.what: The Riveli di anime e di terre — Piedimonte households in 1714 and 1747–1752
rows.note: **This archive has been saying «Sicily begins in 1820, and before that it is parish records or nothing». That is wrong, and the register index says so.** Antenati holds **nine volumes** for Piedimonte from the **Deputazione del Regno**: *Riveli di anime e di terre*, **1714** (`qJkjONB`, 283 images) and **1747–1752** (`noPNme4`, 73 images, plus four more volumes). **A *rivelo* is a household tax return sworn by the head of the house**, and it lists the house, the head, his wife, his children and their ages — a census of souls and land, a century before any civil register in Sicily. For a family whose Sicilian ceiling is **Mariano Mazza, born about 1809**, this is the only source that can reach behind him without a parish archive. **What it can and cannot do.** It cannot prove descent: a Mazza household at Piedimonte in 1747 is not *evidence* that it is this Mazza household. What it can do is give the **shape** — how many Mazza households there were, what given names ran in them, and whether the surname is native to the town or arrived later — which is exactly what the repeated Mariano–Rosario–Orazio naming would be tested against. **Read it for the shape first and make no joins.** Start with the smaller 1747–1748 volume. **THE 1747–1748 VOLUME IS READ, AT LEAST ITS INDEX, AND THE ANSWER IS A NEGATIVE WORTH HAVING.** **Images 1–14 are an alphabetical index** with cut letter tabs down the fore-edge — and it is alphabetised **by given name**, so there is no shortcut: all fourteen openings, about eighty households, were read. **There is no Mazza.** There are two **MAZZEO** — *Onofrio Mazzeo, folio 5* and *Silvestro Mazzeo, folio 29* — and the ending was cropped at native resolution on both because it is exactly the kind of near-match that has fooled this archive before. **Mazzeo is not Mazza until something says it is.** **What makes the negative meaningful is how recognisable the rest of the town is:** Pagano, Currenti, Grasso, Musumeci, Vasta, Puglisi, Torrisi, Moschella, di Mauro, Ricceri, Zappalà, Patanè — the same surnames that fill the birth indexes of the 1870s and 1880s, read this week. The register is legible and the town is continuous, and **the Mazza are not in it**. Set beside the nineteenth-century evidence — no Mazza birth at all in 1844 or 1846, two in 1845, four marriages in sixteen years — that is a second piece pointing the same way: **a small family, possibly a recent one**. [Recorded as probable, not documented](/corrections/). **What is left in this row:** the **1714** volume (`qJkjONB`, 283 images), which is four times the size and may or may not carry an index of its own; and the two Mazzeo folios themselves, 5 and 29, which would say whether that household looks anything like a Mazza one. **AND THE TWO MAZZEO FOLIOS ARE READ.** The folio numbers sit in the top outer corner with an older number struck through, so the map is five probes wide: **folio = image − 16**. **Folio 5:** *«Rivelo che Io ONOFRIO MAZZEO … in virtù di Bando promulgato sotto li 30 Aprile 1747. ANIME: Notato Onofrio Mazzeo d'anni TRENTA; et CARMINA moglie; et GIUSEPPE figlio.»* **Folio 29:** *«Rivelo che Io SILVESTRO MAZZEO … ANIME: M.ro Silvestro Mazzeo d'anni TRENTACINQUE; et MARIA moglie»*, and then his house — *«un loggio terraneo di pietra a cruda, scagliato dentro e di fuori di calce, per proprio abitare, consistente in una stanza in piano»*: one ground-floor room of rough stone, limewashed inside and out. **The surname is settled** — MAZZEO four times over, in two hands, never Mazza. **And the limit of the source is now known, which is worth as much as the content.** A rivelo runs *«Rivelo che Io …»* naming the declarant and the bando, then **ANIME**, then **BENI STABILI** in close detail, then the dues. **At Piedimonte only the HEAD's age is given** — Carmina and Giuseppe and Maria are named and not aged. So a rivelo here will **not** hand over a wife's or a child's birth year, which is the thing one hopes for from a census. It gives the household and the house. **Read it for shape, exactly as this row said.** **THE 1714 VOLUME IS READ TOO, 21 SEPTEMBER, AND ITS OWN ARITHMETIC IS WHAT SAVED THE READING.** Images 1–17 are a summary index — *Nomi | Somme di Lordo | di Netto | Cagione di Riveli | folio* — alphabetised **by given name** again, **142 households**. **Twelve of the seventeen were read first, and two of them looked like blank versos at thumbnail size. The running totals said otherwise:** p6 closes at 1468 and p8 opens with a *riporto* of **2556**; p8 closes at 3774 and p10 opens at **4023**. Eleven households nobody had read. Both pages were fetched at full width and hold entries **73–80** and **106–108**. **A double-entry book checks itself**, and this one caught a negative that would otherwise have been eleven households short. **No Mazza and no Mazzeo in 1714.** So the sequence is: **1714 neither; 1747–1748 two MAZZEO and no Mazza; the civil registers from 1820 Mazza and no Mazzeo** — while Pagano, Currenti, Grasso, Musumeci, Vasta, Puglisi, Torrisi, Moschella and dell'Aquila run through all three. **That is a shape, not a descent.** A rivelo is a tax return; a household can be missing from one; and **Mazzeo is not Mazza until a record says so.** Recorded as *probable*.

rows.what: Mariano Mazza, born 12 February 1872 — the son the naming custom promised
rows.note: **Found in an index opened for somebody else, which is the third time that has happened this week.** The 1872 birth index was being read for a Maria Nicotra. Its M section held **«Mazza Mariano — 32»**. **Act 32, read in the original:** *«L'anno milleottocentosettantadue, nel giorno tredici Febbraro ... è comparso ROSARIO MAZZA DI MARIANO, d'anni ventisette, bracciante ... un bambino di sesso maschile ... nato il giorno dodici corrente Febbraro alle ore dieci pomeridiane, dalla di lui moglie LEONARDA BONANNO DI GAETANO ... contrada SAN BASILIO ... al quale figlio dichiara di dare il nome di MARIANO.»* Witnesses Leonardo Grasso di Sebastiano, fifty, and Carmelo Russo fu Venero, forty. **Three things fall out of one act.** **(1)** Rosario and Leonarda have a **fifth child**, and he is the eldest — the tree gives them four. **(2)** The first son is named **for his father's father**, which is precisely what the Sicilian naming custom predicts, and it is now the third independent pointer at **Mariano Mazza (b. c. 1809)** after the 1845 birth act and the *«di Mariano»* patronymic. **(3)** Rosario is **twenty-seven** in February 1872, so born about **1845** — a third statement against the tree's 1850, this one his own at a registration desk. **One thing not resolved.** Salvatore was born **5 January 1873**, eleven months after this boy. Either Mariano died in infancy or the two births are ten and a half months apart. **The Piedimonte death registers of 1872–1875 would say**, and they are listed and unbought. **And the custom is being used the way this archive says it should be** — to rank a candidate, never to make an identification. It did not find Mariano; the index did. It only explains him.

rows.what: One file at Brisbane would end the Nicotra search: NAA BP25/1, ITALIAN MAZZA M
rows.note: **This archive has read twelve consecutive years of Piedimonte birth registers looking for where Maria Nicotra was born. Her own file probably says.** **NAA: BP25/1, ITALIAN MAZZA M** — Item ID **5041955**, held at **Brisbane**, access **Open**, not digitised. Titled *«Mazza [nee Nicotra], Maria — Nationality: Italian — arrived Sydney 20 April 1962 on PHDCG».* **Why it matters more than another year of registers.** An Italian alien's registration file carries the particulars the holder gave the Commonwealth: **date of birth, place of birth**, last address in Italy, nearest relative. If it says *Piedimonte Etneo* then the twelve negatives mean her year is wrong and the sweep widens; if it names another comune — Catania, Linguaglossa, Fiumefreddo, anywhere — then the sweep stops and this archive goes there instead. **Either answer is worth more than ten more indexes.** **What it needs:** a copy request through RecordSearch, or an hour in the Brisbane reading room. It is already open, so nothing has to be applied for first. **Worth ordering in the same request as [row 150](/worklist/)'s four Brisbane files**, which are also NAA and also not yet examined.  **NO LONGER THE ONLY ROUTE, AND NO LONGER URGENT.** This file was wanted because an alien registration file states a date and place of birth, and that was the one fact the whole Piedimonte sweep could not reach. **It has now been read off her own birth act instead** — Mascali, 8 December 1875. The file is still worth having for the 1962 arrival and whatever else it carries, but it is no longer blocking [row 161](/worklist/).

rows.what: Gaetano Mazza, born 5 May 1880 — and the custom calls a second child in a row
rows.note: **A lead written down as a lead, and then tested.** The 1880 birth index carried «Mazza Gaetano — 66». That was recorded here as *«it may be another child of Rosario and Leonarda or another of the town's Mazza households; not opened, nothing claimed»* — because Piedimonte holds **three** Mazza households and one of them is a second Rosario with a second Leonarda ([row 163](/worklist/) and [the corrections](/corrections/)). **Act 66, read in the original:** *«L'anno milleottocento ottanta, addì nove di Maggio … è comparso MAZZA ROSARIO, di anni trentadue, bracciante … nella casa posta in VIA S. BASILIO … da BONANNO LEONARDA, industriosa, sua moglie … il nome di GAETANO»*, born at half past four on the afternoon of **5 May 1880**. Witnesses Dimauro Salvatore, twenty-two, and Zappalà Sebastiano, twenty-four. Registered before **Ignazio Dr. Fragalà**, assessore delegato, not the sindaco. **What settled it was the street and the mother's surname**, not the name Mazza and not the name Rosario. The other household is in via Grotta Nicodemo and its Leonarda is a **Monacorso**. **And the naming custom has now called two children in a row.** Mariano in 1872 for the father's father; Gaetano in 1880 for the mother's father, **Gaetano Bonanno**, who is named as such in the 1872 and 1873 acts. First son for the paternal grandfather, then the maternal grandfather — the order the custom prescribes. **It still did not find either of them; the index did. It explains them.** **One disagreement recorded rather than smoothed:** Rosario is *«trentadue»* here, which would put his birth in 1848, where he is twenty-seven in 1872 and twenty-eight in 1873 and his own birth act says **2 June 1845**. A declared age is a statement, not a measurement.

rows.what: Caterina Melluso, born Briatico 1860 — a wall with not one record against her
rows.note: **She is on the chart and she is blank.** Caterina Melluso, born at Briatico in 1860, died 1957, married **Alfonso Prostamo** and had six children including **Francessco Prostamo**, who came to Brisbane in 1957. The family tree gives her **no parents**, and this archive has **never opened a single record for her** — her person page carries none. **Two documents would do it:** her birth act of 1860, which names her father with his age and her mother; or her marriage to Alfonso, about 1880, which names both couples. **And the first thing checked was not the records but the listing, because that is what Piedimonte taught today.** `briatico-arks.tsv` holds **eighty** registers. **Briatico has 555** — the facets read *Catanzaro (440)* and *Vibo Valentia (115)*. **So the same under-listing was sitting on the deepest line in the archive.** **What is established and what is not.** A listing at `s_size=500` returned 500 of the 555 and showed the years running **1810 to 1930 with nothing between 1859 and 1910**. **That is not yet a finding.** Fifty-five registers were not in the sample, and the Vibo Valentia holdings are exactly where a later series would sit. A 500-of-555 listing reported as a gap would be the same error as a half-read index section reported as a negative — paid for twice already this week. `s_size` above 500 times out and the rate limiter closed the session before year probes could settle it. **Next, and cheap:** one complete listing, or three year probes — 1860, 1880, 1900. If the gap is real, Caterina is a **Vibo Valentia** archive enquiry or a comune letter, not a search. If it is not, her birth act is one container away.

rows.what: Candeloro Donato × Marta Paladino — a marriage the 1816 error had closed
rows.note: **Found by fixing a sentence, not by a search.** This archive wrote, of Candeloro Donato: *«the first age this archive has ever had for him, and the last it will get — Scilla's civil registration begins in 1816, so his own birth and marriage are pre-civil … HE IS WHERE THE SCILLA LINE STOPS».* **Scilla's registers begin in 1809.** His own birth, about 1783, is still out of reach. **His marriage is not necessarily.** Their son **Michele** was born at Messina about 1814 and **Domenico** at Scilla on 18 December 1816, so the marriage is **before 1814** — and **1809 to 1813 at Scilla are civil and reachable**. **What is already read, from the Arena sweep, at no extra cost:** 1810, 1811 and 1812 through their annual indexes and **1815** groom by groom — **no Donato**. 1816 and 1817 were read groom by groom too, and hold none. **What is left is 1809 and 1813–1814**, the two napoleonic volumes with no index at all — and both fall to the [act-head montage](/searched/) that read 1815, 1816 and 1817 in an afternoon. Containers are banked: 1809 `LD6vJel`, 1813–1814 `0MnkW4l`. **And if it is in neither**, the marriage is pre-1809 and the conclusion this row corrects turns out to have been right for the wrong reason — which is still worth writing down, because a right answer resting on a false premise is not evidence. **SIX YEARS CLEAR, 20 SEPTEMBER, AND THE TWO UNINDEXED VOLUMES ARE READ.** **1809** (twenty-five acts, the first year Scilla ever registered a marriage) and **1813–1814** (forty-four acts) were read groom by groom off the act head, both to their closing statements. **No Donato groom in either.** With 1815, 1816 and 1817 that is **six years clear**. **Three are not clear and this row will not pretend they are:** 1810, 1811 and 1812 were read through their Tavole **for the letter F**, on the Arena hunt — and a *Candeloro* sits under **C** or **D**. Those three openings have to be looked at again, which is three crops, not three volumes. **If they are clear too, the marriage is pre-1809 and parish**, and the conclusion this row corrects turns out to have been right for the wrong reason — which is still worth writing down. **CLOSED THE SAME DAY IT WAS OPENED, AND THE ANSWER IS THE ONE THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HELD.** The three indexed years were re-read **whole** rather than for one letter — and they are richer than expected: **1810's indice names both spouses**, and the **1811 and 1812 Tavole name both spouses AND all four parents**. **1810's C section is one line** (Corro Weingarten); **1811's is one line** (Candido Giordano); **1812 has no C groom at all**. **No Donato appears anywhere in any of the three — not as a spouse, not as a parent.** **So nine consecutive years, 1809 to 1817, hold no Donato marriage at Scilla.** Michele was born at Messina about 1814, so the marriage is before 1814; nine civil years exclude it; **therefore it is pre-1809 and parish**. **The conclusion is what this archive said this morning. The reasoning is entirely different, and that was the point** — it used to rest on a start year that was false. A right answer resting on a false premise is not evidence. It now rests on nine complete readings.

rows.what: More Arena siblings, and the year Orazio and Litteria die
rows.note: **Opened by [row 157](/worklist/) closing.** Finding one sibling took one crop, because the Scilla marriage **Tavole are alphabetised by surname in the Italian-era and restauration years** and name **both spouses and all four parents** — so Arena sits at the top of the book and a whole year is a single A-section crop. **Twenty-one containers are banked, 1820 to 1843**, and 1820 and 1821 are read. **Nineteen years remain and each is one crop.** **What they can give.** More children of Orazio Arena and Litteria Morabito — there is no reason to think Filippo and Giuseppe were the only two. And **the year the parents die**: the Tavola marks the dead with *«fu»*, so the first Arena entry that writes *«fu Orazio»* brackets his death between that year and November 1821. **What they cannot give.** Anything above Orazio. His own marriage is pre-1809 and parish — [row 158](/worklist/). **One caution carried forward:** Scilla holds at least **four** Arena households in this period — Orazio's, Domenico the barber's, Carlo's, and the Rocco of 1821 act 20 whose parents are different again. **The parents' column is the only thing that tells them apart**, and it is in the Tavola, which is why the Tavola is the instrument and not the act. **TWELVE YEARS READ, 1820–1831, AND A SECOND BROTHER.** The method held: one crop a year, except that the Tavola starts at image **n−3** in some years and **n−2** in others, so both get fetched. **1828 opens on him.** *«ARENA ANTONIO e DE LUCA SERAFINA — Scilla — **ORAZIO, e MORABITO LETTERIA** / fu Filippo, ed Alfonzetto Anna — 10 Ag.o 1828 — 26».* **Neither parent carries «fu»**, so Orazio and Litteria were both alive on **10 August 1828** — thirteen years after Filippo's wedding, seven after Giuseppe's. **So Orazio and Litteria had at least three sons:** Filippo (1793), Giuseppe (c. 1794) and Antonio. **And the surname's shape is now plain.** Eight Arena grooms in twelve years, in **seven households**: Rocco (1821, mother Vittoria Fiorenza); Antonio (1822) and Luciano (1827), both sons of *Giuseppe ed Antonia Polimeni* and therefore brothers; Carlo (1826, *fu Antonino e Vittoria Molinari*); Antonino (1827, *Giuseppe e Carmela d'Amico*); Bonaventura (1827, *Rocco e Domenica Samari*); and Orazio's two. **Without the parents' column these eight men are one indistinguishable surname** — which is why the Tavola is the instrument and the act is not. **Four years have no A section at all** (1823, 1829, 1830, 1831) and three have a single A entry that is not an Arena. **Twelve years remain, 1832–1843, containers banked.** **AND THE SWEEP FOUND WHAT IT WAS BUILT TO FIND, 1832–1838.** The 1838 Tavola opens on *«ARENA DOMENICO e POLISTINA TERESA — **FU ORAZIO**, e Lett.a Morabito — 4 7bre 1838 — 20».* **The «fu» is the finding.** Orazio Arena is named **living** in the Tavole of 1821 and 1828 and **dead** in 1838, so **he died between 10 August 1828 and 4 September 1838** — ten years, every one of them covered by a Scilla death register this archive has already listed. **Letteria Morabito outlived him**; she carries no *«fu»*. **And Domenico is a fourth son**, after Filippo, Giuseppe and Antonio. **Two of the four married Polistina sisters** — Giuseppe took Maria Teresa in 1821 and Domenico took Teresa in 1838, both *«figlie di fu Raffaele Polistina e Letteria Morabito»*. Two sisters and two brothers, or one widow marrying her brother-in-law; **nothing read settles it** and the death registers would. **Two more Arena grooms, neither ours:** Francesco in 1833 (*«fu Santo, e Fiorenza Vittoria»*) — which also supplies the cut-off father's name for the Rocco Arena of 1821, same mother, so they are brothers and their father is **Santo Arena**; and Santo in 1836 (*«fu Domenico, e Autieri Santa»*). **Five years remain, 1839–1843.** **THE RUN IS COMPLETE, 1820–1843, TWENTY-FOUR CONSECUTIVE YEARS.** 1839 has no A section; 1840 and 1842 have one A entry each and neither is an Arena; **1841** holds *Arena Rocco × Martello Domenica* («fu Santo») — either the Rocco of 1821 remarrying as a widower or a namesake in the same household — and **1843** holds *Arena Salvadore, **calzolaio**, × Polistina Maria, **filatrice*** («Gaetano e Lomanti Camilla»). **No child of Orazio Arena marries after 1838**, which is what four sons already married by then would predict. **The whole run: twelve Arena grooms in about eight households, three of them Orazio's** — Giuseppe 1821, Antonio 1828, Domenico 1838, with Filippo's 1815 marriage just outside the range. **One form change worth knowing for the next sweep:** from **1842** the Tavola adds a **Professione** column for both spouses. **And one practical warning:** the Tavola's first page sits anywhere between n−4 and n−2 with no rule, so several years cost a second fetch just to find it. **What this row cannot do is go higher.** Orazio's own marriage is pre-1809 and parish. **What follows it is [row 169](/worklist/)** — his death, now bracketed to ten years, and a death act names parents.

rows.what: Orazio Arena's death — ten years, and every volume is listed
rows.note: **The narrowest window this archive has ever had on a death, and it was bought with one word.** The 1828 marriage Tavola names Orazio Arena living; the 1838 one writes *«fu Orazio»*. **He died between 10 August 1828 and 4 September 1838.** **Every volume in that window is already listed.** Scilla's *restaurazione* death series runs **51 volumes, 1817–1865**, in `scilla-arks.tsv` — so the ten years cost ten containers and ten A-section crops, and the annual death Tavole are alphabetised the same way as the marriage ones. **What it would give.** A death act names the age, the trade, the address and often the parents — which is the only remaining route to **Orazio's own father**, a generation this archive cannot otherwise reach because his marriage is pre-1809 and parish ([row 158](/worklist/)). **And LETTERIA MORABITO is in the same window and beyond it.** She outlived him — no *«fu»* in 1838 — so her death is 1838 or later, and the same series runs to 1865. **Read his first:** a widow's death act names her husband, so finding him narrows her, and finding her does not narrow him. **CLOSED THE SAME AFTERNOON IT WAS OPENED, IN THE SECOND YEAR READ.** The death Tavole turn out to be the **same instrument** as the marriage ones — surname order, a parents column, and for a married person the **spouse** in it — so a year costs one A-section crop. **Scilla, Morti 1830:** *«ARENA ORAZIO — Scilla — MARINARO — Mar.to MORABITO LETTERIA — 12 Luglio».* **And the act gives a generation.** Atto 64, reached by walking the dates rather than the index, because the Tavola's number is its own row and not the act: *«ORAZIO ARENA, MARITO LITTERIA MORABITO, nato in questo Comune, **DI ANNI SETTANTANOVE**, di professione MARINARO, **FIGLIO DEL FU FILIPPO ARENA E DELLA FU SANTA UNGARO**»*, dead at six in the morning of 12 July 1830 in his own house, declared by **Diego Arena, twenty-two**, and **Prospero Arena, twenty-five**, both marinari and both *«nipote del defonto»*. **Three things.** The death is exact **to the hour**. He was born about **1751**, **nineteen years** earlier than this archive had inferred by working back from his sons and assuming a young father. And **his parents are named** — **FILIPPO ARENA** and **SANTA UNGARO**, generation nine. **The naming custom, confirmed after the fact rather than used to identify.** Orazio's first son, born 25 March 1793, is a **Filippo** — named for this Filippo. This archive has spent four months using the custom to rank candidates and refusing to make a join with it; this is what it looks like when a record catches up.

rows.what: Litteria Morabito's death, and two young Arena who called him uncle
rows.note: **Three questions left standing by [row 169](/worklist/), all of them cheap.** **LITTERIA MORABITO outlived him by at least eight years.** Orazio died 12 July 1830 and she is named without *«fu»* in the 1838 marriage Tavola, so her death is **1838 or later** and Scilla's death series runs to 1865. **A widow's death act names her husband**, so the A section of each year from 1838 will find her the same way his did — one crop a year, and *«vedova di Arena Orazio»* in the parents column is the whole test. **DIEGO ARENA, twenty-two, and PROSPERO ARENA, twenty-five**, declared his death and the act calls both *«nipote del defonto»* — which in Italian is **nephew or grandson** and the act does not choose. Born about 1808 and about 1805, they are **too old to be sons of Filippo or Giuseppe**, who married in 1815 and 1821 — which points at **nephew**, and a nephew means **Orazio had a brother**. Their birth acts are pre-1809 for Prospero and 1808–1809 for Diego, so one of them may be reachable and the other is parish. **And FILIPPO ARENA THE ELDER and SANTA UNGARO are the end.** Orazio was born about 1751, so they belong to the 1720s, and nothing civil exists. That is [row 158](/worklist/) — the parish books of the Chiesa Matrice, whose custodians the 1815 marriage bundle already names. **SIXTEEN CONTAINERS BANKED, 20 SEPTEMBER** — Scilla deaths 1828–1836 and 1838–1844 — so what is left is reading. **And the first year read has already exposed a flaw in the plan.** The 1838 A section holds no Litteria: *Arlotta Mariano, Arlotta Caterina, Arlotta Antonino, **Arena Rocco** (11 Agosto), Arlotta Mariano, Arlotta Giuseppe*. **But reading the A section is only HALF a search for a married woman**, and this archive knows it: Serafina Arlotta is entered as *«ARENA Serafina, fu Giovanni»* in the 1908 index — her **husband's** surname over her father's forename. **So Litteria Morabito may sit under A for Arena or under M for Morabito**, and the M section has not been read for a single year. **Two crops a year, not one.** Recorded as *part* rather than done so that nobody later mistakes six A sections for a search. **And one name to come back for:** the Arena Rocco who died 11 August 1838 has not been identified against the seven Arena households of the town. **FIVE YEARS READ AT BOTH LETTERS, 21 SEPTEMBER: 1838, 1839, 1840, 1841, 1842.** Each year's **A and M sections both**, which is what the flaw above demanded — and every M section is quoted whole on [the Scilla reads](/scilla/). **Eight Morabito deaths across the five years and not one is a Litteria or a Letteria.** **Still PART, not done.** The window is not closed: Scilla's deaths run to 1865 in the restauration fondo and to 1943 in the Italian one. Containers are banked to 1844. **And the by-product is a warning rather than a lead:** five **Arena** deaths turned up in those A sections and **none belongs to Orazio's household** — Rocco 1838, Giuseppa 1839, Giuseppe and Santo 1841, Giuseppe 1842, whose parents read *«Ant.o e Ros…»*, *«Fran.co e Falcomatà»* and *«Santo e Martello Angela»*. Seven Arena families in one town, and the parents' column is the only thing that tells them apart.

rows.what: A status this archive cannot write: read, and the source is empty
rows.note: **Raised by the Falco archive, 21 September, and it is a real hole.** They found Arienzo births **1836**: a Tavola with a printed heading, ruled columns, and **every cell empty**. Their point is the one that matters: *«that is nastier than absence, because it files itself in your notes as ‘not read’ and somebody re-opens it.»* **`searched.tsv` cannot say it.** The vocabulary is `done`, `outstanding`, `not-yet`, `part`, `superseded`, `wall`, `correction`. A blank-but-present source is not `done` (nothing was found), not `wall` (nothing blocked it), and emphatically not `not-yet`. It would go in as `done` with a note, and the note is the only thing stopping the next person opening it again. **This archive does not have a clean instance yet**, which is why this is a row and not a patch. What it has is the adjacent class: **present but unreadable** — Scilla Matrimoni 1816 catalogued *VOLUME TARLATO*, the 1842 death Tavola carrying an *INCHIOSTRO SBIADITO* card, the 1845 birth index with seven of eighteen lines too faint. Those are recorded in prose and would be better recorded in the status. **Do not invent vocabulary for a case that has not happened.** When the first genuinely blank source turns up here, add ONE word and update `check_searched.py` with it — and tell the estate, because Falco has the same gap and reached it first. **AND THREE CONCRETE CASES ARRIVED THE SAME DAY.** Mascali births **1876 and 1877** were read at the N section, every entry, and their indexes carry **no paternità column** — so the Nicotra entries there are neither found nor absent. 1874, whose index *does* carry the column, is a clean negative from the identical amount of work. **The status this archive cannot write is the difference between those two readings**, and writing them both as «part» loses it. **AND HERE IS THE CASE MADE AGAINST THIS ARCHIVE'S OWN WORK, THREE HOURS APART.** «Cassaniti» in the Antenati name index returns nothing for the whole of Italy, and that was filed as a control-tested real negative. The same afternoon the archive read **Cassaniti Gaetano** in a Piedimonte Tavola and **Venera Cassaniti** in two acts. **The instrument was read correctly, the source was empty, and the emptiness was a fact about the instrument** — Piedimonte and Mascali are not name-indexed. `done` is wrong, `wall` is wrong, and `part` loses the distinction entirely.

rows.what: PIEDIMONTE — sweep the marriage indexes 1866–1885 for a NICOTRA groom
rows.note: **The cheapest unopened route into the thinnest quarter of the family.** Piedimonte's Italian-era marriage volumes each carry an annual index that names **both spouses** for every act, on a single page-pair. One crop-pair per year eliminates the year. **1871 is done** — twenty-six couples, no Nicotra. The rest, 1866–1870 and 1872–1885, need **one batched container lookup** (the arks are in `pe-arks.tsv`; only 1871 carries a container) and then about twenty crops. **What it would settle:** the marriage of **Giovanni Nicotra and Venera Cassaniti**, which names both sets of parents and would carry generation five of the Sicilian quarter — the side [row 161](/worklist/) calls the one nobody has ever searched. **And it tests [row 89](/worklist/)'s candidate** — the Venera Cassaniti born at Piedimonte in 1848 — without another birth sweep. **Mind the DUPLICATA:** these volumes are photographed twice and the numbers at the top right are **folios, not act numbers**.  **1870 AND 1872 DONE, AND 1872 WAS THE ANSWER.** 1870's N section is one line — «Nucifora Michele, Lo Coco Nicoletta, 15». **1872's N section is «NICOTRA GIOVANNI, E CASSANITI VENERA — 20»**, and act 20 is legible whole on a single page. **The instrument worked exactly as predicted: two crops a year, no act opened to eliminate a year.** 1873, 1874 and 1875 have containers banked and are no longer needed for the Nicotra question — but they remain worth reading for the **other** Piedimonte households this archive is tracking, and the Mazza sons' marriages fall in the 1890s and beyond, past Antenati's run.

rows.what: MASCALI — the comune this archive has never opened, and Maria Nicotra was probably born there
rows.note: **A fifth town, and it arrives with a reason rather than a hope.** Matrimoni 1872 atto 20 puts **Giovanni Nicotra «domiciliato e residente a MASCALI»** and his parents Rosario Nicotra and Venera Murabito «residenti pure in Mascali». Venera Cassaniti was the Piedimonte one; he was not. **A wife went to her husband's comune**, so the children of the October 1872 marriage — **Maria (about 1875), Rosa, Venera, Nina, Angela, Rosario and Antonina**, all seven of them in the family's own export — should be in **Mascali's** birth registers, not Piedimonte's. **That is why [row 161](/worklist/) read fourteen consecutive Piedimonte indexes and found nothing.** **What to do, in order.** (1) List Mascali on Antenati with `?localita=Mascali&s_size=500` and **check the count against the facet total**, because a listing at the ceiling is a sample. (2) Bank the ark rows in a `mascali-arks.tsv` and add the comune to `antenati-coverage.tsv` and the holdings table. (3) Read the **annual birth index** for 1873–1885 at the N section — the same instrument row 161 built, on the right town this time. (4) **Rosario Nicotra and Venera Murabito's own marriage**, about 1840, which would carry generation seven. **And check whether Mascali is name-indexed** before sweeping anything: Scilla, Pizzo and Catania are, and one query would replace the lot.  **LISTED, BANKED, AND SHE WAS IN THE SECOND YEAR READ.** The listing is **498 results, 498 distinct arks, and facets that total 498 exactly** — Catania 452, Palermo 46 — so it is the whole holding and not a sample at the ceiling. All 498 rows are in `data/mascali-arks.tsv`. **Mascali runs 1820–1893** like Piedimonte, with processetti from 1841 — **and 46 volumes at Palermo that are not civil registration at all**: riveli from **1616**, a century before Piedimonte's earliest. **One gap recorded: there is no 1844**, in any series. **THEN THE SWEEP.** 1873's index carries a *paternità* column and gives **«Nicotra Venera, 12 Dicembre 1873, Giovanni»** — the couple's first child, fourteen months after the wedding. 1875's index gives **«Nicotra Maria — 144»**, and act 144 read in the original is **MARIA NICOTRA, born at Mascali on 8 December 1875 at half past nine in the evening, in contrada Sopra Pietrafitta, daughter of Giovanni Nicotra and Venera Cassaniti.** **The tree's «born Piedimonte Etneo» was her mother's town.** **What is left here:** the other five children, **Giovanni Nicotra's own birth act** (1841 or 1847 — his two declared ages disagree by six years), and **Rosario Nicotra × Venera Murabito's marriage**, about 1840, which would carry generation seven. **THREE MORE YEARS READ, AND THEY SPLIT INTO TWO KINDS.** **1874 is a true negative** — its index carries a *paternità* column, its N section is two lines, and neither is Giovanni's. **1876 and 1877 have no paternità column**, so their Nicotra entries (Giuseppa 81; Mariano 10 and **Rosaria** 8 — and the export carries a *Rosa*) are **read and unresolved**, which is not the same as absent. The acts must be opened. **And 1874 handed over the namesake trap in person:** Mascali registered a *second* Maria Nicotra, daughter of a **Gaetano**, on 28 March 1874 — eighteen months before ours. An index line alone would have been a coin toss. **AND HIS OWN BIRTH IS NOT IN EITHER YEAR HE NAMED.** Mascali's Bourbon birth Tavole are alphabetical and **name both parents**, so a *Giovanni Nicotra of Rosario and Venera Murabito* would identify itself without an act being opened. **1841's N section is one line** (Nicolosi Salvadore) and **1847's is two** (Nicolosi Domenico; Nicotra Maria of Alfio) — both checked into the next letter before being written down. **He is in neither.** That does not put him in another comune: this archive has now watched him lose six years between two acts and Leonarda Bonanno lose four, so a declared age is a bracket. **Next: Mascali Nati 1838–1850, ten more Tavole, one crop each.** **GENERATION SEVEN ATTEMPTED, AND THE INSTRUMENT IS PROVED EVEN THOUGH THE YEAR WAS EMPTY.** Mascali's restauration **marriage** Tavola is alphabetical by groom and carries a **four-line parents column** — both spouses and all four of their parents, dead ones marked «fu». **Matrimoni 1840's N section is one entry** (Nicolosi Francesco × Mercurio Francesca) and the facing page opens at P, so it is complete: **no Nicotra marriage at Mascali in 1840.** **Better plan than hunting the marriage across fifteen years:** the **birth** Tavole name both parents too, so one «Nicotra [X] — Nicotra Rosario / Murabito Venera» would place the household and bracket the marriage from below. **Fifteen Mascali containers are now banked** (Nati 1839–1843, 1845–1848, Matrimoni 1840), so what is left is reading, not fetching. **And 1842 is out of reach for a physical reason:** its birth Tavola is **torn**, with the archive's own «Torn Page(s)» card over it and the M–P run on the lost side. **That year cannot be recorded as a negative** — the section is missing, not empty. **THE WHOLE DECADE IS READ AND IT CHANGES THE QUESTION.** Mascali births **1839–1848**, every N section, each one checked into the next letter: **1839 has no N section at all** (M runs straight into P); **1843 and 1846 are headed and empty**; 1841, 1845 and 1848 hold one Nicolosi or Neri apiece; **1840 and 1847 hold the only Nicotra in the decade, and both are ALFIO'S** — Nicotra Venera (1840) and Nicotra Maria (1847), mother Carmela Sudieri. **1842 is torn and unreadable**, and 1844 does not exist. **ROSARIO NICOTRA AND VENERA MURABITO ARE IN NONE OF THEM.** They were not at Mascali in the 1840s, so **Giovanni was almost certainly not born there** — the household arrived between about 1848 and 1872. **The next step is not another Mascali sweep**: it is the **1872 marriage allegati**, whose publication certificate prints each spouse's birthplace, as Piedimonte's did for Rosario Mazza. That is one fascicolo, and it names the comune.

rows.what: Re-test this archive's own zeros with the most suspect parameter removed
rows.note: **A control licenses the SHAPE of a query and says nothing about the VALUE.** This archive's standing rule — *a zero is not recordable until a control in the same form and session returns a known result* — was satisfied in the Lerena archive on 21 September and **the zero was still false**. A parent-pair query with the mother's surname returned nothing; dropping the surname returned seven, two of which that archive had already published, one of them displaying the very surname it had asked for. The name sits unparsed in the given-name field, so supplying a surname excluded every record the parser failed on. Larriera has one spelling and controlled fine; **Villademoros has four**. **What to do here.** Every zero this archive has recorded from a MULTI-FIELD query should be re-run **with the most suspect parameter removed** — the rare surname, the `localita`, the year range — to see whether the count moves. The candidates are the [name-index nils](/searched/): *Prostamo* at Pizzo, *Cassaniti* at Catania, *Nicotra* at Catania, *Mariantonia Musolino* at Scilla. **This archive already knows the other face of the same fault** — `localita=` at Antenati matches loosely and returned deaths at Vicopisano, Tuscany, for a Catania query. Loose in one direction, silently exclusive in the other. **A field you did not put there yourself is a field you do not control.** **DONE THE SAME HOUR, AND IT FOUND SOMETHING WORSE THAN A FALSE ZERO.** All four nils were re-run with `localita` removed and the raw page inspected. **The nils are genuine** — «cognome=Cassaniti» with no locality at all returns *«Nessun risultato trovato»*, and the Musolino control still returns 7. **But two things were wrong anyway.** (1) **The detector.** This archive reads a count by matching «N risultati», and **the zero page does not contain that string** — its count is a sentence in a 266 KB page. So «no match» was indistinguishable from a throttled page or a broken selector, and only a second signal told them apart. (2) **The meaning.** «Cassaniti returns nothing» was filed as a negative *about this family*.
